paras: Wang Jing asks what distinguishes the view of democracy embodied in Chinese modernization from the liberal-democratic view that grew out of Western modernization, and why this matters beyond China. The article argues that because capital logic dominates Western modernization, liberal democracy functions as an ideology serving capital accumulation. In Wang's account, the Chinese view is a distinctive, people-centred view of democracy that surpasses it in theory and in practice and offers a model to late-developing countries.

The article first reviews Western democratic theory: transition theorists, postmodern scholars and left-wing deliberative democrats. It judges them unable to transcend liberal democracy because they lack a grounding in democratic practice and do not grasp its capital logic. It then traces how liberal democracy took shape from Montesquieu, Locke and Rousseau to Schumpeter and Dahl, and sets out the Chinese view in terms of democratic values, subject, institutions, process and evaluation. It ends by discussing the view's global significance.

Wang criticises four "myths" of Western liberal democracy. These are the property-rights myth, which subordinates democracy to the market; electoral supremacy, which reduces democracy to elite competition for votes; the history of democracy as a Western story that justifies "democracy export" and capital expansion; and the "end of history" meta-narrative. Against these, the author presents the Chinese view as grounded in historical materialism and the Two Integrations. It treats the people as the real political subject, relies on the people's congress system, multiparty cooperation and whole-process people's democracy, and judges democracy by whether people actually run their own affairs. Wang adds that liberal electoral systems have aggravated ethnic division and polarisation in late-developing states, whereas the Chinese approach links democracy with ethnic unity and the building of a sense of community of the Chinese nation.

Wang concludes that the word "distinctive" does not imply exceptionalism. It marks a systematic difference between a people-centred and a capital-centred democracy, and a Chinese cultural subjectivity that the "Second Integration" establishes. The author claims that this democracy is more broadly, deeply and truly democratic, and that its universality comes from practice. It is therefore presented as a model for developing countries seeking their own paths. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of the official Chinese critique of Western liberal democracy and of how Chinese scholars frame the global claims of whole-process people's democracy.
quoteEn: By placing the people at the core of democracy, the view of democracy embodied in Chinese modernization transcends capitalist relations of production in economic structure and shapes genuinely equal democratic relations.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化蕴含的民主观将人民置于民主的核心，就从经济结构上超越了资本主义生产关系，塑造真实平等的民主关系

glossary.explanation: The official Party concept, elaborated especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022), of a path of modernization with Chinese characteristics, presented as distinct from Western modernization.

A concept put forward by Xi Jinping in 2019 holding that democracy covers all stages of political life, from consultation and decision-making to management and supervision, rather than only elections.
The formula of combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities (the First Integration) and with its fine traditional culture (the Second Integration).
China's fundamental political institution, in which congresses at each level are said to exercise state power on behalf of the people.

glossary.zh: 铸牢中华民族共同体意识
glossary.en: sense of community of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: forging a firm consciousness of the Chinese national community
glossary.explanation: A Party policy slogan on ethnic affairs, prominent since 2017, that stresses a shared national identity among all ethnic groups.

t: The civilisational implications of building a community with a shared future for mankind and the path to realising it
zh: 构建人类命运共同体的文明意蕴及践行理路
paras: Drawing on Volume V of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China, Liu Yang asks what the idea of building a community with a shared future for mankind means for the course of human civilisation. The article argues that the idea is not only a framework for global governance but a plan to move beyond Western-centric modern civilisation and to rethink 21st-century civilisational development as a whole. Liu holds that it answers the question of what kind of world to build and how to build it.

The article has two main parts. The first explains why the idea arose, through three 'changes' (changes in the world, in the era and in history) and through its two intellectual sources: Marx's thought on civilisation and the conception of civilisation in traditional Chinese culture, joined by the Two Integrations. The second sets the idea against what Liu calls the defects of Western civilisation, then lays out five practical tasks tied to the four global initiatives (on development, security, civilisation and governance).

Liu's central claim is that Western civilisation, driven by capital, is 'deconstructive', 'universalist', 'single-dimensional', 'hierarchical' and 'short-sighted'. Against this, the community with a shared future is said to offer a constructive view of civilisation, common values of all humanity in place of 'universal values', a balanced view of economic, political, cultural, social and ecological development, and equal, consultative relations between states. Liu reads this as a sublation of Western economic rationality, and presents the 'end of history' thesis as having failed amid current crises. The practical path has five parts: a community of ideas built on shared values, a development community that corrects the unequal global division of labour, a security community with a new security outlook, an ecological community based on 'common but differentiated' responsibility, and a cooperation community in which power shifts from Western dominance toward 'multi-party co-governance' with a stronger Global South.

Liu concludes that the idea redraws the future of world civilisation and offers new choices and Chinese wisdom for overcoming civilisational difficulties. It presents the idea as part of creating a new form of human civilisation and as a step toward the Marxist ideal of an 'association of free individuals'. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese scholars link Xi Jinping's foreign-policy concepts to Marxist civilisation theory and to a critique of the West.
quoteEn: Building a community with a shared future for mankind aims to transcend the modern civilisation dominated by Western-centrism and to make a new, comprehensive plan for the course of human civilisation in the 21st century.
quoteZh: 构建人类命运共同体，旨在超越西方中心论统治下的现代文明，对21世纪人类文明发展进程重新作出总体性谋划

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.literal: community of common destiny for humankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and global-governance concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2012–2013. It calls for countries of different systems to share interests, rights and responsibilities.
A formula stressing the combination of Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture. It was elaborated under Xi Jinping, especially from 2021–2023.
A term for developing and emerging countries, used in Chinese official discourse to describe a group whose weight in global governance is rising.

glossary.en: a new form of human civilisation
glossary.explanation: A phrase used in Party discourse for a civilisation said to be created by Chinese-style socialist modernisation. It is presented as an alternative to the Western model.

glossary.zh: 全球发展倡议、全球安全倡议、全球文明倡议、全球治理倡议
glossary.pinyin: quánqiú fāzhǎn chàngyì, quánqiú ānquán chàngyì, quánqiú wénmíng chàngyì, quánqiú zhìlǐ chàngyì
glossary.explanation: Four proposals announced by Xi Jinping between 2021 and 2025, on development, security, civilisation and governance. Chinese official texts present them as ways to put the community with a shared future into practice.
A formula introduced by Xi Jinping in 2015 listing peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom. It is offered in contrast to Western 'universal values'.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Understanding the major significance of "upholding the organic unity of governing the country by law and governing the Party by regulations"
zh: 深刻理解“坚持依法治国和依规治党有机统一”的重大意义
paras: This article from Red Flag Manuscripts (2025, no. 24) explains why Xi Jinping's thought on the rule of law treats the organic unity of governing the country by law and governing the Party by regulations as a core principle. Zhou Yezhong argues that the principle is a theoretical innovation that sets Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law apart from Western legal theory. It is now listed as the "twelfth upholding" in the 2025 edition of the Study Outline on that thought.

The article has four sections. The first presents the principle as a core element of Xi's legal thought. The second presents it as a distinctive strength of "governance by the Communist Party of China" and of "Chinese governance". The third treats it as a practical way to address problems specific to a large party and a large country. The fourth presents it as China's contribution to the rule-of-law civilisation of humankind.

Zhou's central claim is that the principle joins political logic and legal logic. Placing Party-regulation governance alongside state-law governance, in Zhou's account, brings both governing the Party and governing the country onto a legal track. The result is a "grand rule of law" with both Party rules and state law. Zhou sets this against Western theory's habit of treating law and political parties as relatively separate. Zhou also links the principle to the "two answers" to the historical cycle of rise and fall. Law-based governance gives practical force to the first answer, popular supervision of government. Regulation-based Party governance is described as the legal instrument for the second, the Party's self-reform. Zhou adds that it addresses the "unique problems of a large party" and the governance problems of a large country.

Zhou concludes that the principle gives world party governance a legalised path built on intra-Party regulations. These emphasise duties that come before rights, self-discipline, and Party discipline stricter than state law. In Zhou's view it also offers non-Western countries experience in exploring their own legal paths. It further shows that Party and law are mutually reinforcing, not opposed. Read the original if you want a representative statement of the official Party-theory case for combining Party regulations with state law, and of how it is contrasted with Western legal thought.
quoteEn: Only when governing the Party by regulations takes root in the hearts of Party members can governing the country by law take root in the hearts of the people.
quoteZh: 依规治党深入党心，依法治国才能深入民心。

glossary.literal: governing the Party according to rules
glossary.explanation: The practice of managing the Communist Party through its own intra-Party regulations (党内法规), headed by the Party Constitution. It is presented as parallel to governing the state by law.
The official formula for rule of law in China, in which the state is governed according to the Constitution and statutes under Party leadership.

glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law
glossary.explanation: The body of Xi Jinping's ideas on law, formally articulated around 2020. It is treated as a component of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.

Official shorthand for two replies to the question of how to escape the historical cycle of dynastic rise and fall. The first is Mao Zedong's 1945 answer, popular supervision of government. The second is Xi Jinping's, the Party's self-reform.
A term for the Party's continuous internal correction and discipline, presented since the 2010s as its second answer to the historical cycle.

keywords: Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law

t: Publication, distribution and dissemination of the Selected Works of Mao Zedong in China's border ethnic minority regions
zh: 《毛泽东选集》在边疆民族地区的出版发行与传播
paras: How did the Selected Works of Mao Zedong reach China's border ethnic minority regions, and what did their spread do for national cohesion? Di and Wang note that earlier research has concentrated on translation and publication of the ethnic-language editions. They argue instead that publication, distribution and study of the Selected Works in these regions turned Party theory into a resource for governance and culture, and strengthened identification with the Party, the state and the Chinese nation.

The article covers roughly 1951 to 1965, from the first volume's release to the completion of the four-volume set. It first traces translation and publishing: Uyghur, Kazakh, Mongolian, Tibetan and Korean editions, with figures for Xinjiang, Inner Mongolia and Tibet. It then examines the media and distribution channels, the Party-led study system, and the effects on ideological identification, cadre training, new socialist culture and ethnic relations. Examples come from Xinjiang, Inner Mongolia, Ningxia, Tibet, Yanbian, Guangxi, Yunnan and Hainan.

Di and Wang describe a combination of organised promotion and popular response. Local newspapers, radio in minority languages, Xinhua Bookstore working groups and mobile book-sellers carried the volumes to remote areas. Party committees set study plans, and workplaces, schools, newspaper-reading groups and night classes took up the texts. The authors say the study was adapted to local language and production conditions and was not mere indoctrination. They report that, by their account, the books shaped a concrete sense of belonging to the Party and the new China, equipped growing numbers of minority cadres, and supplied authoritative arguments against both "Han chauvinism" and "local nationalism". Evidence includes sales figures, reported readers' comments and accounts of local practice.

The authors conclude that the Selected Works served as both a cultural product and a guiding ideological banner, and that their circulation built an ideological foundation for forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. They call for inheriting and developing the useful practices of this period and for new ways of strengthening national cohesion today. Read the original if you study the history of Party theory dissemination, ethnic-minority policy in the 1950s and 1960s, or Chinese official scholarship on the sense of community of the Chinese nation, and want the regional examples and figures.
quoteEn: In essence, the publication, distribution and dissemination of the Selected Works was a process of turning the Party's theory, governing ideas and policy arrangements into resources of social governance and cultural forms in the border ethnic regions, shaping the peoples' identification with the Party and the state.
quoteZh: 《毛选》的出版发行和传播，实质上是将党的理论、执政理念、政策安排等转化为边疆民族地区社会治理资源与文化形态，塑造各族群众对党和国家认同的过程。

glossary.explanation: A Party term for attitudes in which the Han majority disregards or dominates minorities. It is usually paired with "local nationalism" as the two errors to be opposed.
A Party term for minority-group nationalism seen as placing local ethnic interests above national unity. It is the counterpart of "Han chauvinism" in official ethnic-policy discourse.

t: Understanding the "Second Integration" through the grand historical outlook
zh: 以大历史观理解把握“第二个结合”
paras: Gao Changwu asks how the "Second Integration", the combination of the basic tenets of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture, should be understood. The article, published in Party Literature in 2025, answers that it must be read through the "grand historical outlook" (da lishi guan). Gao treats this as a way of placing the concept in long historical time, a broad field of view, a coherent internal structure and a layered set of goals. The author presents the Second Integration as an original, signature theoretical innovation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, especially of Xi's thought on culture.

The article is organised around four senses of the "grand" in the outlook: looking far, looking wide, looking through, and looking deep. The first section traces the idea from the Party's early explorations to its formal announcement on 1 July 2021 and its later elaboration. The second examines its significance for the Party, the country and the world. The third analyses its internal structure as an integrated whole of standpoint, viewpoint and method. The fourth sets out its aims in three dimensions.

Gao argues that the Second Integration should be seen as a line, not a point. Mao Zedong's 1938 call to inherit China's cultural heritage critically, the 1943 call to join Marxism-Leninism deeply with China's history and culture, and examples such as seeking truth from facts and regional ethnic autonomy are read as earlier stages. Xi's statements from 2012 to 2021 then led, in Gao's account, from quantitative accumulation to a qualitative leap. Gao claims that the concept answers three questions: what the Party is, where China comes from and is going, and what is to be done about the world. It is said to establish cultural subjectivity, to explain why socialism with Chinese characteristics is a necessary road, and to supply ideas for a community with a shared future for mankind. Its goals are said to run from theoretical innovation, through cultural innovation, to the evolution of civilisation, with theory as the basic dimension.

Gao concludes that the Second Integration must be upheld and deepened on the new journey. This means holding to Marxism as the "soul-root" while keeping Chinese traditional culture as the "root-vein". The author calls for creative transformation and innovative development of that culture, for building a socialist cultural powerhouse, and for further resolving the dispute between ancient and modern, Chinese and Western. Seen from a long historical perspective, the concept is said to open space for Chinese modernization and for a new form of human civilisation. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-historical account of how the Second Integration is traced and framed in official theory, with dated citations from Mao and Xi.
quoteEn: The study of the "Second Integration" should not be "a point" but "a line".
quoteZh: 对“第二个结合”的考察,不应是“一个点”,而应是“一条线”。

t: The philosophical foundations of a theoretical narrative of Chinese modernization: based on a critique of Western-centrism
zh: 中国式现代化理论叙事的哲学基础——基于对西方中心主义的批判
paras: Sun Hui asks how a self-reliant, original theoretical narrative of Chinese modernization can be built when Western-centrist accounts have long distorted the interpretation of China's modernization. Citing Xi Jinping's remark that Chinese social science is still in a position of 'having reason but being unable to state it', the article argues that Western-centrism must first be criticised and overcome at the philosophical level. Only then, Sun contends, can theoretical confidence and methodological awareness be established.

The article first dissects Western discourse through three questions: the source of China's modernizing drive, the choice of path, and the global impact. It traces three foundations of that discourse: a fragmented view of history, linear historicism and teleology, and a narrative of civilizational superiority. Sun then sets out an alternative based on the 'grand view of history' and applies it to the same three questions. The article engages Fairbank, Levenson, Pomeranz, Huntington, Hegel and Fukuyama, and draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Xi.

In Sun's critique, the 'impact–response' paradigm, the 'high-level equilibrium trap' and the 'Great Divergence' all fix on the nineteenth-century 'time lag', which strips Chinese civilization of its subjectivity. Hegelian teleology is said to underlie the equation 'modernization = Westernization', and civilizational-conflict theory conceals the contradictions of capital-centred Western modernity. Against these, Sun draws on historical materialism. The Western impact was an external condition, not the first mover. China's modernization is said to arise from 'economic necessity' in its own social contradictions, and the Party's activation of the 'cultural subjectivity' of Chinese civilization through the Two Integrations turned it from passivity to initiative. Sun presents Chinese modernization as Engels's 'third conception' of industrialization, uniting the development of productive forces with their ownership by the people.

Sun concludes that Chinese modernization is the self-sublation, self-development and self-transcendence of Chinese civilization. In the author's account it creates a new form of human civilization across five spheres: material, political, cultural-ethical, social and ecological. Because it is people-centred rather than capital-centred, Sun says, it avoids the Western pattern in which a strong state inevitably seeks hegemony, and it offers answers to modernity's problems. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese theorists use historical materialism and the 'grand view of history' to rebut Western accounts of China's modernization.
quoteEn: The so-called modernization 'time lag' that arose before the collision of Chinese and Western history is in essence a difference in timing produced by each civilization's own inner logic and rhythm, not a binary opposition between backward and advanced civilizations.
quoteZh: 所谓中西历史碰撞前产生的现代化“时差”,本质上是中西文明基于各自发展的内在逻辑与节奏而产生的时序差异，而非中西文明落后与先进的二元对立。

glossary.explanation: The official Party concept of China's own path to modernization, led by the Communist Party and presented as distinct from Western models. It has been prominent since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
Xi Jinping's formula of integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture.
A methodological notion promoted by Xi Jinping: analysing change from the long course of history, the tide of the times and global developments.
A concept stressed by Xi Jinping from 2023, referring to Chinese civilization's capacity to develop itself and respond to challenges on its own terms.
The official description of what Chinese modernization is said to create, developing material, political, cultural-ethical, social and ecological civilization together.

t: The generative mechanism, value implications and practical requirements of the "Second Integration"
zh: “第二个结合”的生成机理、价值意蕴和实践要求
source: Journal of China Jinggangshan Cadre College, 2025 no. 6
paras: Su Xinghong and Chen Ruixia take up the "Second Integration", the proposition that Marxism should be combined with China's fine traditional culture, which they call the signature proposition of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. They argue that existing scholarship has treated its political and theoretical logic well but its philosophical underpinnings only weakly. Their thesis is that, read through ontology, axiology and a theory of practice, the Second Integration is necessary, needed and workable.

The article is organised in three parts that correspond to these philosophical levels. The first addresses its generative mechanism through Marxist practice-ontology. The second addresses its value implications, covering socialism with Chinese characteristics, cultural subjectivity and the modern transformation of Chinese civilisation. The third addresses its practical requirements.

On the first point, the authors treat Marxism as the universal law of human history and fine traditional culture as the particular law of the Chinese nation, so that the universal shows itself through the particular. They list seven Marxist-compatible elements in traditional culture, including worldview, dialectics, epistemology, people-based thinking and the Confucian "Great Harmony". They also claim that Chinese thought indirectly fed into Marxism through Hegel and utopian socialism, and they cite Marx's and Engels's many references to China. They further trace the idea through Mao Zedong's 1938 formulation of Marxism's adaptation to China and the way later Party leaders reworked classical Chinese expressions. On value, they argue that the Second Integration is the "golden key" to understanding the Chinese path, consolidates cultural subjectivity (standpoint, awareness, innovation) and gives the modern transformation of Chinese civilisation its direction, standpoint and openness. In practice, they propose adapting Marxist cultural theory to China and to the times, creating a new cultural form of Chinese modernization, answering real problems at home and globally, and combining safeguarding fundamentals with innovation under Party leadership.

The authors conclude that the Second Integration is the necessary route for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, for modernising traditional culture and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. They describe it as the greatest asset for building a strong socialist cultural nation and call for continued work on the cultural path, theory and institutions. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of Marxism grounds the Second Integration in philosophical categories and in claims about Marxism's links to Chinese thought.
quoteEn: The "Second Integration" is the fundamental method for advancing the modern transformation of Chinese civilisation, and that transformation is its goal; the two stand in a relationship of means to end.
quoteZh: “第二个结合”是推动中华文明现代转型的根本方法，中华文明现代转型是“第二个结合”的奋斗目标，两者之间是手段和目的的关系。

glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's formulation, prominent from 2023, of combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture. It is paired with the "First Integration", the combination of Marxism with China's concrete realities.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since the reform era, combining Party leadership with a market economy and Chinese conditions.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for the Party's project of fitting Marxist theory to China's conditions and to the contemporary era.
A concept emphasised in Xi Jinping's thought on culture, referring to a culture's self-reliance, self-awareness and creativity as a basis for cultural confidence.
The official term for China's own path to modernisation, presented as distinct from Western models.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's overarching national goal of restoring China's strength and international standing, closely associated with Xi Jinping's "Chinese Dream".

t: The Communist Party of China's exploration of an independent Chinese knowledge system in the Yan'an period
zh: 延安时期中国共产党对中国自主知识体系的探索
source: Journal of Renmin University of China, 2025 no. 6
paras: Taking up Xi Jinping's 2022 remark that building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics ultimately means building China's own independent knowledge system, Dong Jia and Wen Ruiqin look for its historical roots in the Yan'an period (1935–1948). They argue that the Communist Party of China was both the leading force and a direct builder of such a system. In their account, this period settled key terms, concepts and methods of what they call the Yan'an chapter of an independent knowledge system.

The article begins with the background: the modern clash between Chinese and Western learning, the May Fourth critique of tradition, and the failure of earlier reform and revolutionary programmes. It then traces the early Party's wish to adapt foreign theory, from Yun Daiying and Li Dazhao to Mao Zedong's 1938 formulation of the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions. The body is organised around the contribution of Mao Zedong Thought, the academic climate fostered by Party leaders, and the movement for the sinification of scholarship.

The authors' core argument has several parts. Knowledge is independent, they say, when it rests on Chinese experience and addresses Chinese problems, and when it is systematic, as Mao and Ai Siqi stressed. Mao, Zhang Wentian, Zhou Enlai and others encouraged scholars such as Fan Wenlan, He Ganzhi and Hou Wailu, and set up research bodies such as the Central Research Institute. The Party then guided the movement for the sinification of scholarship, begun in Chongqing, towards the 'new-democratic culture' of Mao's 1940 essay. The authors present this as a shift from a vague appeal to a leading framework that combined inheriting the national heritage with localising foreign learning. They also note that some works over-emphasised service to current politics.

The authors conclude that Yan'an built on Marxism as the guiding principle, critically inherited traditional culture, grounded scholarship in practice, and raised professional standards. They cite Hou Wailu and Hu Sheng to argue that scholars had moved from imitating the West to using their own methods. For the present, they call for continued adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era running through teaching and research. They also call for greater international academic influence. Read the original if you want a detailed account, with many period sources, of how Yan'an-era Party leaders and scholars shaped the idea of an independent Chinese knowledge system and how it is used in current discourse.
quoteEn: The Communist Party of China is both the leading force in building China's independent knowledge system and the agent that actually builds it.
quoteZh: 中国共产党既是中国自主知识体系建构的领导主体,又是中国自主知识体系的建构主体。

glossary.explanation: A concept emphasised by Xi Jinping since 2022. It refers to Chinese-originated disciplines, academic theories and discourse in philosophy and the social sciences, as distinct from reliance on Western frameworks.
A late-1930s intellectual movement, led largely by Communist or left-wing scholars, that sought scholarship rooted in Chinese realities. It followed Mao's call for the sinification of Marxism.
Mao Zedong's 1940 concept of a national, scientific and mass culture suited to the stage of New Democracy, the Party's programme for the pre-socialist revolution.
The Party's official term for the sinified Marxism developed by Mao and his colleagues. It was written into the Party constitution at the 7th Party Congress in 1945.

t: On relational civilization and its place in the new form of human civilization
zh: 论关系文明及其在人类文明新形态中的地位
source: Journal of Peking University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2026 no. 1
paras: Qiu Gengtian asks what "relational civilization" is, why it should be built, where it sits within the new form of human civilization, and how it can be created. The article, guided by the Marxist conception of civilization and Xi Jinping's thought on culture, argues that civilization has so far been built mainly through domain-specific forms. It contends that the growing "disharmony" of development calls for a distinct civilization of human relations, to stand alongside the existing five.

The article begins from the contradiction of today's world, which Qiu summarises as insufficient development and discordant development. It defines relational civilization and sets out its practical, theoretical and institutional components. It then grounds the concept in Marx's theory of "all-round production" and in classical Marxist ontology, and traces precursors in Chinese tradition, communicative-practice philosophy and the Party's record, from the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence (1954) to the global initiatives. The last sections discuss its theoretical and international significance and how to build it.

Qiu's central move is to place relational civilization in the logic of production. Material, spiritual and ecological civilization rest on their own forms of production, and relational civilization rests on the production and reproduction of human relations. Because the existing five civilizations are domain-based and "entity-type", the author holds that they cannot cover relations between domains or relations such as international ties. Relational civilization is therefore a "relational" form that cannot be reduced to social civilization. Qiu also cites relational ontology, arguing that matter exists as both entity and relation. Together these give a "5+1" structure, and the author argues that the new form of human civilization would be incomplete without it.

On the practical side, Qiu proposes a shift in ideas from egocentrism to symbiosis (gòngshēng zhǔyì), and a shift in practice from mutually harmful to mutually beneficial development. Qiu presents China's development as a leading example of relational civilization and links the concept to the Global Development, Security, Civilization and Governance Initiatives. Qiu says it also enriches Marxist civilization theory. Read the original if you want to see how a Party School scholar derives a new sixth civilization from Marxist production theory and ties it to China's foreign-policy concepts.
quoteEn: Relational civilization should not be confined within social civilization; its meaning, status and role go far beyond the scope of social civilization in the narrow sense, and it should be set apart as a new form of civilization alongside the other five.
quoteZh: 关系文明不应该局限于社会文明之中，它的意涵及其地位、作用远远超出了狭义的社会文明的范畴，它应该被独立出来，成为和其他五种文明相并列的新的文明形式。

glossary.en: the new form of human civilization
glossary.explanation: A concept in official Party discourse, listed in the 20th Party Congress report (2022) as one of the essential requirements of Chinese modernization. It describes the civilizational outcome the Party says Chinese modernization is creating.
The author's proposed concept: the positive results of efforts to make human relations coordinated, balanced and harmonious. It is not an established official term.
A value outlook that the author builds on the idea of coexistence and mutual benefit. The author offers it in place of egocentrism as the ideological basis of relational civilization.

t: On the major significance of the concept of a community with a shared future for mankind for world modernization
zh: 论人类命运共同体理念对世界现代化的重大意义
source: Journal of Peking University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2025 no. 6
paras: Wu Zhongmin asks what the concept of a community with a shared future for mankind means for the course of world modernization. The article argues that the concept is more than a diplomatic slogan: it concerns how modernization worldwide can be advanced as a whole. In Wu's view, without building such a community world modernization has no future, and the concept is an original Chinese contribution that fits historical materialism and the basic trend of modernization.

The article first sets out the historical and practical grounds for the concept, then examines its effects on four conditions of sustainable world modernization. It then turns to the obstacles to building the community and to what states should do. It draws on Marx, Engels and Xi Jinping, together with cited Western scholarship on globalization, and gives figures for China's GDP and trade for 2018–2023.

Wu grounds the concept in historical materialism. Modern large-scale industry and the market economy produce economic globalization, which makes states mutually dependent. This globalization spreads social risks and ecological damage that no single state can handle alone. On that basis, Wu says the concept supports four things: a healthy world economy through free movement of production factors and fair competition instead of jungle-law zero-sum play; a more balanced modernization that gives developing countries a voice; harmony between humans and nature; and a just international order. Wu presents the concept as going beyond the principles of sovereignty, equality and peaceful coexistence, which aim only at passive coexistence, by pursuing active common prosperity. The article describes China as a responsible leader on ecology and as an example of fair-competition cooperation, and it describes US hegemony and withdrawal from climate agreements as obstacles.

Wu concludes that the community is the direction of history but will take a long and difficult process. The article names three obstacles: no world government with enforcement power, slow cultural adaptation, and tangled disputes that feed reverse globalization. It proposes that states build an economic community of shared destiny as the foundation, jointly govern risks to deepen mutual empathy, and build a fair order through multilateral consultation centred on the United Nations. Wu adds that the UN needs reform, with better global governance and a stronger voice for developing countries. Read the original if you want a Chinese sociologist's systematic case linking the community with a shared future for mankind to theories of modernization and globalization.
quoteEn: In a certain sense, without the building of a community with a shared future for mankind, world modernization has no future, and human society as a whole has no prospects.
quoteZh: 从一定意义上讲，如果没有人类命运共同体的建设，世界现代化就没有未来，整个人类社会也就没有前景。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.literal: community of common destiny for humankind
glossary.explanation: A concept put forward by Xi Jinping in 2013 and later written into Party and state documents. It calls for cooperation, mutual benefit and multilateralism in international relations.
Wu's term for the modernization of all countries taken together as one process, as opposed to the modernization of any single state.
A situation in which one side's gain is another's loss. Chinese official discourse uses it to criticise Cold War-style confrontation and contrasts it with 'win-win cooperation'.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Chinese modernization and the logic of value change in creating a new form of human civilization
zh: 中国式现代化与人类文明新形态创造实践的价值观变革逻辑
source: Journal of Peking University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2025 no. 6
paras: Yuan Zushe asks what Xi Jinping means when he lists a distinctive 'outlook on values' among the features of Chinese modernization, and how that outlook differs from the values behind Western modernization. Drawing on Marxist historical materialism and modern value philosophy, the article argues that Chinese modernization has identified and practised a genuinely universal 'true value'. In Yuan's account, this has corrected the value basis of Western modernization and supplied the value logic for creating a new form of human civilization.

The article begins with the place of values in modernization, drawing on Ulrich Beck, Jürgen Habermas, Cyril Black, Talcott Parsons, Anthony Giddens and Jacques Derrida to describe the costs of Western modernity. It then turns to the value premises of Enlightenment modernity, quoting Marx and Engels on capitalism's productive power and on the general law of capitalist accumulation. The second half sets out the value content of Chinese modernization, first in four points, then in three claimed contributions, and finally in six areas of value change.

Yuan argues that Western modernization rests on one-sided values: capital logic, wealth maximization, individualism and hedonism, and the slide from a market economy into a 'market society'. In the author's reading, this produces ecological crisis, spiritual emptiness, an 'acquisitive personality' and claims to 'universal values' that serve narrow national interest. Chinese modernization is said to unite three value sources: the Marxist ideal of the free and all-round development of the person, excellent traditional Chinese culture, and the common values of all humanity. It is also said to offer a relational, 'public value' logic and to rest on a socialist market economy that differs in kind from a market society. The six areas of change are ecological harmony, social justice and common prosperity, development aimed at a better life, a people-centred approach, common values of humanity with a community with a shared future for mankind, and a pluralist view of civilizations.

Yuan concludes that the values in Chinese modernization are 'Chinese values'. The author presents them as the outcome of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and as the basis for Chinese discourse power on values. They are also described as a way past the binaries of universalism versus particularism and efficiency versus equality. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese philosopher builds a value-theoretic case for Chinese modernization and how the article frames Western modernity critically.
quoteEn: The values of Chinese modernization are the crystallization of adapting the basic Marxist theory of values to the Chinese context and the needs of our times; they contain reflection on, critique of and transcendence of Western social values, and the creative transformation and innovative development of the values of excellent traditional Chinese culture.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化的价值观，是马克思主义基本价值观理论中国化、时代化的结晶，包含着对西方社会价值观的反思、批判与超越，包含着对中华优秀传统文化之价值观的创造性转化与创新性发展。

glossary.explanation: The official Party-state term for China's own path of modernization, which has been prominent since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as an alternative to the Western model.

glossary.en: a new form of human civilization
glossary.explanation: A phrase in official discourse for the civilizational outcome claimed for Chinese modernization, set against the Western model.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept for international relations, stressing shared interests, multilateralism and common development.
Xi Jinping's formula naming peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom as shared values. It is offered as an alternative to 'universal values' of Western origin.
An official goal of prosperity shared by all the people, stressed in recent Party policy as a defining feature of socialism.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for developing Marxism by combining it with Chinese conditions, culture and contemporary demands.

t: The logic and enhancement paths of whole-process people's democracy empowering the modernization of a super-large-scale country
zh: 全过程人民民主赋能超大规模国家现代化的逻辑理路与提升路径
paras: Cai Wencheng and Liu Bojian ask how whole-process people's democracy can help a country of more than a billion people complete modernization. Taking as their starting point the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called whole-process people's democracy an essential requirement of Chinese modernization, they argue that it turns the problem of scale into an advantage. In their account it does so by offering a workable answer to the governance problems peculiar to a super-large-scale country.

The article first sets out the governance dilemmas that population size creates for democracy, then identifies the theoretical, practical and historical foundations of the Chinese answer, and then explains four mechanisms. It closes with four paths for improving whole-process people's democracy: values, institutions, content and technology. Its sources range from Aristotle, Robert Dahl and Arrow's impossibility theorem to Marxist state theory, Party history and imperial-era administration.

The authors name four problems of scale: divergent interests, a shortage of government responsiveness, distorted expression of demands, and obstructed participation. They argue that whole-process people's democracy resolves each by combining paired elements. It unites Party leadership with the primacy of the people, vertical (representative) with horizontal (grassroots) democracy, electoral with deliberative democracy, and digital with traditional democracy. Grassroots self-government, they claim, lets people handle small matters themselves and lowers the burden on government, while the people's congress system concentrates on major issues. Marxist state theory supplies the normative guidance, the Party's earlier experience with democratic governance supplies the practice, and the multi-level administration of imperial China is treated as a historical precedent.

To raise governance effectiveness, the authors call for stronger democratic education and a people-centred orientation, better grassroots democratic institutions and deliberative mechanisms before, during and after decisions, and content that innovates around grassroots forms. They also call for digital platforms, AI-assisted decision-making and information-management systems for people's congress deputies. They present these steps as ways to strengthen the popular base of modernization and reduce the cost of political participation. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language account of how scholars link democratic theory on scale to the official concept of whole-process people's democracy.
quoteEn: Whole-process people's democracy unites Party leadership with the primacy of the people, and through correct guiding principles resolves the problem of "divergent interests" in governing a super-large-scale country.
quoteZh: 全过程人民民主实现了党的领导和人民至上相统一，以正确的原则导向破解了超大规模国家治理中的“利益分化”难题。

glossary.explanation: A concept put forward by Xi Jinping in 2019 and written into Party documents. It describes the Chinese system as combining elections with consultation, decision-making, management and oversight, and as being led by the Party.
The official name for China's own path of modernization, set out prominently at the 20th Party Congress in 2022. Official texts stress features such as a huge population and common prosperity.
An official principle holding that the interests of the people come first in Party and state work.

In China this refers to consultation among Party, government and social groups, for example through the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference and grassroots forums. Official texts present it as a distinct form alongside electoral democracy.
China's fundamental political institution, a system of congresses from township to national level whose deputies are elected indirectly at the higher levels.
The system of village committees and urban residents' committees through which residents manage local public affairs. Official texts count it among China's basic political institutions.

t: Our Party's understanding of the laws of high-quality development continues to deepen
zh: 我们党对高质量发展的规律性认识不断深化
paras: Published in the People's Daily on 9 March 2026, this commentary takes up the draft outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan submitted to the National People's Congress, whose first major strategic task is "promoting high-quality development". Gu Hailiang argues that, since the 19th Party Congress (2017), Xi Jinping's successive statements have steadily deepened the Party's understanding of the laws governing high-quality development, which Gu calls an original, signature concept of Xi Jinping's economic thought.

The article has three parts. The first explains why high-quality development is an inherent requirement of Chinese modernization. The second traces how the concept was enriched in drafting and implementing the 13th, 14th and 15th Five-Year Plans. The third examines how the concept is extended in response to the problems of the present era.

In the first part, Gu draws on the Marxist distinction between extensive and intensive expanded reproduction. The shift from quantity-led to quality-led growth is presented as following from the change in the principal contradiction in Chinese society, from the full and faithful implementation of the new development philosophy, and from the building of a modern economic system. In the second part, Gu reads the 13th Plan as stressing quality and efficiency, the 14th as tying high-quality development to innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing, and the 15th as adding high-level scientific and technological self-reliance and new quality productive forces. In the third part, Gu points to three examples of deepened understanding: building a modern industrial system; moving from "letting go effectively and managing tightly" to "letting go effectively and managing well", which Gu reads as a refinement of the understanding of the government's role; and combining investment in physical assets with investment in people.

Gu concludes that these understandings enrich Xi Jinping's economic thought and guide a good start to the 15th Five-Year Plan period. High-quality development is described as a systemic undertaking, and Gu calls for systems integration and for pooling resources in advancing Chinese modernization, along with greater ability to recognise, adapt to and seek change amid external uncertainty. Read the original if you want an authoritative Party-theorist account of how high-quality development is framed in the 15th Five-Year Plan and linked to Xi Jinping's economic thought.
quoteEn: The new development philosophy and high-quality development are inherently unified.
quoteZh: 新发展理念和高质量发展是内在统一的

glossary.explanation: An official formula, introduced at the 19th Party Congress (2017), for a shift from high-speed growth to growth stressing quality, efficiency and innovation. It is now the stated main theme of China's economic and social development.
The Party's official term for China's own path to modernization, set out prominently at the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.
A framework put forward in 2015 comprising innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing. It is officially treated as the guide for China's development policy.
A term Xi Jinping introduced in 2023, referring to advanced productive forces driven by technological breakthroughs and emerging and future industries.
The official name for the body of economic ideas attributed to Xi Jinping, treated as part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.
The 19th Party Congress (2017) redefined it as the contradiction between people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development. It sets the Party's central tasks.

t: Chen Yun's view of economics and politics and its implications for Chinese modernization
zh: 陈云的经济政治观及其对中国式现代化的启示
source: Studies on Mao Zedong Thought, 2025 no. 5
paras: Marking the 120th anniversary of Chen Yun's birth in 2025, Yin Xiao'en asks how Chen Yun handled the dialectical relationship between economics and politics, and what this offers Chinese modernization. The article defines Chen Yun's "economic-political view" as a political-philosophical outlook, grounded in historical materialism, that runs through his economic thought. Yin argues that it has three parts: treating economic problems from a political standpoint, stressing the economy's foundational role over politics, and insisting on their dialectical unity in practice.

The article follows Chen Yun's work across the revolutionary war years, the early People's Republic and the reform era. Its examples include his handling of the "greater public" and "lesser public" in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region, his correction of leftist errors in the Central Soviet Area in 1933–34, and his financial unification after 1949. It also covers his 1950s–60s calls for balanced, steady growth, his 1970s study of capitalism, and his 1980s views on reform. A final section draws lessons for Chinese modernization.

Yin's core claim is that Chen Yun treated economic work as political work, while holding that politics rests on material interests. His formula "seven parts economics, three parts politics" is read as a creative application of Lenin's "inculcation" principle: ideological education of finance personnel is to keep construction socialist. Yin presents Chen Yun's insistence that central economic authority underpins central political authority as a response to the inflation and disorder that followed fiscal decentralisation in the 1980s. His statement that reform is the "self-improvement and development of the socialist system" is said to have separated reform from liberalisation. Reform, development and stability are read as a political-economic relationship.

Yin concludes that Chen Yun's ideas bear on deepening reform to advance Chinese modernization. The article calls for upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee, including the Two Upholds, and for strengthening the Party's self-reform. It also calls for coordinating reform, development and stability to avoid an "interruption" of modernization, and for keeping a people-centred stance through common prosperity and high-quality development. It further urges guarding against Western hostile forces and using ideological and political education to build consensus. Read the original if you study Chen Yun, or how Party scholars link the history of socialist economic management to current Chinese modernization discourse.
quoteEn: Chen Yun explicitly put forward that economic structural reform is the self-improvement and development of the socialist system.
quoteZh: 陈云明确提出经济体制改革是社会主义制度的自我完善与发展

glossary.explanation: Official Party concept for China's own path to modernization, developed prominently since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.
A Party formula, adopted in 2018–2019, calling on members to uphold the core position of General Secretary Xi Jinping and the authority and centralised leadership of the Party Central Committee.
A goal of shared wealth for all, now officially presented as an essential requirement of socialism and of Chinese modernization.
Official term, prominent since 2017, for growth that emphasises quality, efficiency and innovation rather than speed alone.
Official term for the Party's efforts to discipline and renew itself, associated with the anti-corruption campaign and Party-building under Xi Jinping.

glossary.pinyin: qī fēn jīngjì, sān fēn zhèngzhì
glossary.en: seven parts economics, three parts politics
glossary.literal: seven parts economy, three parts politics
glossary.explanation: Chen Yun's formula for the work of finance and economic cadres. It holds that economic work should be central but must be accompanied by political and ideological education.

t: A review of research on Chen Yun since the turn of the century
zh: 新世纪以来陈云研究综述
source: Mao Zedong Thought Studies (《毛泽东思想研究》), 2025 no. 5
paras: Marking the 120th anniversary of Chen Yun's birth in 2025, this literature review surveys Chinese scholarship on Chen Yun, a member of both the first and second generations of the Party's central leadership, published since 2000. Chen and Zhang argue that the steady publication of source materials, a large body of monographs and articles, and the work of research institutions have made the field flourish. They also see it shifting from assessing historical contributions towards multi-dimensional readings of his thought.

The review first covers documentary editions: Chen Yun's selected manuscripts, the three-volume Collected Works, the revised chronology and the biographies issued around the 100th and 110th anniversaries. It then counts output: over 150 books, about 4,500 journal articles and 198 master's and doctoral theses by 2024. Next it describes institutions and the annual symposium "Chen Yun and Contemporary China", whose themes follow the Party's priorities. The main body then sorts the scholarship into four themes: philosophy, Party building, economic thought and personal character.

On philosophy, the authors report scholars (Lu Jianjie, Liu Jiadong, Zhu Jiamu and others) who centre Chen's thought on "seeking truth from facts" and the fifteen-character formula "not simply following superiors, not simply following books, only following reality; exchange, comparison, repetition". On Party building, they note broad agreement that his work on Party conduct, cadre selection and discipline supplemented Mao Zedong Thought and Deng Xiaoping Theory. On economics, they set out two approaches: tracing the development of his ideas on planning and markets, and identifying core principles such as seeking progress while maintaining stability, comprehensive balance and the "birdcage economy". Livelihood thought has drawn growing attention, and the review cites the American scholar David M. Bachman's praise of Chen's economic legacy. Studies of his character stress practical-minded, incorruptible, studious conduct.

Chen and Zhang propose four directions. These are to place Chen within a century-long history of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times; to combine holistic study with comparisons, for example of investigation methods used by Mao, Liu Shaoqi and Chen; to link Chen with Chinese modernization; and to deepen study of his character through archives and interdisciplinary methods. Read the original if you want a bibliographic map of Chen Yun scholarship in China and a sense of how the field ties itself to current Party priorities.
quoteEn: Chen Yun's life and thought are in themselves a whole, so the related research cannot be sharply divided.
quoteZh: 陈云的生平和思想本身是一个整体，因而不能把相关研究截然分割开来

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for the Party's project of applying Marxism to Chinese conditions and updating it for each era. The review treats Chen Yun's thought as part of this process.
The official term, prominent since the 20th Party Congress (2022), for China's path to modernization under Party leadership. The review suggests studying Chen Yun's contribution to it.
Chen Yun's metaphor from the early 1980s: the market is a bird that must be kept alive within the cage of state planning.

t: Mao Zedong's thought on independence and self-reliance in cultural development and its contemporary value
zh: 毛泽东关于文化建设独立自主的思想及其当代价值
paras: Chu Haoyu asks how Mao Zedong understood and practised independence and self-reliance in cultural development, and what that legacy means today. The article argues that Mao, drawing on the basic principles of Marxism and on fine traditional Chinese culture, charted a path of self-reliant cultural construction. Chu holds that studying it deepens understanding of the Party's cultural path and supports the building of a strong socialist culture in the new era.

The first half is a chronological survey. It starts with Mao's early habits of independent thought in Hunan, his May Fourth-era calls for a new culture, and the rural cultural movements of the Great Revolution. It then covers the Party's counter-campaign against the Kuomintang's cultural "encirclement" in the land revolution period, the new-democratic culture of the War of Resistance, and the post-1949 "Hundred Flowers, Hundred Schools" policy, set against Soviet practice. The second half draws out features of the thought and then turns to its relevance today.

Chu identifies three features. First, Marxism provides the guiding ideology, the historical-materialist method and the principle of seeking truth from facts, so independence is not self-isolation. Second, the thought is rooted in a critical inheritance of fine traditional culture: Mao opposed both swallowing foreign things whole and cutting off history, and favoured keeping the essence while discarding the dross. Third, it holds to a people's standpoint, treating peasants and workers as creators and main audience of culture, as in literacy drives and in the rural cultural policies of the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region. Chu adds that Mao never used the term, but his thinking contains the idea of cultural leadership.

Chu concludes that Mao's thought laid foundations for later cultural work. For the present it offers lessons on four points. The Party's cultural leadership should be strengthened, with Xi Jinping's 2023 formulation of it cited. The Two Integrations should carry forward Mao's "first integration" and the implicit logic of the "second". Cultural work should answer the demands of each era. Cultural subjectivity should be upheld in building a modern Chinese civilisation. Read the original if you want a Chinese account that links Mao's cultural policies to current Party discourse on cultural leadership and the Two Integrations.
quoteEn: Although Mao Zedong never explicitly put forward the concept of "cultural leadership", his cultural theory contains a wealth of ideas about it.
quoteZh: 毛泽东虽未明确提出“文化领导权”这一概念，但他的文化理论中蕴含着丰富的文化领导权的思想。

glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's formula for combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities (the first) and with fine traditional Chinese culture (the second). The second integration was stressed from 2021–2023.

glossary.literal: let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools contend
glossary.explanation: A policy Mao announced in 1956 to encourage diversity in the arts and scholarly debate under Party leadership. The article contrasts it with Soviet cultural policy.

Mao's 1940 programme in On New Democracy for a "national, scientific and mass" culture opposed to imperialism and feudalism. It was meant to serve the new-democratic revolution under proletarian leadership.

The Party's authority over the direction of ideology and culture, akin to but not identical with Gramscian hegemony. Xi Jinping used the phrase "the Chinese Communist Party's cultural leadership" in June 2023.

t: Inheritance and transcendence: a review of research on Hunan-Xiang culture and Mao Zedong
zh: 继承与超越：湖湘文化与毛泽东研究述评
paras: This is a literature review, published in Mao Zedong Thought Studies (2025, no. 5), of scholarship on how Hunan-Xiang culture (the regional culture of Hunan) shaped Mao Zedong and Mao Zedong Thought. Pang and Sun note that existing work mostly treats Hunan-Xiang culture and Mao studies separately and lacks systematic sorting. They aim to supply scholarly reference for the Two Integrations, in particular the integration of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture.

The review organises the field into three strands: Hunan-Xiang culture and the formation of Mao's personality; Hunan-Xiang culture and Mao's personal thought; and Hunan-Xiang culture and Mao Zedong Thought proper. The first covers ideals and beliefs, worldview, temperament, character and self-awareness. The second covers philosophy, historiography, military, diplomatic and legal thought, literature and art, and sport. The third covers the "living soul" of Mao Zedong Thought, the Practice and Contradiction essays, and the "three magic weapons".

Across these strands, the reviewed studies trace Mao's traits and ideas to regional traditions such as statecraft-oriented practical learning, the people-as-foundation outlook, patriotism and a spirit of perseverance. They link these to thinkers such as Wang Fuzhi, Zeng Guofan, Tan Sitong and Yang Changji. On seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence, the review reports a recurring claim that Mao both inherited and went beyond Hunan-Xiang culture. After accepting Marxism, he is said to have discarded idealist elements and the "hero" view of history, and to have removed the historical and class limits of traditional people-centred thought.

Pang and Sun identify weaknesses. Concepts such as character, personality and temperament are loosely defined, producing repetition. Studies of Mao's personal thought are scattered, and the armed struggle is thinly treated. The authors also see weak integration of the two fields, with some works selecting Mao Zedong Thought concepts and then searching Hunan-Xiang sources for support, which they call "running the film backwards". They also see too little dialogue among scholars and a one-way view of influence. They call for placing Mao in historical context and for studying how Mao enriched Hunan-Xiang culture in return. Read the original if you want a map of Chinese scholarship on regional culture and Mao Zedong Thought, or its authors' view of the field's methodological gaps.
quoteEn: In fact, only through a two-way examination can the relationship between Hunan-Xiang culture and Mao Zedong be deeply understood and grasped.
quoteZh: 事实上，只有在双向度的考察中，才能深刻理解和把握湖湘文化和毛泽东之间的关系。

glossary.explanation: The regional culture of Hunan province, associated with practical statecraft learning, patriotism and a reformist, perseverant temperament. Thinkers such as Wang Fuzhi and Zeng Guofan are treated as its representatives.
Official formula: integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The second integration is the one this review invokes.
The Party's official term for the Marxist-Leninist theory adapted to Chinese conditions, developed by Mao and other Party leaders and summarising the experience of the Chinese revolution.
A principle of starting from actual conditions and linking theory with practice. It is treated in Party doctrine as a core of Mao Zedong Thought and has roots in classical Chinese scholarship.
The Party's method of work: everything for the masses, reliance on the masses, and 'from the masses, to the masses'.
Mao's summary of the Party's revolutionary experience: the united front, armed struggle and Party building.

t: Mao Zedong's exploration of Party propaganda work in the Yan'an period and its contemporary implications
zh: 延安时期毛泽东对党的宣传工作的探索及其当代启示
paras: How did Mao Zedong lead the Communist Party's propaganda work during the Yan'an period, and what does it offer propaganda work today? Zhao and Nie argue that Mao treated propaganda as a "major task" of the revolution. In their account, flexible strategies and wide use of available resources broke the Japanese and Kuomintang news blockade, built a positive image of the Party and won domestic and international sympathy.

The article first sets out Mao's view of propaganda as a vehicle of ideological leadership, tied to political, military and diplomatic work. It then examines the Yan'an situation and the principles Mao drew from it, the mobilisation of different propaganda actors, and the strategies used, including domestic methods and outreach abroad. It closes with lessons for the present, linked to statements by Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

The authors' central claim is that Mao's work rested on a sober reading of the situation: attacks on the Party abroad, Kuomintang smears, and subjectivism, sectarianism and "Party stereotyped writing" inside the Party. From this came three principles: Party leadership, seeking truth from facts, and distinguishing audiences ("look at the target before shooting the arrow"). Mao also drew on cadres, journalists, writers, theorists, students and correspondents under the slogan of "opening the door" to run newspapers. The authors add vivid language, popular forms, newspapers and radio, and foreign journalists such as Edgar Snow and Anna Louise Strong, plus overseas Chinese. They cite figures such as nearly 30,000 correspondents by 1945.

Writing against the background of the "two overall situations", the authors propose four lessons. These are upholding Party leadership and top-level design; mobilising diverse actors, including self-media, foreign influencers and overseas Chinese; adopting a "user mindset" and new discourse for differentiated audiences; and following communication laws with a full-media system using AI, big data and short video. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how Mao's Yan'an propaganda experience is being tied to current propaganda and communication policy.
quoteEn: Mao Zedong always led propaganda work from the standpoint of grasping the underlying laws.
quoteZh: 毛泽东始终坚持从把握规律的高度来领导开展宣传工作。

glossary.explanation: A formulation in recent Party discourse referring to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and profound changes in the world unseen in a century, which together frame current strategy.
A principle associated with Mao Zedong's Yan'an-era writings, stressing that policy and work should start from investigated reality rather than dogma.
Mao's term, from his 1942 essay Oppose Stereotyped Party Writing, for formulaic, empty and jargon-laden writing that ignores real conditions and audiences.

glossary.en: opening the door to run newspapers
glossary.explanation: A Maoist approach in which newspapers draw contributions from many cadres, workers and ordinary people, not only professional journalists.

t: Mao Zedong's exploration of and contribution to inheriting and developing China's fine traditional culture after 1949
st: A text analysis based on volumes 4–9 of the Chronology of Mao Zedong
zh: 新中国成立后毛泽东对传承与发展中华优秀传统文化的探索及贡献
zhSub: 基于《毛泽东年谱》(第4—9卷)的文本分析
paras: Liu Yanwu asks how Mao Zedong approached the inheritance and development of China's fine traditional culture in the years after the founding of the People's Republic, and why Chinese communists present themselves as its faithful heirs. The article, published in Mao Zedong Thought Studies in 2025, argues that Mao and his generation made a preliminary but distinctive contribution within the Two Integrations: combining Marxism's basic tenets with Chinese realities and with traditional culture. Liu also holds that this contribution was uneven and marked by errors.

The study takes volumes 4–9 of the Chronology of Mao Zedong as its source and extracts 289 entries from 1949 to 1976 concerning traditional culture. Liu sorts them by theme (theoretical background, policy, remoulding of old culture and intellectuals, key fields, cultivation, commentary, practice) and by period: 67 entries for 1949–1956, 137 for 1957–1965 and 85 for 1966–1976. Entries about errors already judged in the Party's 1981 historical resolution are excluded. Method follows grounded-theory coding, in three stages: initial, focused and theoretical.

Liu's reading draws out several threads. On policy, Mao's slogans "let a hundred flowers bloom, weed through the old to bring forth the new" and "make the past serve the present, foreign things serve China" called for critical, discriminating use of the heritage. Liu cites Mao on protecting cultural relics and museums, reforming old education and intellectuals, and promoting opera and traditional Chinese medicine. Mao judged traditional figures and works by four yardsticks: popular character, historical context, the needs of the present, and comparison with the West. Liu also counts 42 entries where Mao used classical allusions to explain international and domestic affairs.

Liu concludes that the policies protected many relics and advanced opera and Chinese medicine. The author also says Party understanding of cultural laws was still limited, so interference in the arts was excessive, the "hundred flowers" line was not well carried out, and the material heritage was better protected than traditional ideas, which were often criticised. Liu cites Xi Jinping on the continuity of the pre- and post-reform periods. The article names four factors for further study: politics, the principal contradiction, the Party's historical position and intellectuals. Read the original if you want a source-based, coded survey of Mao's remarks on traditional culture, with specific entries and an official-line assessment of its mistakes.
quoteEn: Mao Zedong's evaluations of traditional culture reveal the distinctive historical vision of a great leader of his generation.
quoteZh: 毛泽东对传统文化的评价彰显着一代伟人独特的历史大局视角。

glossary.explanation: Formula in Xi Jinping-era Party theory: combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with China's fine traditional culture.

glossary.en: let a hundred flowers bloom, weed through the old to bring forth the new
glossary.literal: a hundred flowers bloom together; push out the old to bring forth the new
glossary.explanation: Mao's 1951 inscription for the Chinese Opera Research Institute, which became a guiding line for the arts. It is related to the 'Double Hundred' policy of the 1950s.

glossary.pinyin: gǔ wéi jīn yòng, yáng wéi zhōng yòng
glossary.en: make the past serve the present, foreign things serve China
glossary.explanation: Mao's guideline for critically using ancient and foreign culture to serve contemporary socialist China.
Official term for the parts of China's traditional culture the Party considers worth inheriting, as distinct from what it regards as outdated or feudal.

t: The Chinese Communists' theoretical exploration of the people as the main body: a three-dimensional analysis
st: Political integration, institutional construction and value guidance
zh: 中国共产党人民主体思想的理论探索历程
zhSub: 基于政治整合、制度建构与价值引领的三维分析
paras: How has the Communist Party of China understood "the people" as the main body (renmin zhuti) of history and development, and how has that understanding changed over a century? Zhang argues that the Party's thinking evolved through three core values, "each in its proper place", common prosperity and shared development. Over this course, the Party moved from a strategy of mobilisation to a role of value guidance, uniting the people as subject of material production, holder of political power and realiser of values.

The article, published in Mao Zedong Thought Studies in 2025, proceeds chronologically and is organised around political integration, institutional construction and value guidance. It covers the New Democratic Revolution and the Anti-Japanese War, then the early reform and opening-up period, and finally the digital economy of the "new era". Zhang draws on Mao Zedong's class analysis, Marx's remarks on distribution and ownership, Xi Jinping's statements on sharing, and figures on income distribution, taxation and migrant workers.

Zhang makes three main moves. First, for the wartime years, Mao's picture of a society "small at both ends, large in the middle" is said to have led to a "double recognition" of class identity and political rights, through rent and interest reduction and the "three-thirds" system, producing the united front as a new political community. Second, after reform and opening up, "allowing some to get rich first" is presented as legitimising socialism through growth while distinguishing inequality from unfairness; it also reshaped the people into four identity groups, and the author flags unresolved tensions in primary, secondary and tertiary distribution. Third, digitalisation produces four new groups, including platform workers and "new workers", and moves the core value from common prosperity to shared development, with data rights framed as a successor to "land to the tiller".

Zhang concludes that through economic empowerment, political confirmation of rights and value empowerment, the Party has united the people as material, rights-bearing and value-bearing subject. The people thus become an end, not a means, and the "revolutionary community" gives way to a "community with a shared future for mankind". Read the original if you want a periodised account of how Party scholarship frames the people-centred idea, with the wartime class data, distribution figures and digital-economy case material that support it.
quoteEn: The Communist Party of China has explored an original line of thought on the people as the main body, whose core value system consists of "each in their proper place", "common prosperity" and "shared development".
quoteZh: 中国共产党探索了一条以“各得其所”“共同富裕”“共享发展”为核心价值体系的人民主体原创性思想脉络

t: The endogenous logic and basic experience of the Communist Party of China in establishing cultural confidence since 1949
st: An interview with Professor Zhang Ji of the School of Marxism, Hebei Normal University
zh: 新中国成立以来中国共产党确立文化自信的内生逻辑与基本经验——访河北师范大学马克思主义学院张骥教授
paras: This is an interview, published in Studies on Marxism, with Professor Zhang Ji of the School of Marxism at Hebei Normal University, a specialist in Marxist cultural theory and cultural soft power. The interviewers ask how the Communist Party of China has established cultural confidence since 1949, what logic underlies the process and what lessons it offers. Zhang answers that the process unites theoretical, historical and practical logics and reflects both inheritance of Marxist cultural thought and fine traditional Chinese culture and a firm belief in creating modern culture.

The conversation opens with the meaning of cultural confidence. Zhang defines it as a people's, state's or party's strong identification with its own cultural ideals and values, and presents it as the most basic of the Four-sphere Confidence. It then takes up the theoretical logic, the historical logic across three periods, and the practical logic of the present. The final questions concern the experience gained: Party leadership, people-centredness, innovation, the Two Integrations, and the balance between material and spiritual civilisation.

On theory, Zhang sets out Marx and Engels on the two-way relation of culture and the economy and on human beings as the subjects of culture. He then covers Lenin on the Party's cultural leadership, on seizing bourgeois cultural achievements and on respecting the pace of cultural work. Zhang adds Mao Zedong's cultural policies, Deng Xiaoping's spiritual civilisation, later leaders' contributions and Xi Jinping's thought on culture, together with fine traditional culture as the "cultural gene" of the Party. Historically, he traces a progression from cultural self-awareness and self-reliance to cultural self-direction, strength and confidence. He admits that cultural work in the early decades took some detours. For the present, he points to the Two Integrations, to the "two overall situations" of national rejuvenation and global change, and to cultural subjectivity as the root of confidence.

Zhang names comprehensive Party leadership as the first lesson, exercised through political leadership, ideological guidance, mass organisation and social mobilisation. He adds the people's主体 role, innovation in keeping with fundamental principles, and coordinated material and spiritual progress. He lists domestic challenges, including coexisting cultures, digital cultural security, cultural arrogance or inferiority, historical nihilism and weak identification. Internationally he cites cultural competition and the struggle for discourse power, which he says call for exchange and mutual learning. Read the original if you want an authoritative Chinese academic statement of how Party theorists periodise and justify the Party's cultural policy from 1949 to the present.
quoteEn: Cultural confidence fundamentally answers the questions of who we are, where we come from and where we are going.
quoteZh: 文化自信从根本上回答了“我们是谁、我们从哪里来、我们到哪里去”的问题。

glossary.explanation: A concept given prominence by Xi Jinping from 2014 onwards, meaning firm identification with and confidence in China's own cultural values, including traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture.
