Zhang concludes that livelihood work should do its best while acting within the country's means, advance step by step and persistently, combine Party leadership with popular participation and shared benefits, and tilt resources toward rural areas, the west and disadvantaged groups to narrow gaps. The text is a Party-theory commentary that restates and organises current official positions rather than adding new empirical material. Read the original if you want a compact view of how official Party scholarship links livelihood policy to the Party's nature, the socialist system and the contrast with Western modernization.
quoteEn: The greatest flaw of Western modernization is that it is centred on capital rather than on the people; it pursues the maximisation of capital's interests, which leads to wide wealth gaps and serious polarisation.
quoteZh: 西方现代化的最大弊端是以资本为中心而不是以人民为中心，追求资本利益最大化，导致贫富差距大、两极分化严重。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party's model of national development, elaborated since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as socialist, led by the Party and distinct from Western modernization.
A traditional Chinese term now used officially for the material well-being of ordinary people, covering education, jobs, income, health care, housing and social security.
A goal of shared wealth for all, described in official discourse as an essential requirement of socialism. It has been emphasised especially since 2021.
An official economic policy concept, prominent since 2017, that stresses quality, efficiency and balance over simple growth in output.

t: Keep advancing Chinese modernization on the new journey of the new era
zh: 新时代新征程上把中国式现代化不断推向前进
authors: Management Committee of the Party School of the CPC Central Committee (Chinese Academy of Governance)
paras: Published in Qiushi (2024, no. 13) under the name of the Party School's management committee, this is an authoritative study-and-implementation piece rather than a research article. It argues that Chinese modernization is the central task of the Party and state, and that completing it requires guidance from Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the spirit of the 20th Party Congress (2022) and Xi's statements on Chinese modernization.

The text has three parts. The first reviews how, in the new era, the Party led the people to advance and extend Chinese modernization in understanding, strategy and practice. The second presents Xi's statements as a scientific guide: Party leadership, the Chinese characteristics, essential requirements and major principles, the handling of major relationships, great struggle, and a new form of human civilization. The third sets out four tasks: deepening reform, high-quality development, raising cadres' capabilities, and implementation.

The article contends that Xi's discourse has begun to form a theoretical system of Chinese modernization, which it says enriches Marxist modernization theory and breaks the myth that modernization equals Westernization. It sorts the content into five Chinese characteristics (what it is), nine essential requirements (what to do) and five major principles (how to do it). It presents Party leadership, backed by the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, as decisive for the direction and success of the project. It lists paired relationships to be balanced, such as top-level design and local exploration, efficiency and fairness, and vitality and order, and calls for a spirit of struggle against external pressure. In its account, Western-led modernization has left some imitating countries in political turmoil, economic stagnation and social division, whereas Chinese modernization offers a path for the Global South and a community with a shared future for mankind.

The authors conclude that Chinese modernization is the only correct road to national strength and rejuvenation. They call for deepening reform, pursuing high-quality development in line with the new development philosophy, developing new quality productive forces according to local conditions, training officials, and carrying out decisions with a nail-driving spirit. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of how the Party's own training institution frames Chinese modernization in mid-2024, including its official structure of characteristics, requirements and principles.
quoteEn: Chinese modernization is a process of accumulating small victories into a great one; the key lies in action and in hard work.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化是一个积小胜为大胜的过程，关键在行动，关键靠实干。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's modernization path under Party leadership, elaborated since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is characterised by five features, including a huge population, common prosperity and peaceful development.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution in 2017 and the state constitution in 2018.
A formula from the 2021 Party resolution on history. It affirms Xi Jinping's core position in the Central Committee and the whole Party, and the guiding role of his thought.
A Party requirement to uphold Xi Jinping's core position and the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee.
An official economic goal that stresses quality, innovation and efficiency over raw growth. The article calls it the primary task of building a modern socialist country.
A concept Xi Jinping introduced in 2023–24. It refers to productivity driven by technological breakthroughs and innovation.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's foreign-policy concept, in use since 2012–13, of shared global interests and cooperative international relations.

t: Modernization alone is not enough; what matters more is the "Chinese-style" path
st: A critical assessment of Jiang Tingfu's A History of Modern China
zh: 只讲现代化是不够的，更重要的是“中国式”
zhSub: 蒋廷黻著《中国近代史》评析
source: Journal of Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育导刊), 2024 no. 5
paras: Prompted by a student's question about why Jiang Tingfu's A History of Modern China (1938), which narrates modern Chinese history around modernization, is praised by some and dismissed by others, Wang Xianming and Liu Yanhong offer a critical assessment. They argue that the book has real academic merits and lasting appeal, but that its theoretical framework is heavily Westernized and that it has two serious political flaws. In the authors' view, talking only about modernization is insufficient: the correct path and the right leadership matter more.

The article opens with the book's publication history. Jiang wrote it in Wuhan in 1938 and described it as a preliminary report. The authors say it was out of favour after 1949, then reissued in dozens of editions since reform and opening up, and gradually elevated to a pioneering masterpiece. They note that contemporaries such as Cao Juren did not rank it among the three best works on the period. The authors then set out three parts: why the book has drawn long-term attention, why its framework is Westernized, and what its political defects are.

On its appeal, the authors credit four features: the "Jiang Tingfu question" (can China modernize?), a simple structure built around four rescue plans (self-strengthening, the reform movement, the Boxers, Sun Yat-sen's programme), a comparative global setting including Japan, Russia and Turkey, and accessible prose. They contend, however, that its recent popularity mainly reflects the rise of Western modernization thinking, and that some use a "modernization paradigm" to displace the revolutionary narrative guided by historical materialism. Wang and Liu argue that Jiang equates modernization with Westernization, draws on Western-centrism and the "stagnant China" thesis of Hegel and H. B. Morse, and echoes imperialist justifications, for instance in treating Mongol and Manchu rule as invasions and describing China as an imperialist power. Politically, they link the book to the Kuomintang-backed Yiwen Research Society, whose leaders later defected to Japan, and say its "science first" logic amounts to defeatism. They also fault it for placing hopes of national rejuvenation in Chiang Kai-shek while disparaging the Communists.

The authors conclude that Jiang the historian lacked sufficient moral and intellectual judgement. In their account, a semi-colonial, semi-feudal country could neither resist imperialism nor industrialize without a popular anti-imperialist, anti-feudal revolution. They close with Jiang's later quarrel with his former student John K. Fairbank, who adopted his paradigm but rejected his anti-Communist politics. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of a widely reissued history, and of the modernization paradigm in modern Chinese historiography.
quoteEn: To speak only of modernization, without addressing the correct path and necessary preconditions for achieving it, or recognising who its true leader is, can only end in futility, and the dream of modernization cannot be realised.
quoteZh: 只讲现代化，不讲实现现代化的正确道路和必备的前提，不认清谁是现代化的真正领导者，其结果只能是竹篮打水一场空，其现代化的梦想亦无法实现。

glossary.explanation: An approach that organises modern Chinese history around the pursuit of modernization, often identified with Western models. The authors present it as a rival to the revolutionary-history framework based on historical materialism.

glossary.literal: theory of the West as centre
glossary.explanation: The view that Western history and values are the universal standard for progress. The authors treat it as a theoretical support for colonialism and imperialism.
The idea, associated with Hegel and later Western sinologists, that China had no internal impetus for change and required external impact to modernize.

t: From development philosophy to form of civilization: the evolution of terminology and knowledge production in Chinese modernization
zh: 从发展理念到文明形态：中国式现代化的术语演进与知识生产
paras: Zhang Mingzhi asks how the vocabulary of modernization in China has evolved, and how Chinese modernization, as a body of practice, produces a distinctive discourse, knowledge system and channels of communication for the wider world. The article argues that the shift from the "two civilizations" to the five-sphere overall plan, together with the new development philosophy, has given Chinese modernization its own character and opened what the author calls a new form of human civilization.

The article has three main parts. The first traces the terminology from the "four modernizations" through the 1978 truth-criterion debate and the evolving reform goals to the Five-sphere Integrated Plan (economic, political, cultural, social and ecological construction). The second reads Chinese modernization through the new development philosophy, covering its essential attributes and its "new era" features. The third treats knowledge production, an autonomous knowledge system, international communication and civilizational significance, before closing with directions for future research.

Zhang's central move is to treat development concepts as products of practice that then guide it. Chinese modernization is presented as socialist modernization led by the Communist Party. Its core is common prosperity and a people-centred approach, and its outward character is peaceful, open and shared. The author sets this against a Western path driven by capital, which is said to produce class polarisation, a "centre–periphery" structure and ecological crisis. A second move links the new development stage, new development philosophy and new development pattern, with innovation and new quality productive forces as the main driver. Zhang then argues that the practice yields original concepts and narratives, offers developing countries an alternative to Western modernization and gives world socialism a new form. The author claims that this undermines the "end of history" thesis and the "clash of civilizations" thesis.

In the conclusion, Zhang holds that traditional Western modernization theory cannot explain Chinese modernization and that the classics offer no ready answer. Four tasks follow for research: more rigorous concepts and terms, a wider range of methods (including AI-based modelling of discourse), a systematic autonomous knowledge system, and shared values. The author also calls for stronger international discourse power and for East–West dialogue mechanisms. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese scholars frame modernization terminology, the new development philosophy and the building of an "autonomous knowledge system" as a theoretical project.
quoteEn: Development philosophy is the forerunner of development action.
quoteZh: 发展理念是发展行动的先导

glossary.explanation: The Party's formula for China's own path of modernization, systematised at the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as socialist, people-centred and distinct from the Western model.
A set of five concepts (innovation, coordination, green, openness, sharing) put forward under Xi Jinping in 2015 to guide economic and social development.
The Party's overall plan, adopted at the 18th Party Congress (2012), to advance economic, political, cultural, social and ecological progress together.
A goal described by the Party as an essential requirement of socialism: prosperity shared by all, with narrower gaps in income and development.
A term Xi Jinping introduced in 2023 for productive forces driven by technological innovation, notably digital technology, rather than by traditional resource-intensive growth.
A Party formulation, prominent since 2021, claiming that Chinese modernization creates a form of civilization that goes beyond the Western capitalist model.
A slogan from recent Party calls for Chinese social science to build its own concepts and theories rather than rely on Western ones.

t: Putting people's livelihood first: a key guideline for Chinese modernization
zh: 民生为大：中国式现代化的重要遵循
paras: This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2024, takes up Xi Jinping's remark during an inspection in Chongqing on 22 April 2024 that in Chinese modernization, "people's livelihood comes first" (民生为大). Pan Xun and Cui Jianxi argue that the statement clarifies the essential character of Chinese modernization as people-centred, identifies what decides its success or failure, and sets out a practical guideline for it.

The article is organised in three parts. The first traces how livelihood expresses the 'people first' nature of Chinese modernization, through the Party's century-long history, the Marxist view of the people, and the need to meet the people's growing aspiration for a better life. The second examines livelihood as the key to the direction, mission and outcome of modernization. The third derives three practical principles.

On the first two points, the authors read the Party's history from its 1921 programme to the new era as a continuous effort to realise modernization for the people's wellbeing. They contend that Chinese modernization has broken the 'modernization equals Westernization' myth and gone beyond Western modernization's logic of capital by following a human-centred logic. They link livelihood to the national mission of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and to common prosperity, citing figures that rural per capita disposable income in poor areas rose from 6,079 to 12,588 yuan between 2013 and 2020.

For practice, the authors call for strengthening primary-level Party organisations and grassroots governance so that livelihood projects reach people concretely, citing the 255,000 village-based work teams of the poverty-alleviation campaign. They also call for improving livelihood through development, treating better living standards as a measure of development, and relying on the people as the driving force of history. They present this as the Party's value stance and a code of action for modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary connects Xi's livelihood remarks to Marxist theory and Party history.
quoteEn: Chinese modernization is a modernization that follows a human-centred logic, which determines that it must put people's livelihood first.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化是遵循人本逻辑的现代化，这决定着中国式现代化必须做到民生为大

glossary.explanation: The official term for the Party's path of national development, set out prominently at the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models of modernization.

glossary.literal: people's livelihood is the greatest matter
glossary.explanation: A phrase used by Xi Jinping in April 2024 to stress that the welfare of ordinary people, such as food, housing, health care and education, is the central concern of government work.
An official goal of shared wealth for all, described as an essential requirement of socialism. It has been given renewed emphasis since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's long-term national goal of restoring China's strength and international standing, closely tied to Xi Jinping's idea of the Chinese Dream.
A principle in Xi Jinping's thought that the Party's work should put the people's interests above all else.

t: The Way of China: a philosophical interpretation of the outstanding characteristics of Chinese civilization
zh: 中华之道：中华文明突出特性的哲学阐释
source: Historical Theory Studies (史学理论研究), 2024 no. 3
paras: Zhang Zhiqiang takes up the five "outstanding characteristics" of Chinese civilization named by Xi Jinping at the 2023 symposium on cultural inheritance and development: continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness. The article argues that these are not a loose list of traits but the law of development of Chinese civilization, which Zhang calls "the Way of China". Zhang presents the Way of China as both the result of Chinese history and the premise that keeps generating China. The text is the introduction to Zhang's 2024 book of the same title.

The article first sets out why five characteristics, and why in this order, and proposes that they form three pairs: continuity and innovation, unity and inclusiveness, inclusiveness and peacefulness. It then takes each characteristic in turn, drawing on classical sources such as the Book of Changes, the Gongyang Commentary, the Doctrine of the Mean and the Book of Rites, as well as on Qian Mu and Fei Xiaotong. A closing section ties the argument to the Second Integration, building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation, and the future of world civilization.

Zhang's central move is to read continuity as the continuity of a unified historical subject. Through the notion of "tongji" (thread-gathering), legitimate succession and the state form are said to unify time, so that continuity and innovation presuppose each other as change and constancy, or the one and the many. Zhang links innovation to the Book of Changes idea of "casting off the old and taking up the new" and to the Party's self-reform. Unity is traced to the "great unity" tradition and to the ideal of "all under heaven as one family", and inclusiveness to the ethic of conscientiousness and reciprocity ("zhong-shu"). Zhang claims this ethic produces "common values", which differ from "universal values" in the way they are established: through mutual communication rather than by one side imposing them. Zhang contrasts a worldview of heaven and humanity as one with Western subject–object opposition and monotheism, and attributes peacefulness to the same cosmology, citing the absence of expansion and colonial plunder in Chinese history.

Zhang concludes that adapting Marxism to Chinese tradition means using Marxist principles to activate these characteristics and bring out the laws of Chinese civilization. A modern civilization of the Chinese nation must therefore modernize all five and discard none of them. Zhang adds that such a civilization would not replace other civilizations with a single one, but would help form a larger community of human civilizations, a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-affiliated scholar derives Xi Jinping's five characteristics from classical Chinese philosophy and links them to the Second Integration.
quoteEn: Continuity is continuity achieved through innovation; and equally, innovation exists only on the premise of continuity.
quoteZh: 连续是通过创新实现的连续，同时也只有在连续的前提下才有所谓创新。

glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's formula for combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities (the first) and with China's fine traditional culture (the second). The second was stressed from 2021 and especially at the 2023 cultural symposium.
Xi Jinping's 2023 summary of Chinese civilization as marked by continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness.
Zhang's own term for the law of development of Chinese civilization, which he identifies with the five characteristics.
A classical ideal, found in the Gongyang Commentary, of a unified political and temporal order. The author reads it as the source of the modern idea of unity in diversity.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's foreign-policy and civilizational concept, put forward from 2012–13, of a world bound by common interests and responsibilities.
An official term for the Communist Party's claimed capacity to correct itself and renew its discipline and ideology. The article links it to the classical idea of changing the old.

t: The inner drivers, methods and laws of theoretical innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化理论创新的内在动因、方法和规律
source: Journal of Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育导刊), 2024 no. 5
paras: Wang Gang asks what drives theoretical innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, which methods achieve it, and which laws it follows. The article answers that innovation is driven internally by practice, problem-orientation and the Party's mission. It is carried out through methodological requirements and governed by three laws. Wang treats the three as unified: drivers supply the impetus, methods the path, laws the direction of development.

The article has three parts, written in 2024 and published in a journal on ideological and political education. The first part treats the drivers across the Party's history, from the new-democratic revolution through socialist construction and reform and opening up to the new era. The second sets out methodological requirements. The third formulates the laws of innovation. Wang repeatedly maps Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era onto this scheme.

On drivers, Wang argues that each stage of Chinese practice posed questions the classic authors could not have met. Each also posed a defining question of its age, and the Party's mission as a Marxist "mission-oriented party" spurred it to answer them. On method, Wang stresses upholding fundamental principles while innovating, which means holding to Marxism as the "soul" and to fine traditional Chinese culture as the "root". The article presents the Two Integrations and the "six musts" from the 20th Party Congress (2022) as the basic guide, and it adds systematization and scholarly grounding of theory as an internal requirement. On laws, Wang names three: the dialectical unity of upholding and developing Marxism, with dogmatism and pragmatism as the two errors to avoid; the positive interaction of theoretical and practical innovation; and learning from the creativity of the people.

Wang concludes that the three sets of factors are mutually unified and jointly advance the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article treats the Party's mission and tasks as without limit, so theoretical innovation too has no end. It calls for following the mass line in theory-building, on the grounds that the people's practice is the inexhaustible source of theory. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how Party theorists present the logic, methods and regularities of theoretical innovation from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping.
quoteEn: Talking about development apart from upholding is like water without a source or a tree without roots and leads to the error of pragmatism; talking about upholding apart from development falls into a rigid rut and leads to the error of dogmatism.
quoteZh: 脱离坚持谈发展，犹如无源之水、无本之木，就会犯实用主义错误；脱离发展谈坚持，就会陷入刻板的窠臼，就会犯教条主义的错误。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formulation for the Party's project of fitting Marxism to China's conditions and to the present era. It extends the older term 'sinification of Marxism' and was given prominence in the 2021 Party history resolution and the 20th Party Congress.
Xi Jinping's formula for combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture.

Six requirements set out in the 20th Party Congress report: put the people first, be confident and independent, uphold fundamental principles while innovating, be problem-oriented, adopt systematic thinking, and have a global vision.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's current official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution in 2017.

glossary.literal: guarding what is correct and innovating
glossary.explanation: An official formula meaning that innovation must proceed from fidelity to Marxism and the Party's core positions.
A Party method, associated with Mao Zedong, of drawing ideas and experience from the masses, turning them into policy and returning them to the masses.

keywords: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context

t: The threefold logic and pathways of coordinated urban–rural development from the perspective of Chinese modernization
zh: 中国式现代化视角下城乡协调发展的三重逻辑与推进路径
paras: The article asks how urban–rural relations can be coordinated within Chinese modernization, and why coordination must precede integration. Zhou and Zhong argue that coordinated development is the precondition for urban–rural integration, and that the main weakness still lies in the countryside. Their answer is that comprehensive rural revitalization, rather than integration alone, is the strategic basis for narrowing the urban–rural gap.

The study is organised around three "logics". The theoretical logic draws on Marx's account of urban–rural opposition and on the "synchronised development of the Four Modernizations" (industrialization, urbanization, informatization, agricultural modernization), alongside rural revitalization and the drive to build a strong agricultural country. The historical logic traces policy-driven phases from the planned-economy division of the two sectors to the present push for integration. The practical logic identifies six current difficulties, and the final section proposes seven pathways.

Zhou and Zhong's central claim is that outside forces (industry supporting agriculture, cities leading the countryside) must combine with the countryside's own endogenous momentum. Using statistics, they report that the urban–rural income ratio fell from 2.88 in 2012 to 2.39 in 2023, but that the absolute gap widened from 15,738 to 30,130 yuan. They also report that inequality within the rural population exceeds that in towns, and that rural pension levels are far below urban ones. The six difficulties are weak county economies, thin village collective economies, rural ageing and a weakened farm workforce, and a fragile rural industrial system in which smallholders struggle to reach large markets. The authors also stress that revitalization cannot save every village and must follow population trends and local conditions.

The authors propose invigorating county economies, strengthening village collective and cooperative economies, raising farmers' employability, innovating rural investment mechanisms, raising rural social security (including a large rise in the basic pension minimum by 2025), and improving rural governance under Party leadership. They present this as essential to common prosperity and to a modernized socialist country. Read the original if you want a data-rich, policy-oriented account of China's urban–rural gap and the measures an academic policy analyst proposes to close it.
quoteEn: Coordinated urban–rural development is the precondition and necessary condition of urban–rural integration, and integration must be promoted through coordinated development.
quoteZh: 城乡协调发展是城乡融合的前提和必要条件，必须要以城乡协调发展来促进城乡融合。

glossary.explanation: The official concept of China's own path to modernization, set out prominently at the 20th Party Congress (2022). Coordinated development is listed among its basic features.
A national strategy first announced at the 19th Party Congress (2017). It seeks to modernize agriculture and the countryside through industry, ecology, culture, organization and talent.

glossary.en: synchronised development of the Four Modernizations
glossary.explanation: The official policy of advancing industrialization, informatization, urbanization and agricultural modernization together rather than in sequence.
A stated goal of socialism with Chinese characteristics, meaning prosperity shared by all, which has been given high priority in recent policy.
A policy concept first put forward at the 19th Party Congress (2017). It aims at two-way free flow of factors between town and country and the removal of the urban–rural dual structure.
A goal stressed at the 20th Party Congress (2022): moving China from a large agricultural producer to one with strong supply security, technology and competitiveness.

t: Creative transformation and innovative development of China's fine traditional virtues in the new era
zh: 新时代中华优秀传统美德的创造性转化创新性发展
source: Ideological and Political Education Research (思想教育研究), 2024 no. 5
paras: Xiao Guiqing and Long Zhengwu ask how China's fine traditional virtues can be turned into something suited to the new era. Taking Xi Jinping's statements as their starting point, they argue that creative transformation and innovative development of these virtues must rest on the historical position of the new era and on the Two Integrations. The result, they say, should carry Chinese characteristics, style and manner.

The article has three parts. The first sets out why inheriting traditional virtues matters: as the ethical basis of the Two Integrations, as spiritual strength for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and as a store of governing wisdom for the Party. The second divides the virtues into six levels: personal character, family virtues, professional ethics, public morality, virtue in government, and virtue in foreign relations. The third sets out a scientific attitude and method for inheritance.

The authors' central claim is that traditional virtue and Marxism fit together closely, so that inheriting the first is part of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Ideas such as 'the world belongs to all' and 'the people as the foundation of the state' are said to match communist ideals and the principle of putting the people first. At each level the authors pair a traditional virtue with a present-day practice: moral exemplars, family-conduct campaigns, honesty in a market economy, rural civility and poverty alleviation, the Party's self-reform and consultative democracy, and the Belt and Road Initiative. They also say that traditional virtue nourishes the core socialist values.

On method, the authors call for critical inheritance guided by a Marxist view of ethics. They cite Engels that no universal morality fits all eras and peoples, and they urge keeping what is vital while discarding dross. They also insist on a people-centred stance, on using stories and moral models, and on avoiding doctrinaire indoctrination so that virtues are internalised as real values. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Party theorists connect Confucian-era ethics, the core socialist values and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.
quoteEn: The creative transformation and innovative development of traditional virtues should help turn them into value identification among the people and spur moral agents to take up moral requirements of their own accord.
quoteZh: 传统美德的创造性转化和创新性发展，应当推动传统美德内化为人民群众的价值认同，激发道德主体主动实践道德要求。

glossary.explanation: A formula in Xi Jinping's thought: combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities, and with China's fine traditional culture. The second integration was stressed from 2021 onwards.
A set of twelve values promoted since the 18th Party Congress (2012), at three levels: national, social and individual.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's long-term goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing, closely tied to the Chinese Dream.
An official term for the Party's efforts to discipline itself and correct its own problems, emphasised under Xi Jinping.
China's international infrastructure and economic cooperation programme, launched in 2013.

t: The dialectical logic of the development of Chinese modernization
zh: 中国式现代化的辩证发展逻辑
paras: Wang Jie asks how Chinese modernization should be understood in light of the dialectic of universality and particularity in contradiction. The article argues that, seen as universal, Chinese modernization shares historical, theoretical and practical continuity with the modernization of the Chinese nation, of socialist countries and of human society. Seen as particular, it has distinctive advantages and features that drive the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and offer a Chinese experience and Chinese approach to others.

The article is organised in four parts. The first three each set Chinese modernization against one of the three larger processes: the Chinese nation's modernization efforts since the Opium War, the modernization of socialist states since the October Revolution, and world modernization. In each, Wang separates what Chinese modernization shares from what is new in it. A fourth part draws out its significance for Chinese, socialist and human civilization.

In the first part, Wang traces over a century of exploration at the levels of material objects and industry, institutions and culture. Against this background, Chinese modernization is said to reach a new height through four features: a more advanced leading class, broad mass mobilisation under the Communist Party, comprehensive content, and a distinct path. In the second part, it is placed within the socialist modernizations that began from backwardness, relied on public ownership and a proletarian party, and faced competition from capitalism. Its innovations are the socialist market economy, support for the non-public sector alongside a stronger public sector, and distribution that breaks with egalitarianism. In the third part, it follows general laws, such as technology, industrialisation and markets. Wang adds five particular features: huge scale, "parallel" rather than sequential development, a people-centred orientation, peaceful development, and a socialist direction.

Wang concludes that Chinese modernization continues and renews Chinese civilization and defends and confirms socialism against the "end of history" thesis associated with Fukuyama. It also enriches the forms of human modernization. In the author's account, it shows that developing countries can find a path that does not depend on developed countries and suits their own conditions. Read the original if you want a systematic official-style account of how Chinese modernization is positioned against national, socialist and global histories.
quoteEn: What Chinese modernization has opened up is a comprehensive path of modernization.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化开创的是一条全面的现代化之路

glossary.explanation: The official concept of China's own path to modernization, which the Communist Party has promoted especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as socialist in character and distinct from Western models.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing after the "century of humiliation" that began with the Opium War.
The official description of China's economic system since the 1990s, combining market mechanisms with public ownership as the main body and Party leadership.
Xi Jinping's term for China's industrialisation, informatisation, urbanisation and agricultural modernization proceeding together, in contrast to the sequential ("series") path of Western countries.

t: How human liberation generates enormous momentum for modernization
zh: 论人的解放何以催生巨大的现代化动力
paras: Wu Zhongmin asks how the historical tide of "human liberation" produces the driving force of modernization, and what limits that liberation needs. Wu defines liberation as the rise of people's practical and cognitive capacities with modern science and productive forces, which frees them from the constraints of traditional society. The article argues that without it modernization has no momentum, but that liberation can slip out of control and must be given reasonable boundaries.

The article has four sections. Three examine the sources of momentum: the autonomy of society's members, the wide space for their activity, and their growing needs. The fourth sets out four limits. Wu contrasts traditional and modern society throughout, drawing on medieval Europe and traditional China. Marx supplies much of the framework, and Xi Jinping's statements are cited on Chinese modernization.

In the first section, Wu argues that modern values of freedom and equality replace dependence with autonomous behaviour. Its features are independence, stronger self-interest, rationality and competitiveness, which the market economy rewards through distribution by contribution. The second section holds that large-scale social mobility, openness to the outside world, wider choice, more exchange and better cooperation raise creativity. Wu cites patent filings, including a rise in Chinese resident filings from 25,346 in 2000 to 1,344,817 in 2020. The third section claims rising needs push the economy up through successive sectors, from agriculture to industry to services.

Wu then identifies four boundaries: liberation must not outrun the stage of productive forces, capital must not grow "wildly", materialistic demand must not dominate spiritual and cultural needs, and the ecological environment must not be damaged. Wu presents these as conditions for healthy, lasting momentum and for the goal of free and all-round human development. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's account of how Marxist ideas of human emancipation are linked to Chinese modernization and its stated limits.
quoteEn: Human needs follow a law of evolution from the lower to the higher.
quoteZh: 人的需求遵循由低到高的演化规律。

glossary.explanation: The official term for China's own path of modernization, promoted by the Party leadership especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.

glossary.pinyin: rén de zìyóu ér quánmiàn fāzhǎn
glossary.explanation: A Marxist ideal of individuals developing their capacities fully. Official Chinese discourse treats it as the ultimate aim of modernization.

t: New quality productive forces and national competitive advantage: inner logic and strategic priorities
zh: 新质生产力与国家竞争优势：内在逻辑与战略重点
source: Teaching and Research (Jiaoxue yu Yanjiu), 2024 no. 6
paras: Zhou Wen and Yang Zhengyuan ask how new quality productive forces can be turned into lasting national competitive advantage as the new round of technological and industrial revolution deepens and great-power rivalry intensifies. They argue that, unlike the incremental innovation of traditional productive forces, new quality productive forces rest on disruptive innovation. Their logical starting point, in the authors' view, is rebuilding independent innovation capacity through an organic combination of government and market.

The article has four parts. It first treats productive-force progress as the decisive factor in national advantage, contrasting incremental innovation (the expansion of existing stock) with disruptive innovation (the reconstruction of increments), with historical cases from Portugal and Spain, Britain's steam power and the United States' electrification. It then presents industrial competition as the modern form of rivalry between states. Next it criticises three theoretical misconceptions, and it ends with four strategic breakthroughs. The authors draw on Smith, Marx, Porter, Freeman, Acemoglu and Robinson, Stiglitz and others.

The authors say that new quality productive forces mean original, disruptive breakthroughs, "from 0 to 1", rather than marginal technical improvement. Developed countries, they contend, protect patents and restrict technology cooperation, which forces developing countries to rely on independent innovation. Drawing on Freeman, Wen Yi and others, they hold that state action is needed to supply infrastructure and overcome market gaps. The three misconceptions are: full marketisation, as in institutionalist economics and the Latin American case; industrial hollowing-out and over-financialisation, which they analyse with Marx's account of credit and fictitious capital; and static comparative advantage, which they say locks developing countries into the middle and lower links of value chains. They cite US semiconductor controls as an example.

The authors propose four priorities: building a new-type whole-nation system (xinxing juguo tizhi) that combines government and market and links science, industry and finance; integrating the digital and real economies, with platform regulation and anti-monopoly enforcement; building a modern industrial system that climbs to the middle and upper reaches of global value chains while safeguarding supply-chain security; and creating world-class enterprises, with state-owned firms as sources of original technology and private "little giants" in close cooperation. Read the original if you want to see how a Fudan political-economy team links new quality productive forces to industrial policy, technological rivalry and critiques of Western development theory.
quoteEn: New quality productive forces are not ordinary technological progress, nor marginal improvement in productive forces, but the realisation of breakthroughs and innovation in original, disruptive technologies.
quoteZh: “新质生产力”不是普通的科技进步，也不是生产力边际上的改进，而是要实现原创性颠覆性技术的突破和创新。

glossary.explanation: A concept put forward by Xi Jinping in 2023–24 for advanced productive forces driven by innovation, high technology, high efficiency and high quality, and distinct from traditional growth paths.

A model that mobilises state, market and institutional resources nationwide for major scientific and technological goals, such as core technology breakthroughs. It updates the earlier whole-nation system.

t: The distinctive advantages of Chinese modernization
zh: 中国式现代化的独特优势
paras: This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in June 2024, asks what makes Chinese modernization distinctive and why this path could only have emerged in China. Chen Congkai argues that its advantages can be understood from cultural, historical, theoretical and practical angles, and sets out six: strong leadership, a distinctive cultural tradition, theoretical innovation, a people-centred value orientation, ecological civilization values, and a contribution to world peace.

The piece is organised as six short sections, each pairing a feature of Chinese modernization with a contrast to Western modernization. It draws on speeches by Xi Jinping, on the five features of Chinese modernization named in official discourse, on Marx and Engels, and on Thomas Piketty's work on inequality. It also cites figures on forest cover and a list of twentieth-century pollution incidents in the West.

Chen's central claim is that leadership by the Communist Party of China determines the nature, direction and momentum of modernization, whereas Western parties are described as offering slogans, short-term promises and a rotation of power controlled by large capital. The author traces each of the five features to Chinese traditional ideas such as 'harmony between humanity and nature' and 'enriching the people', and presents the Two Integrations and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the theoretical guide. Chen contrasts a people-centred path, which is said to have eliminated absolute poverty, with a capital-centred Western path marked by rising inequality and a 'pollute first, clean up later' model.

The article concludes that Chinese modernization pursues peaceful development, has no record of foreign aggression or colonies in the author's account, and offers an alternative to equating modernization with Westernization. Chen presents it as an opportunity for countries that want to develop without dependence, and as a step towards a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official-line commentary summarises the claimed advantages of Chinese modernization against a Western comparison.
quoteEn: Chinese modernization is socialist modernization led by the Communist Party of China.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化是中国共产党领导的社会主义现代化。

glossary.explanation: The official concept of China's path to modernization, set out by the Party from 2021–2022. It is described by five features, including a huge population, common prosperity and peaceful development.
Xi Jinping's formula for combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution in 2017 and the state constitution in 2018.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept of international relations, promoting cooperation and shared interests among states.

t: Some theoretical questions on the formation and development of new quality productive forces
zh: 新质生产力形成与发展的若干理论问题
source: Fujian Tribune (Humanities and Social Sciences Edition), 2024 no. 5
paras: Hou Weimin takes up the category of new quality productive forces, put forward by Xi Jinping in 2023 and endorsed by the Central Economic Work Conference (2023), and asks how it should be understood in theory and how it should be built in practice. Hou argues that the concept extends Marxist productive-force theory and answers the needs of a new stage of Chinese modernization. In Hou's view, it must be read through Marx's own texts, and its formation depends on state-led, publicly owned economic power.

The article has four parts. It first separates the essential definition of new quality productive forces from their concrete forms, comparing Marx's "new productive forces", labour productive power and the subject–object relation. It then identifies three theoretical breakthroughs. The third part treats the new relations of production that fit these forces, and the fourth sets out the leading role of the state-owned economy. Hou draws throughout on Marx's Grundrisse, Capital, The German Ideology and letters, and on Xi's statements.

Hou holds that Marx's "new productive forces" refer to qualitative change in total productive power tied to a change of social formation. The Chinese concept instead stresses the advanced quality of particular factors of production. A scientific discovery or invention is not a productive force until it is embodied in material means of production and absorbed into social production, so the concept cannot be reduced to technological determinism or to higher labour productivity. Hou counts data, computing power and artificial intelligence as new factors that extend the concept. On the relations of production, Hou argues that new quality productive forces call only for adjustments within direct production, not a change of social formation. These adjustments cover exchange and distribution, stable regulation of labour relations and the training of innovative talent.

Hou concludes that public ownership should lead the process. Marx's remark that freedom depends on whether productive forces belong to the people is read as support for state-owned capital's decisive role. Hou says state-owned enterprises have greater cooperative productive power, and calls for state control of large digital platforms, state-led AI regulation, heavier state investment and policy support. Hou rejects the view that private firms are the main vehicle, and the proposal to capitalise labour-power through new share schemes. Read the original if you want a Marxist-political-economy argument, closely tied to Marx's texts, for a state-owned-economy-centred reading of new quality productive forces.
quoteEn: Whether new quality productive forces can benefit the people depends crucially on the institutional character of the agents that form them.
quoteZh: 新质生产力能否为人民造福，关键在于新质生产力的形成主体的制度属性。

glossary.explanation: A concept Xi Jinping put forward in 2023. It denotes advanced productive forces driven by technological breakthroughs, new factors of production such as data, and upgraded industries.
The official name for China's development path under Party leadership. It is presented as distinct from Western models of modernization.

t: The path and method by which Mao Zedong created the philosophical system of "practice theory"
zh: 毛泽东创立“实践论”哲学体系的路径与方法
source: Journal of Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育导刊), 2024 no. 5
paras: Li Weiwu asks how Mao Zedong created the philosophical system of "practice theory" (shijianlun), which the article treats as the core of Mao Zedong Thought. The author sets out to trace the stages of exploration, the logical links between them and the research method involved. The thesis is that the system arose from the needs of the Chinese revolution and was built step by step, moving from concrete reality to philosophical abstraction and back to concrete reality.

The article is organised as six sections that follow Mao's path in order. It begins with the problem of the relation between the universal truth of Marxism and China's concrete conditions, which Mao met in rural investigation in the 1920s and 1930s and in the anti-dogmatist struggle within the Party. It then covers the materialist-dialectics movement in Shanghai and Beijing around 1930, his reading notes on Soviet textbooks, the 1937 lecture outline, and the texts "On Practice" and "On Contradiction". It ends with the 1943 decision on leadership methods and Mao's wartime writings on military, revolutionary and state theory.

Li makes three main moves. First, Mao shifted the emphasis of dialectical materialism from ontology, the focus of Ai Siqi and Li Da, to epistemology, because his opponent was now dogmatism within the Party. Li argues that he justified this through Lenin's unity of dialectics, epistemology and logic. Second, the core is built from the concept of "social practice" and two formulas: "practice–cognition–practice" and "particular–general–particular". Mao's 1943 mass line, "from the masses, to the masses", adds a third formula, "masses–leadership–masses". Li reads this as folding historical materialism and political philosophy into the system, with collective subjects of cognition. Third, Mao derived a methodology from the system, the principles of "hitting the target with the arrow" and "seeking truth from facts". Li argues this produced a Chinese Marxist military theory (On Protracted War), a theory of revolution and a theory of the state (New Democracy).

Li concludes that the system was not created at a stroke. In his account it answered the question of universal truth and Chinese reality in both theory and practice, and it armed the Party and the masses for victory in the revolution. He presents it as a model of adapting Marxist philosophy to the Chinese context that still guides that task in the twenty-first century. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based reconstruction of how Mao's philosophical writings of the 1930s and 1940s fit together and how a leading Chinese philosopher interprets them.
quoteEn: Mao Zedong's creation of this philosophical system was by no means accomplished at a stroke, but went through a long process of exploration.
quoteZh: 毛泽东创立这一哲学体系决非一蹴而就，而是经过了一个长时期的探索历程。

glossary.explanation: The label the author gives to Mao Zedong's philosophical system, built around the essay "On Practice" and its extensions. It stresses that knowledge arises from social practice and serves it.

The Party's method of leadership, formulated by Mao in 1943 as collecting the masses' views, systematising them and returning them to the masses as policy. The Party continues to present it as a basic working principle.
A classical Chinese phrase that Mao reinterpreted in 1941 as studying the internal laws of objective things. It later became a core slogan of the Party's ideological line.

Mao's theory, set out in 1940, of a stage of revolution in colonial and semi-colonial China. It envisaged a republic led by the proletariat and based on a joint dictatorship of anti-imperialist and anti-feudal classes, preceding socialism.
In Party discourse, applying Marxist texts or Comintern directives mechanically without regard to Chinese conditions. Mao criticised it as a main error within the Party in the 1930s.

t: Building a modern Chinese civilisation requires firmly grasping both the "root" and the "soul"
zh: 建设中华民族现代文明要牢牢把握“根脉”和“魂脉”
paras: Li Jie takes up Xi Jinping's goal, set out at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development, of building a modern Chinese civilisation. Li asks what direction that work should take and argues that it rests on two lines of continuity: Marxism as the "soul vein" (hunmai) and excellent traditional Chinese culture as the "root vein" (genmai). The article, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2024, takes both from Xi's remark at the 20th Political Bureau's sixth collective study session that neither can be abandoned.

The article has three parts. The first treats traditional culture as the root, placing it within China's 5,000-year history, the humiliations after 1840 and the Party's present aim of a culturally strong socialist country. The second treats Marxism as the soul, through the Two Integrations. The third sets out three questions on which, Li says, "political clarity" is needed: how to understand Chinese civilisation, Marxism, and the Two Integrations.

In the first part, Li argues that cultural confidence, which the article calls more basic and more lasting than other forms of confidence, is needed to resist what Li calls a Western view of civilisation. In Li's account, that view treats Western modernity as the only modern civilisation and so confuses plurality with unity and equality with hierarchy. Li contrasts it with China's openness and inclusiveness, which Li sees as matching Marxism's own openness. In the second part, Li presents the First Integration (Marxism with China's concrete realities) and the Second Integration (Marxism with traditional culture) as two sides of one process. Li says traditional values such as "the world belongs to all" and "the people are the root of the state" fit scientific socialist values. Li concludes that without Marxism, modern civilisation lacks a soul and head, and without tradition it lacks a foundation and feet.

Li holds that the Two Integrations are the necessary path to a modern civilisation. In this account they rest on mutual fit, produce "a new cultural life form", and consolidate cultural subjectivity, which Li sees embodied in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Li describes Chinese civilisation as continuous, innovative, unified, inclusive and peaceful. On that basis Li says it follows that China will go its own way, and that national unity is the core of China's core interests. Read the original if you want to see how a senior Party historian ties the Two Integrations to the root-and-soul metaphor and to the project of a modern Chinese civilisation.
quoteEn: If, without the guidance of Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, one one-sidedly stresses inheriting and promoting excellent traditional Chinese culture and neglects its creative transformation and innovative development, then building a modern Chinese civilisation is tantamount to having no soul and no head.
quoteZh: 如果脱离了中国化时代化的马克思主义指导，片面强调继承和弘扬中华优秀传统文化，忽视了对中华优秀传统文化的创造性转化、创新性发展，中华民族现代文明建设就等于没有了灵魂和头脑。

glossary.literal: modern civilisation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A goal Xi Jinping set out at the June 2023 symposium on cultural inheritance and development. It refers to a modern civilisation that combines Marxism with traditional Chinese culture and goes with Chinese modernization.

The Party's formula for combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with excellent traditional Chinese culture. The second integration was added to official discourse in 2021–2023.
A Party concept, prominent since the 2010s, that stresses confidence in China's culture and in socialism with Chinese characteristics. It is counted among the Four-sphere Confidence.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology since 2017, written into the Party and state constitutions.

t: Advancing the building of a modern Chinese civilization through research on the history of Chinese civilization
zh: 以中华文明史研究推动中华民族现代文明建设
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 27 June 2024
paras: This newspaper commentary, published in June 2024, asks how research on the history of Chinese civilization should serve the building of a modern civilization of the Chinese nation, which Xi Jinping named a new cultural mission. Chen argues that history as a discipline should take this goal as its central task in the new era.

The article defines civilization as the sum of material, spiritual and institutional achievements. It then sets out four tasks: the Project to Trace the Origins of Chinese Civilization, scholarly explanation of civilization's "five outstanding characteristics", mutual learning among civilizations, and new ways of writing civilizational history.

On origins, Chen holds that the usual checklist of writing, bronzes, cities and ritual centres cannot fit every civilization. The author endorses the "Chinese approach" to civilizational criteria developed by the origins project: productive growth and cities, class differentiation, and kingship and the state. On the five characteristics (continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness, peacefulness), Chen calls for combining archaeology with documents and breaking the topic into case studies, such as the shift from mixed commandery-and-kingdom rule to commanderies and counties, or the coexistence of Song, Liao and Jin regimes. Chen also wants a civilizational history guided by historical materialism, with a holistic view, multidisciplinary work, and room for agricultural, steppe and maritime civilizations.

Chen concludes that building a modern civilization means creative transformation and innovative development of fine traditional culture, not a return to the past. Research should identify positive and modern elements in Chinese institutions and thought, strengthen historical consciousness and cultural confidence, and supply intellectual resources for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a short statement of how an archaeologist at CASS links civilization studies to current cultural policy.
quoteEn: The history of Chinese civilization is neither a synthesis of various specialised histories nor a fusion of general and specialised history, but must proceed under the guidance of historical materialism, start from the economic base, and focus on the civilization and progress of human society.
quoteZh: 中华文明史不是各种专史的综合,也不是通史与专史的融合,而是要在唯物史观的指导下,坚持从经济基础出发,聚焦人类社会的文明和进步。

glossary.en: a modern civilization of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A cultural goal announced by Xi Jinping in 2023 at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development. It is presented officially as building a new civilization on the basis of traditional Chinese culture and socialism.

glossary.en: the Project to Trace the Origins of Chinese Civilization
glossary.explanation: A multidisciplinary state-backed research programme, begun around 2002, that studies the origins and early development of Chinese civilization through archaeology and related sciences.
A formulation by Xi Jinping in 2023 describing Chinese civilization as marked by continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness.
The official term for China's path of modernization under Party leadership, presented as distinct from Western models.

glossary.zh: 创造性转化、创新性发展
glossary.explanation: An official formula for how traditional Chinese culture should be adapted to contemporary needs rather than simply preserved.

t: The value of Mao Zedong Thought in China–Africa diplomatic practice
zh: 毛泽东思想在中非外交实践中的价值意蕴
source: Journal of Xiangtan University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2024 no. 3
paras: He Jian and Liu Shuaijun ask how Mao Zedong Thought, and the diplomatic thinking within it, shaped China–Africa relations in the Mao era and what value it retains today. They argue that Mao's foreign-policy ideas guided the move from almost no contact to a relationship of mutual support. In their view these ideas have historical, theoretical and contemporary value, and they still offer guidance for present-day China–Africa ties.

The article has three parts. The first traces the history of China–Africa relations in four stages: early Chinese awareness of Africa before 1949, tentative contacts in 1949–54, the 1955 Bandung Conference, and aid and China's return to the United Nations in 1956–76. The second examines four strands of Mao's thinking: the three diplomatic guidelines of the early 1950s, the 'intermediate zone' idea, the international peace united front, and the theory of the three worlds. The third turns to the value of this legacy today.

The authors read each strand as raising Africa's place in China's strategy. Mao's 'intermediate zone' formulations of the 1940s–50s and 1960s, they say, first gave Africa a conceptual place, then made it a force China could unite with. The peace united front, expressed in the Bandung principle of 'seeking common ground while setting aside differences', is presented as the basis for equal, non-interfering relations. Chinese aid, cited at about 7.7 billion yuan from the 1950s to the 1970s, is credited with winning political support. The authors note that 16 of the 23 sponsors of the 1971 UN resolution, and 26 of the 76 states voting in favour, were African. They also interpret the three-worlds theory as an application of dialectical materialism and as a rebuilding of China's international discourse power.

The authors conclude that Mao-era thinking on national interest, independence and peaceful coexistence still helps China read the international situation and place itself within it. They describe the 'community with a shared future for mankind' as inheriting and going beyond Mao's diplomacy, and as moving China–Africa ties from 'all-weather friends' towards a China–Africa community with a shared future. They also hold that China's response to the 'two overall situations' draws on this legacy. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how Mao-era diplomatic doctrine is linked to China–Africa policy and to current foreign-policy discourse.
quoteEn: The theory of the 'three worlds' is, moreover, a practical application of the methodology of dialectical materialism in Marxist philosophy.
quoteZh: “三个世界”划分理论更是对马克思主义哲学当中辩证唯物主义方法论的实践运用。

glossary.explanation: A concept Mao Zedong set out in 1946 to describe the territories lying between the United States and the Soviet Union. In the 1960s it was revised into 'two intermediate zones'.

glossary.literal: theory of dividing the three worlds
glossary.explanation: Mao Zedong's early-1970s scheme placing the United States and the Soviet Union in the first world, other developed countries in the second, and developing countries in the third. China counted itself in the third.

glossary.en: seeking common ground while setting aside differences
glossary.explanation: A principle put forward by Zhou Enlai at the 1955 Bandung Conference. It stresses cooperation on shared aims despite differences in systems and ideology.
Mao-era idea of uniting all countries willing to resist hegemony and war, regardless of social system.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping-era foreign-policy concept calling for shared responsibility and cooperation among states. Official texts apply it to bilateral ties, including those with Africa.
Official formulation pairing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation with 'great changes unseen in a century' in the world. It is used to frame strategic planning.

t: The basic core, main features and value implications of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation
zh: 中华民族现代文明的基本内核、主要特征与价值意蕴
paras: Taking up Xi Jinping's call at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development to "build the modern civilization of the Chinese nation", Li Mengyun asks what this civilization consists of, how it is characterised and why it matters. The article argues that it is a Marxist-guided civilizational form with modern value orientations, rooted in fine traditional Chinese culture and carried forward through Chinese modernization.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the basic core of the concept, the second its main features, and the third its value implications. Li draws on Hegel's distinction between what is actual and what merely exists, on Marx and Engels, and on Xi's speeches. The article also refers to earlier scholarship on the concept's theoretical emergence, philosophical narrative and practical exploration.

On the core, Li argues that "modern" refers to a civilization's nature as well as its time. Western capitalist civilization, in Li's account, merely "exists" and lacks necessity, whereas the modern civilization of the Chinese nation is actual, inheriting and transforming the past while bearing the future. Its core has four elements: Marxism as guiding theory, fine traditional culture as intellectual root, Chinese modernization as practical basis, and the modernization of the human being as its value aim. Li identifies four features: inheritance, a people-centred character, inclusiveness and peacefulness. Western modern civilization is described as driven by the logic of capital and alienation, which the Chinese form is said to surpass.

Li presents four implications: continuing the Chinese historical cultural line, gathering strength for building a modern socialist country, advancing the Second Integration, and taking on the mission of constructing a new form of human civilization. The author contends that the project strengthens cultural confidence, helps coordinate material and cultural-ethical progress, and offers developing countries an alternative to the Western single model. Li also criticises Western theories of a "clash of civilizations" and civilizational superiority. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-theory account of how this concept is justified from Marxist and traditional sources, including its positioning against the West.
quoteEn: The modern civilization of the Chinese nation is a form of civilization with a modern value orientation, formed under the guidance of Marxism.
quoteZh: 中华民族现代文明是在马克思主义指导下形成的具有现代性价值指向的文明形态。

glossary.en: the modern civilization of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A concept put forward by Xi Jinping in June 2023 at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development, described as a new cultural mission of the new era. Scholars are still elaborating its content.

The official name for China's path of modernization under Party leadership, said to combine a huge population, common prosperity, balanced material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony with nature and peaceful development.

The Party formula, from Xi Jinping in 2023, for combining the basic tenets of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. It is the second of the Two Integrations, the first being with China's concrete realities.

keywords: modern civilization of the Chinese nation

t: The historic contribution of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics
zh: 中国特色社会主义政治经济学的历史性贡献
source: Social Sciences in China (Zhongguo shehui kexue), 2024 no. 4
paras: Zhang Yu asks what the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics has contributed to the development of Marxist political economy. The article argues that it has taken Marxist political economy, and especially its socialist branch, to a new stage. In Zhang's account, four features mark this advance: a distinct subjectivity, prominent originality, a complete system, and a rich body of theoretical results that state general principles.

The article first traces how Marxist political economy divides into a capitalist part rooted in Capital and a socialist part. It then follows the Chinese line: Mao Zedong's call to learn from the Soviet Union but find a separate path, the market-oriented reforms after reform and opening up, and Xi Jinping Thought on the economy since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Four sections follow, one for each feature. The first section covers the sources of subjectivity. The second lists some fifteen original theories. The third compares the traditional socialist economics textbook with the Chinese system. The fourth deals with the relation between the particular and the universal.

Zhang contends that the theory has subjectivity because of theoretical self-awareness, a distinctive economic form, a Marxist worldview and method, and practical achievements. Western economics is described as an ideologically loaded summary of Western experience, to be borrowed from critically rather than copied. Zhang says the Chinese theory differs from traditional socialist economics in four ways. It starts from the primary stage of socialism, takes the socialist market economy as its premise, borrows critically from Western economics, and widens its scope to basic economic institutions, the economic system, operation, development and opening up. On principles, Zhang distinguishes three kinds of development of Marxist theory: deepening it (public ownership alongside other forms), innovating (economic modernization) and correcting it (capital under socialism). Zhang rejects the view that Chinese theory is only an application of classical principles, and argues that general principles also rise from particular practice, as Marx drew his from Britain.

Zhang concludes that China, as the most developed real-world form of socialism, is the main object from which general principles of socialist political economy can now be drawn. The article presents Chinese socialism as a banner of twenty-first-century scientific socialism and as an option for developing countries. It calls on scholars to turn practical experience into a systematic economic doctrine. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese economists present Xi Jinping's economic thought as a theoretical advance within Marxism.
quoteEn: These views both uphold the Marxist basic principle of public ownership of the means of production and, proceeding from reality, set out the nature, position, role, specific features and forms of realisation of socialist public ownership in the primary stage of socialism, giving the principle new content.
quoteZh: 既坚持了马克思主义关于生产资料公有制的基本原理，又从实际出发阐明了处于社会主义初级阶段的社会主义公有制的性质、地位、作用、具体特点和实现形式，赋予了这一原理以新的内涵。

glossary.zh: 中国特色社会主义政治经济学
glossary.pinyin: Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì zhèngzhì jīngjìxué
glossary.en: the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics
glossary.explanation: The official name for the body of economic theory that Chinese authorities say sums up China's reform-era experience. Xi Jinping called for it to be developed from the 18th Party Congress (2012) onwards.

glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on the economy
glossary.explanation: The economic component of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Official sources describe it as the latest result of Chinese socialist political economy.
The official thesis that China is, and will long remain, in an early and underdeveloped phase of socialism. It is used to justify market mechanisms and mixed ownership.

keywords: political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics
Xi Jinping Thought on the economy

t: The contemporary significance of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation
zh: 中华民族现代文明的时代意蕴
paras: Following Xi Jinping's call at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development to build a modern civilization of the Chinese nation as a new cultural mission, Fang Zheng asks what this project means for its time. The article argues that the modern civilization of the Chinese nation embodies three qualities of the Communist Party's theoretical character: seeking truth from facts, keeping pace with the times, and upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground.

The article is organised in three sections, one for each quality. The first treats the concept as a summation of the Chinese nation's history, from ancient civilization through the modern humiliations to the Party-led revival. The second places it within a Marxist view of civilization, the development of the productive forces and the contrast between Western and Chinese paths to modernity. The third deals with Party leadership, cultural subjectivity and national spirit.

In the first section, Fang presents the concept as a systematic reading of socialist, Party, People's Republic, reform-era and national history. In the second, Fang argues that civilization and the productive forces are essentially linked, so that civilizational continuity requires rapid productive development. The author describes Western modernization as bound up with colonial plunder, neo-colonialism and cultural colonialism, and presents Chinese modernization as breaking the equation of modernization with Westernization. Marx and Engels, Fang notes, could not foresee a socialist modernization of a large, backward Eastern country, which had to be explored independently, with the Two Integrations as guidance. In the third section, Party leadership is called the key to building this civilization, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented as the expression of cultural subjectivity. The great founding spirit of the Party and the great national spirit are said to supply its spiritual content.

Fang concludes that the modern civilization of the Chinese nation is at bottom a socialist civilizational form and a marker of national rejuvenation. Only by adhering unwaveringly to Party leadership and Xi Jinping's cultural thought, the author contends, can its content be explained, its theoretical system built and its practical paths widened. Read the original if you want to see how Party-affiliated scholarship in 2024 justifies the concept of a modern Chinese civilization in Marxist and historical terms.
quoteEn: The modern civilization of the Chinese nation is, in the final analysis, a socialist form of civilization.
quoteZh: 中华民族现代文明归根到底是社会主义文明形态。

glossary.en: modern civilization of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A concept put forward by Xi Jinping in 2023 as part of the new cultural mission, referring to a modern form of Chinese civilization built under Party leadership on the basis of Marxism and traditional culture.
The Party's formula of combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture.
The Party's official term for China's own path to modernization, presented as distinct from the Western model.
A term in Xi Jinping's cultural thought for a culture's independent identity and capacity to stand and develop on its own foundations.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's current guiding ideology, written into its constitution in 2017.

keywords: modern civilization of the Chinese nation

t: Intellectual characteristics of the peaceful nature of Chinese civilization and its contemporary presentation
zh: 中华文明和平性的思想特点及其当代呈现
paras: Liu Feng takes up one of the "five outstanding characteristics" that Xi Jinping has attributed to Chinese civilization (continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness) and asks what philosophical roots lie behind its peaceful nature. The article argues that this peacefulness rests on Chinese philosophy's view of the cosmos as harmonious and on the doctrine of the unity of heaven and humanity. It holds that these roots shape the present-day Chinese commitment to peaceful development.

The article has four sections. It first sets out the ontological basis of peacefulness, drawing on the Laozi, the Book of Changes and the Song philosopher Zhang Zai's idea of "supreme harmony". It then examines the unity of heaven and humanity in three forms: following the seasons, correspondence between heaven and humanity as in Dong Zhongshu, and the unity of human virtue with heaven and earth in Confucian and Neo-Confucian thought. A third section identifies three features of the Chinese idea of harmony, and the last turns to its contemporary expression.

Liu's central claim concerns the three features of "harmony" (he). First, it is many-sided, linking self, family, society, nature and "all under heaven" in a single line from self-cultivation to bringing peace to the world. Second, it presupposes order and difference rather than erasing them. Liu draws on Yan Ying's contrast between harmony and sameness, on the Confucian pairing of ritual and music, and on the saying that "the gentleman seeks harmony but not conformity".
