On that basis the article argues that adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times has to be understood through its concrete historical settings. Cao holds that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era unites the localisation of Marxism in China with its adaptation to the age, and that the new context must be linked to earlier ones.

The article has five parts. It first clarifies concepts: the relation between 'Chinese' and 'of the times' content, and the universal significance of localised Marxism. It then sets out the setting in which Xi Jinping Thought emerged, at home and abroad since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Next it compares the settings of socialism with Chinese characteristics and Chinese modernization, and then the setting for combining Marxism with traditional Chinese culture. It closes with the Party's historical experience and the risks it faces.

Cao argues that 'of the times' is the key content of the formula, since each theoretical advance bears the mark of its period. In Cao's account the 'Chinese characteristics' formula originally contrasted with the Soviet and East European model, whereas Chinese modernization is defined against Western capitalist modernization. The author describes a favourable strategic window after the 1970s that was followed by Western containment after the 2008 financial crisis. From this the author concludes that opening up cannot be relied on and that self-reliance and independent innovation are needed. Cao also claims that a developing country on the capitalist road would be suppressed anyway, so only socialism can bring national rejuvenation. The cultural combination is presented as a defence against capitalist corrosion and against a revival of feudal ideas, the 'two preventions'.

Cao names three sources of risk for the Party: external containment by the West, divergent interests within society after market development, and corruption inside the Party. Cao calls for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the Party's self-reform, common prosperity and the Four-sphere Confidence. The present setting is described as composite: reform-era modernization, the new era and 'great changes unseen in a century' in the world. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar reads current theory through domestic and international history, and how the article frames risks to Party rule.
quoteEn: The 'of the times' content is an important part of the new leap in adapting Marxism to China, and contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism are concentrated in the new-era thought of the Chinese communists represented by Comrade Xi Jinping.
quoteZh: 时代化内涵是马克思主义中国化新飞跃的重要内容，当代中国马克思主义和21世纪马克思主义集中体现为以习近平同志为主要代表的中国共产党人的新时代思想。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: An official formula for the Party's project of applying Marxist principles to Chinese conditions and to the demands of the present era. It is used to describe the Party's theoretical innovation.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīnshídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017 and 2018.
The official term for China's path of modernization. It was elaborated at the 20th Party Congress (2022) as socialist modernization under Party leadership.
Confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
An official term for the Party's efforts to address its own problems, including through anti-corruption campaigns.
An official goal of prosperity shared by all, presented as a feature of socialism.

t: Rebuilding the community: a historical-materialist examination of Chinese modernization
zh: 共同体的重建：中国式现代化的历史唯物主义审视
paras: Yan Song asks how Chinese modernization relates to the problem of community under modernity. The article argues that Western modernization dissolved traditional communities and replaced them with a "false community" serving one class against another. Chinese modernization, in Yan's reading, rebuilds community, and this rebuilding is expressed in what the author calls Xi Jinping's thought on community. Yan says existing scholarship treats individual community concepts separately and neglects their overall unity and internal links.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs, mainly from Marx and Engels, how Western modernization dissolved community. It covers the split between civil society and the political state, the atomised individual, the "false community" of the capitalist state, and the consequences within nations and across the world market. The second part sets out four forms of community in Xi's discourse: the community with a shared future for mankind (including its cyberspace version), the Chinese nation as a community, the social governance community, and the community of life between humans and nature. The third part assesses the theoretical, institutional and practical significance of this rebuilding.

Yan argues that Western modernization produced atomised wage-labourers, whose lives are governed by commodity and capital fetishism and by reified relations. Welfare and citizenship are described as devices that stabilise capitalist rule. Against this, the four forms of community are presented as one system, each tied to a feature of Chinese modernization: a huge population, common prosperity, harmony between humans and nature, and peaceful development. Yan adds that Chinese modernization is socialist, so its value orientation is communism and Marx's "real community". The author also contends that it skipped the bloody primitive accumulation of the West by following a "parallel" rather than "serial" path.

Yan concludes that rebuilding community is one comparative advantage of Chinese modernization and shows the strengths of the socialist system. The author also presents it as an option for developing countries that want modernization without losing independence. The framework is described as unfinished and still developing, and not a return to premodern community. Instead it is said to combine the "common good" of traditional communities with the features of modern society. Read the original if you want to see how Xi Jinping's community concepts are fitted into a Marxist critique of Western modernity and linked to Chinese modernization.
quoteEn: One comparative advantage of the path of Chinese modernization is that, facing a modern world in which capital logic has dissolved community and produced many problems of modernity, it has reshaped a new paradigm of communal life for humankind.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化道路比较优势之一就体现在中国式现代化面向资本逻辑主导下共同体消解的现代世界及其产生的种种现代性问题，重塑了人类生活的新共同体范式

glossary.explanation: The official term for China's path of modernization under Communist Party leadership, set out prominently at the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from the Western model.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept associated with Xi Jinping. It calls for cooperation, peace and shared development in international relations.

glossary.en: the Chinese nation as a community
glossary.explanation: A concept stressing a shared national identity above the identities of China's 56 officially recognised ethnic groups. The Party promotes it as "forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation".

A concept first put forward at the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019). It describes governance in which Party committees lead, government is responsible, and society and the public take part.
A goal of shared wealth for all the people, emphasised by Xi Jinping as a feature of socialism.

t: The expression and characteristics of whole-process people's democracy from the perspective of "China's governance"
zh: 中国之治视域下全过程人民民主的表达与特征
paras: Writing amid what the article calls a "great change unseen in a century", Zhang Shuhua asks how China answers the question of democracy, and argues that the answer is whole-process people's democracy. The author places this democracy within "China's governance" (zhongguo zhi zhi), a concept treated as the political dimension of Chinese modernization and as the counterpart of what Zhang describes as growing disorder in the West.

The article has six sections. It sets out the theoretical and international significance of China's governance; compares Chinese modernization with Western and Soviet-bloc paths; and lists the civilizational traits and advantages of China's governance. It then draws out the "principles" (zhongguo zhi li) behind it, traces the Chinese people's search for democracy from the late Qing to the new era, and ends with the characteristics of whole-process people's democracy. Zhang draws on foreign scholars such as Barry Buzan, George Lawson, Martin Jacques and Russian sinologists, and also notes critics such as Nadège Rolland.

Zhang contends that China's governance rests on an independent path rather than imitation of foreign models, on Party leadership as a stable political core, and on the people's principal position. Politically it is marked by stability, development, practicality, coordination and efficacy, and it unifies democracy, order and efficiency. On this basis Zhang says it has produced a "new view of democracy", a comprehensive view of development and a view of global governance linked to a community with a shared future for mankind. Whole-process people's democracy is presented as rooted in Chinese soil, socialist in essence, consensus-based, effective through election, consultation, decision-making, management and oversight, and continually innovating. Zhang cites grassroots legislative liaison offices as an example. By contrast, the author portrays Western democracy as suffering institutional failure and as a source of global disorder.

Zhang concludes that whole-process people's democracy is China's choice and reply to the world's question about democracy. It must uphold the organic unity of Party leadership, the people as masters of the country and law-based governance. The author holds that it offers Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach to political civilization, and that no country has a monopoly on democracy. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese political science presents whole-process people's democracy as a comparative and civilizational claim against Western democracy.
quoteEn: Democracy must suit a country's basic national conditions, answer to the people's needs, be practised by the people and be tested by the people.
quoteZh: 民主必须与一个国家的基本国情相适应，服从于人民需求，由人民来实践，由人民来检验。

glossary.explanation: A formulation Xi Jinping advanced in 2019 and later, written into the 20th Party Congress report (2022). Officially it describes a democracy that covers every stage from election to consultation, decision-making, management and oversight.
The official name for China's path to modernization, set out by Xi Jinping and the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.
A slogan used since the 19th Party Central Committee's Fourth Plenum (2019) for the order and governing effectiveness of China's system. In the article it is set against "Western disorder".

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept for international relations, centred on joint consultation, development and shared benefit. The article links it to a shift from national to common governance.

t: Marx's decoding of the process of modernization and the distinctiveness of Chinese modernization
zh: 马克思对现代化进程的解码与中国式现代化的独特性
source: Journal of Fujian Normal University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2023 no. 1
paras: Responding to the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which says Chinese modernization shares features with other countries' modernization but has Chinese characteristics, Liu Weibing asks how to grasp its distinctiveness on the basis of modernization's general laws. The article argues that Marx, though he never proposed a concept of modernization, in fact developed a theory of it, and that this theory lets us see what sets Chinese modernization apart. For Liu, the distinctiveness rests on adapting to national conditions while using the Party's historical initiative.

The article has three parts. The first traces three shifts in Marx's logic: from alienation to production to capital. The second sets out the dual character of modernization as a historical process. The third turns to Chinese modernization, which Liu discusses under three headings: Party leadership, the free and all-round development of the human being, and the move from spontaneous to conscious history.

In Liu's reading, Marx moved from criticising political, labour and historical alienation (1844 texts), through the division of labour and the forces and relations of production, to capital as a social relation whose self-valorisation shapes production, distribution, exchange and consumption. From this Liu derives three paired features of modernization: time acceleration with spatial expansion, totalisation with difference, and alienation with liberation. Marx, Liu stresses, criticised capitalist modernity rather than modernization as such, and allowed the East a path that might avoid the 'Caudine Forks' of capitalism. Chinese modernization, Liu argues, is led by a mission-driven party that differs from parliamentary parties, and the Party's self-reform guides the broader social revolution. Capital is treated as a means rather than the subject of modernization. Through the socialist market economy, public ownership as the mainstay and distribution according to work, surplus labour time is said to be converted into free time for people. Liu describes the process as conscious in theory, values and path.

Liu concludes that studying Chinese modernization requires Marxist perspectives, knowledge of modernization's general laws, and attention to Chinese conditions and Party practice. Chinese modernization, in this account, will increasingly show world-historical significance and may open a new form of human civilization. Read the original if you want a Marxist-theoretical case, framed through Capital and the Grundrisse, for why Chinese modernization is held to differ from capitalist modernization.
quoteEn: Compared with other models of modernization, Chinese modernization makes clear that capital is only a means of modernization, that the subject of modernization is the human being, and that its core is the modernization of the human being.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化相比较于其他现代化模式，明确了资本只是现代化的手段，现代化的主体是人，核心是人的现代化。

glossary.explanation: The Party's official term for China's path of modernization under Communist Party leadership. It was given prominence at the 20th Party Congress (2022).
A characterisation of the Communist Party of China as driven by a historical mission, in contrast with parliamentary parties that represent part of the electorate.
An official term for the Party's efforts to correct its own problems and maintain its vanguard character, stressed in Xi Jinping-era discourse.
The official name for China's economic system since the 1990s, combining a market mechanism with public ownership as the mainstay.

glossary.en: a new form of human civilization
glossary.explanation: A Party phrase for the civilizational outcome claimed for Chinese modernization, presented as an alternative to the Western modernization model.

t: Understanding and grasping the scientific content of the theory of Chinese modernization
zh: 认识和把握中国式现代化理论的科学内涵
paras: Writing shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Pei Changhong asks what the theory of Chinese modernization rests on and what makes it scientific. The article argues that the theory, systematised in the Congress report as part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, rests on three bases: the Party's understanding of its own governing laws, of the laws of socialist construction, and of the laws of human social development.

The article is organised in three main sections, followed by a short conclusion. The first treats the practice and theory of scientific socialism, the second the logic of Marxist political economy, and the third the logic of historical materialism. Pei compares China with Britain, the United States, Japan, South Korea, India, Latin America and Africa, and traces the evolution of Party formulations from the Four Modernizations to the Five-sphere Integrated Plan and the Four-pronged Comprehensive Strategy.

In the first section Pei contends that Chinese modernization differs from the Western path in its political foundation (a people's republic led by the Party rather than a bourgeois republic), its basic economic system (public ownership as the mainstay, a socialist market economy centred on the people rather than on capital), its values, its peaceful development and its independent, self-reliant opening up. The second section holds that China's path differs in the government–market relationship, in compressing industrialisation, informatisation, urbanisation and agricultural modernization into parallel development, and in aiming at the people's wellbeing rather than GDP alone, with the digital economy and modernised governance as markers. The third section draws on Marx to argue that civilisation is the overall expression of a given level of productive forces, that it is diverse, and that exchange and mutual learning among civilisations are its norm. Pei criticises Huntington's clash-of-civilizations thesis and the 'end of history' idea.

Pei concludes that the theory is an original theoretical achievement that deepens scientific socialism, Marxist political economy and historical materialism. In the article's account, it shows that modernization is not a Western monopoly, that it requires Party leadership in China, and that it offers other developing countries seeking independence a new option. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a leading economist in the Party-state system grounds Chinese modernization in Marxist theory and contrasts it with Western and other developing-country paths.
quoteEn: Modernization is not the patent of Western civilization.
quoteZh: 现代化不是西方文明的专利。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution in 2017 and the state constitution in 2018.
The official concept of China's own path to modernization, elaborated in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Deng Xiaoping used the phrase in 1979 and 1983.
The overall layout of socialist construction across economic, political, cultural, social and ecological civilisation spheres, formulated at the 18th Party Congress (2012).
Xi Jinping's strategic layout from 2014: building a moderately prosperous society in all respects, deepening reform, governing the country by law and governing the Party strictly.

t: Five methods of Mao Zedong's investigation and study
zh: 毛泽东开展调查研究的五种方法
paras: Xu Zhongyuan, writing in Study Times in April 2023, presents Mao Zedong as the Party's model of personally practising investigation and study (diaocha yanjiu). The article opens with Mao's remark that when he was at a loss for a solution, he went to investigate, and that once he had done so, the answer appeared. Xu's thesis is that Mao's investigations were distinctive because they followed identifiable methods, which the piece sets out as five.

The text is a short commentary built from anecdotes rather than theoretical exposition. It draws on episodes from the Jinggangshan and Jiangxi period, the Yan'an years, the early People's Republic and Mao's last decades. Each method is introduced with a heading-like phrase and illustrated by one or more stories involving ordinary villagers, bodyguards, newly appointed ambassadors and commanders.

The first method is to read people's faces and manner (chayan guanse): Xu recounts Mao telling the cadre Jiang Hua to observe how villagers eat, dress and feel. Second, Mao used his security guards, sending them home to investigate rural conditions and asking for their letters. Third, he found major issues by reading newspapers and historical works, for example choosing northern Shaanxi as the Long March destination after a newspaper report, and urging a regional commander to read Gu Zuyu's geographical work. Fourth, he took villagers' grievances and complaints as prompts for inquiry, as when he looked to his own policy failures after a farmer's angry remarks and then helped cut a grain levy. Fifth, he helped people solve practical problems while investigating, citing the Shazhouba well, his concern over the Yellow River, and a conversation with an unrecognised fisherman at Beidaihe.

Xu concludes implicitly through these cases that Mao's investigation combined genuine feeling for the people, self-examination and attention to detail. The article does not draw explicit policy lessons, but it presents these practices as an example for cadres. Read the original if you want a compact set of anecdotes from official Party commemorative writing on Mao's working style, or if you study how investigation and study is being promoted as a model of leadership practice.
quoteEn: Mao Zedong cared deeply for the people, with a sincere feeling that came from the heart, and was accustomed to treating the process of investigating among the masses as a process of helping them solve difficulties in production and daily life.
quoteZh: 毛泽东对人民群众关心备至，有一股发自内心的真挚情感，习惯把向人民群众作调查的过程当作是帮助人民群众解决生产生活困难的过程。

glossary.explanation: A Party working method of gathering first-hand information from the grassroots and analysing it before making decisions. It is associated with Mao Zedong's 1930s writings and has been repeatedly promoted in Party campaigns, including in 2023.
An idiom for judging people's moods from their speech and expressions. Mao used it to mean observing how ordinary people eat, dress and feel as a first step in understanding their lives.
The Red Army's retreat of 1934–36 from the Jiangxi base area to northern Shaanxi, a foundational episode in Party history.

t: Advancing Chinese modernization in the historical process of the new era
zh: 在新时代历史进程中推进中国式现代化
paras: Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Song Caifa asks how Chinese modernization was established, how it advances in the new era, and what it contributes to humankind. The article argues that Chinese modernization is socialist modernization under Communist Party leadership, rests on the basic socialist economic system, and has created a "new form of human civilization" that offers developing countries an alternative to Western modernization.

The article has three main sections. The first traces how the Party established and leads Chinese modernization, from Sun Yat-sen's early blueprints through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second links modernization to the transformation of the principal social contradiction in the new era. The third assesses the world significance of Chinese modernization and its relation to a community with a shared future for mankind. Throughout, Song draws heavily on Xi Jinping's speeches and Party documents.

Song's central moves are as follows. First, Party leadership and public ownership as the mainstay of the economy are presented as the foundations of modernization: the nature of ownership shapes production relations, so modernization must be "of all the people" and move from public ownership to common ownership to common prosperity. Second, the shift in the principal contradiction, now between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development, defines modernization's priorities. Song cites the elimination of absolute poverty, the passage from a moderately prosperous society to a modern socialist country, and high-quality development as the route to common prosperity. Third, the author contends that Chinese modernization breaks with Eurocentric and single-model theories and surpasses capital-centred, polarising and expansionist Western paths as well as the rigid Soviet model. Song also criticises a minority view that stressing a Chinese model means self-isolation, and rejects "universal values" promoted by Western hegemonism.

Song concludes that Chinese modernization is an original contribution that rewrites the world map of modernization, given China's population of over 1.4 billion, and that it enriches scientific socialism in the twenty-first century. The author adds that modernization is a stage in socialist development, not its final aim, which remains communism. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese academic writing presents the Party's official narrative of modernization, with extensive references to Party documents.
quoteEn: Chinese modernization is the theoretical sublimation of the practice of China's modernization drive, and a landmark conceptual category.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化是中国现代化建设实践的理论升华，是一个具有标志性意义的概念范畴。

glossary.explanation: The official Party concept of modernization led by the Communist Party and adapted to China's conditions. The article traces the phrase to Deng Xiaoping in 1979 and to Xi Jinping's elaboration of it at the 20th Party Congress.
A concept the article says Xi Jinping formally put forward in 2021. It describes Chinese modernization as a civilizational model distinct from Western capitalist modernization.

A goal of prosperity shared by all the people, which the Party leadership has given great prominence since the 18th Party Congress. It is presented as the opposite of polarisation between rich and poor.

A Party formulation of the main contradiction in society at a given stage. Since the 19th Party Congress (2017) it has been defined as that between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development.

glossary.zh: 社会主义基本经济制度
glossary.explanation: The official formula combining public ownership as the mainstay with diverse forms of ownership, distribution according to work as the mainstay, and the socialist market economy. It was formally defined in this form at the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019).
The first of the 'Two Centenary Goals', declared achieved in 2021. It is linked in the article to the elimination of absolute poverty.

t: A three-dimensional logical examination of the emergence of contemporary "soft" historical nihilism
zh: 当代软性历史虚无主义思潮登场的三维逻辑审视
paras: Cheng and Gao take up what they call "soft" historical nihilism, which they present as a recent variant of historical nihilism. They argue that, after sustained criticism by the Party, the state and academia, historical nihilism has taken a more concealed form, with subtler methods that make it easier to mislead people's understanding of history. Their thesis is that this variant can be understood, and countered, by examining three connected logics: its intellectual roots, its real-world conditions and its inner mechanism, all from the standpoint of historical materialism.

The article is organised in three sections. The first, the "ideological logic", traces soft historical nihilism to postmodernism and to nihilism in the line of Nietzsche, Heidegger and Weber. The second, the "practical logic", looks at the domestic and external environment and at cyberspace. The third, the "mechanism logic", examines the ideological impact of the trend and the way it distorts historical narrative. The authors illustrate their claims with examples drawn from the War of Resistance against Japan, representations of Mao Zedong, and comparisons of Republican-era and early People's Republic economic data.

The authors argue that postmodern historiography, with its stress on the reader's subjective reading of history as "text", supplies the root of the trend, while nihilism supplies its philosophical base by negating historical value, especially the Communist Party's leadership and the socialist path. In their account, it flourishes because mainstream criticism has forced a softer disguise, because visual and entertainment culture and Western consumerist and ideological influence give it channels, and because the internet speeds its spread through memes, parody videos and self-media. They contend that its content assaults historical materialism in ontology, by promoting subjectivism and a "heroes make history" view, and in epistemology, by promoting subjective truth. Its core method, they say, is narrative distortion: it misuses microhistory to decentre narrative, positivist historiography to blur objectivity, and comparative history to steer values, as in the \"two 30 years\" argument.

Cheng and Gao conclude that, whatever form it takes, historical nihilism remains nihilistic about history, so criticism of it is an important task for safeguarding ideological security. They call both for exposing its substance through the "weapon of criticism" and for removing its real-world foundations through the "criticism of weapons". Concretely, they propose stronger study of Party history and national history, a cleaner climate of public opinion and deeper understanding of historical materialism. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese academic writing defines and categorises the latest forms of historical nihilism and the cases it cites.
quoteEn: However historical nihilism changes the form in which it appears, its nihilistic essence regarding history will not change.
quoteZh: 历史虚无主义无论如何转变呈现形态，其对于历史的虚无本质不会改变。

glossary.explanation: A term used in official and academic Chinese discourse for views seen as denying or belittling the history of the Communist Party, the revolution and socialism. It is a key target of Party ideological campaigns since the 18th Party Congress (2012).
The authors' label for a supposedly more covert, entertainment-oriented and implicit form of historical nihilism, spread through insinuation, parody and online media rather than open denunciation.

The Marxist theory of history that treats material production and social existence as basic to historical development. The authors use it as the standpoint from which they criticise subjectivist readings of history.
A concept in Chinese Party-state discourse that treats the stability of the dominant ideology as part of national security, which is why opposing erroneous trends of thought is stressed.

t: How a community with a shared future for mankind changes the world
zh: 人类命运共同体何以改变世界
paras: Chen Shuguang asks what the Chinese proposal to build a community with a shared future for mankind contributes to global governance and to world history. The article argues that the proposal changes how global governance is conceived, offers a vision of international order, and marks out a new form of human civilization. It also holds that the proposal opens room for socialism and capitalism to coexist and sets the programme for the present stage of world history. Chen presents it as a contemporary Chinese form of the Marxist theory of world history and universal intercourse.

The text is organised in five parts: a shift in the paradigm of global governance thinking; the Chinese proposal for reconstructing world order; a new form of civilization; a contemporary design for coexistence of the two systems; and a programme of action for world history. Chen draws on Marx's idea of world history, Durkheim's "organic solidarity", Hegel on relations between states, and Western authors such as Huntington and Michael Barr. The article also cites speeches by Xi Jinping and Deng Xiaoping.

Chen's central claim is that the existing order is a "centre–periphery" structure serving transnational capital. On this account, Western-led governance no longer fits the material content of globalization, so a crisis arises between its "social form" and that content. Against this, the community with a shared future replaces homogeneous, linear and subject–object thinking with pluralist, complex and intersubjective thinking. It is said to rest on five concepts of equal status, common security, cooperative development, civilizational diversity and ecological harmony. Chen insists it reforms the UN-centred system rather than overthrowing it, and denies that it is nationalist or an "Eastern-centrism". Drawing on Marx's "two never" principle, Chen holds that capitalism still dominates the world while the balance is shifting "east rises, west declines". The community is therefore the only realistic option, ahead of a "true community" that remains the long-term goal.

Chen concludes that the community with a shared future for mankind is China's contribution to international relations theory, a banner of new civilization, and the stage-specific goal of world history, to be pursued through six action plans. These include the Belt and Road Initiative and the Global Development, Global Security and Global Civilization Initiatives. Chen acknowledges that the task is long, faces unilateralism and Cold War thinking, and is not the end of human emancipation. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese Marxist theoretical defence of the concept, set within world-history and two-systems debates.
quoteEn: Building a community with a shared future for mankind is not meant to reconcile the contradictions between the two systems or to gloss over problems, but to open a new path of intercourse between states of the two systems towards lasting world peace.
quoteZh: 构建人类命运共同体，不是为了调和两制国家的矛盾，不是为了粉饰太平，而是为了开创世界永久和平的两制国家交往新路。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2012–13 as China's vision for international relations and global governance, stressing shared interests, equality and cooperation among states.
A Chinese infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative launched in 2013, linking China with countries across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.

Marx's statement in the 1859 Preface that no social order perishes before its productive forces are fully developed, and new relations never appear before their material conditions mature. Chinese theorists use it to argue for long coexistence of capitalism and socialism.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Building a discourse system for institutions from the perspective of conceptual history
zh: 概念史视角下的制度话语体系建构
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today, 30 March 2023, p. 3
paras: Yang Binbin asks how a discourse system for the institutions of socialism with Chinese characteristics can be built so that institutional confidence is strengthened and China's institutional story is told well. The commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2023, argues that conceptual history, which traces how concepts evolve in order to present the underlying historical logic, is a feasible path. Yang holds that this discourse is a developing and open system whose concepts, assertions and propositions have different historical sources, cultural roots and practical uses.

The article does not survey schools of conceptual history in detail. It notes that social history, the history of ideas and the history of words are distinct approaches, and says the method as a whole is valuable for examining a concept's historical starting point, logical starting point, semantic turning points and internal features. Yang then sorts institutional concepts under three headings: cultural origin, historical position and form of present-day generation. Each heading yields a threefold typology.

By cultural origin, Yang distinguishes endogenous or indigenous concepts, characterised by originality; exogenous or imported concepts, whose meaning shifts in transfer into Chinese; and fusion or interactive concepts, in which old Chinese terms receive new content from Party practice, which Yang links to the Two Integrations. By historical position, there are summarising or reflective concepts (historical), guiding or anticipatory concepts (future-oriented, normative) and responsive or judgemental concepts (tied to present reality, often combining fact and value). By form of generation, there are inherited, borrowed and transformed concepts, plus a case of concepts re-imported. Yang insists that concepts must be read in their specific historical context, using historical materialism, or the result is misattribution and unfair criticism of predecessors.

Yang concludes that bringing conceptual history into the study of the history of socialism with Chinese characteristics, the Communist Party, reform and opening up, the People's Republic and socialist development has real value. In Yang's account it offers a window onto building China's own knowledge system and onto the transformation of traditional culture. It would also help excavate discourse resources, make institutional explanation more self-aware and thorough, and show the values and wisdom in China's political path. Read the original if you want a compact typology of how Chinese scholars classify the sources of institutional concepts and a sense of how conceptual history is being enlisted for discourse construction.
quoteEn: Concepts are a historical, fluid form of expression, and conceptual-history methods can strengthen the tracing and analysis of concepts in China's distinctive political theory, political practice and political institutions.
quoteZh: 概念是一种历史性的流动表达，通过概念史的研究方法加强对中国特色政治理论、政治实践、政治制度中的概念追溯与辨析

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's path and system since reform and opening up, combining Marxist principles with China's conditions.
Official formula for combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture.
Confidence in the socialist system with Chinese characteristics, part of the official 'Four-sphere Confidence' formula.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in China in 1978.

t: The influence of traditional Chinese culture on the early spread of Marxism in China
zh: 中国传统文化对马克思主义在中国早期传播的影响
source: Journal of Social Sciences of Hunan Normal University, 2023 no. 2
paras: Wu Zengli and Hu Peng ask how traditional Chinese culture shaped the early transmission of Marxism in China. Writing in the framework of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, they argue that the process of making Marxism Chinese was also one of continual influence by traditional culture. The influence was complex: it created tension, steered the selection and interpretation of Marxist content, and made transmission both winding and gradual.

The authors define the early-transmission period as running from 1899, when the missionary Timothy Richard's Datong xue first mentioned Marx and socialism in Chinese, to the late 1920s. The article has three main sections: how traditional culture affected the entry of Marxism, the content that was chosen and how it was interpreted, and the course of dissemination. It draws on figures such as Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu, Liang Qichao, Sun Yat-sen, Qu Qiubai, Hu Shi and Mao Zedong, and on press and education statistics.

In the first section, Wu and Hu stress the heterogeneity of Confucian-centred, agrarian culture and Marxism, which they describe as a modern Western doctrine that arrived amid anti-Confucian radicalism. They argue, however, that the decline of traditional culture opened conditions for Marxism: the end of the examination system and the monarchy, the new culture movement, a changed view of the West, a booming periodical press, and a new-style educated intelligentsia. In the second section they argue that Chinese intellectuals combined old and new and kept Chinese needs central. They often rendered socialism in traditional terms such as the Great Harmony, the well-field system or equalising wealth, and emphasised different parts of Marxism according to practical needs. The authors say this made early understanding partial and unsystematic. In the third section they claim that cultural inertia, habitual thinking, custom and warlord repression slowed transmission. They also hold that the openness of Chinese culture and its affinity with Marxist values, as in the Sinicisation of Buddhism, aided it.

The authors conclude that traditional culture, as a rich resource, helped Marxism take root in Chinese soil. They add that influence ran both ways: Marxism now guides the creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture. They present a precise grasp of the fit between fine traditional culture and Marxism as necessary for developing contemporary Chinese Marxism. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-rich account of the cultural-historical conditions and mechanisms of Marxism's early reception in China, as presented in current Chinese scholarship.
quoteEn: Traditional Chinese culture had an important influence on the early introduction of Marxism into China, on the choice of its content, on the course of its dissemination and on the effects it achieved.
quoteZh: 中国传统文化对马克思主义在中国早期的传入、内容选择、传播过程及效果发挥等均产生了重要影响。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.literal: Sinicisation and modernisation (of the age) of Marxism
glossary.explanation: The official formula for applying Marxism to China's concrete conditions and to each historical period. It was elaborated in Party documents, including the 20th Party Congress report (2022).
An intellectual movement from about 1915 that criticised Confucian tradition and promoted science, democracy and vernacular writing. It prepared the ground for the spread of socialist ideas.
A Confucian ideal of a world of shared public good, used by late Qing and early Republican thinkers to explain socialism.

t: New understandings of the essence of socialism
zh: 关于社会主义本质的新认识
source: Journal of Shanxi University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2022 no. 6
paras: Bao Xinjian takes up what he calls a fundamental question of socialist theory and practice: what the essence of socialism is. Writing thirty years after Deng Xiaoping's 1992 southern tour talks, he argues that Deng's definition of socialism's essence was an original contribution, and that Xi Jinping's thinking has developed it into a fuller, four-dimensional formulation suited to the new era.

The article has three parts. The first assesses Deng's definition: liberating and developing the productive forces, eliminating exploitation, eliminating polarisation and ultimately achieving common prosperity. The second reconstructs Xi's statements on the essence of socialism and condenses them into a new formulation. The third draws out what this means for grasping socialism's essence comprehensively in the new development stage. Bao relies heavily on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Deng and Xi, and on the 2021 Party resolution on its century of struggle.

Bao argues that Marx, Engels and Lenin never systematically defined the essence of socialism, and that Mao's exploration was marred by errors such as "taking class struggle as the key link". In his account Deng clarified the relationship between essence, characteristics and principles, and freed thinking from disputes over whether a measure is "socialist or capitalist". For Bao, Deng's definition also kept reform and opening up on course. Bao then summarises Xi's contribution as a new formulation: upholding Marxist party leadership and the people's position as masters of the country; fully liberating and developing the productive forces; upholding fairness and justice and achieving common prosperity; and promoting all-round social progress and human development. Each element corresponds to a level: fundamental nature, mode of production, core values and ultimate goal. Bao contrasts the "people-centred logic" of socialism with the "logic of capital".

Bao concludes that, in the new development stage within the primary stage of socialism, the essence of socialism must be grasped as a whole. He calls for upholding the principle of putting the people first, keeping to the socialist market economy with an effective market and a capable government, and giving greater weight to common prosperity and all-round human development. These measures also include regulating capital and curbing its disorderly expansion. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theory account of how Deng's definition of socialism is presented as continuing into Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.
quoteEn: The essence of socialism is to uphold the leadership of a Marxist party and the people's position as masters of the country, fully liberate and develop the productive forces, safeguard fairness and justice and achieve common prosperity, and promote all-round social progress and the free and all-round development of the human being.
quoteZh: 社会主义的本质，是坚持马克思主义政党领导、坚持人民当家作主，全面解放生产力、发展生产力，维护公平正义、达到共同富裕，促进社会全面进步、实现人的全面发展。

glossary.explanation: A goal of shared wealth for all the people. Deng Xiaoping named it as the final aim of socialism, and Xi Jinping has made it a central policy theme.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official name for Xi Jinping's body of ideas, written into the Party constitution in 2017.
The official judgement that China is still in an early, long stage of socialist development. It was formalised in the 1980s and underpins Party policy on the market and mixed ownership.
A Xi-era principle holding that development should serve the people's interests and wellbeing. The Party presents it as the core of its governing philosophy.

t: An economic interpretation of Chinese modernization: a "six-in-one" logical framework
zh: 中国式现代化的经济学阐释：“六位一体”的逻辑框架
source: Social Science Journal (Shehui kexue jikan), 2023 no. 2
paras: Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhou Mi and Liu Lifan ask how Chinese modernization can be explained in economic terms. They argue that existing studies mostly restate official documents and leave its logic unclear. To fill the gap they propose a "six-in-one" framework and derive from it a set of implementation paths.

The article opens by tracing the idea of modernization from the 1950s "four modernizations" to Deng Xiaoping's 1979 use of the term. It then reviews foreign theories (Rostow's stages, Chenery's three-stage account) and Chinese scholarship on industrial, technological and social modernization. It then sets out the framework and its six strands. It ends with six paths for putting the framework into practice, and a short conclusion.

The framework has six parts: government action as an endogenous variable; a return to the labour theory of value; active matching of heterogeneous labour to the national economic circulation; effective combination of supply and demand; guidance by a multi-level vision linking people, nation and world; and high-quality development. The authors contrast Western modernization, which they say rests on a technology theory of value, with a Chinese path that combines it with the labour theory of value. They argue that Smith, Ricardo and Marx all assumed homogeneous labour, whereas Chinese practice recognises productive, research, cognitive and distributive labour. They describe four stages of matching: distributive labour with natural resources, productive labour with foreign capital, research labour with knowledge, and entrepreneurs' cognitive labour with the market. They present the government's roles as guide, shock absorber and amplifier, citing dual-track pricing and local experimentation as examples.

The authors conclude that Chinese modernization has a complete logical framework and is a blueprint for future modernized states. They propose six paths: upholding Party leadership to modernize governance; cultivating craftspeople, scientists, entrepreneurs and officials; unblocking production, distribution, circulation and consumption; meeting varied demand through measures on housing, trade and rural consumption; pursuing a national vision tied to a community with a shared future for mankind; and advancing high-quality development. Read the original if you want an economist's attempt to build a systematic theoretical scheme around Chinese modernization, including a heterogeneous-labour argument that revises the classical labour theory of value.
quoteEn: The source of Chinese modernization is labour; Chinese modernization is a combination of the technology theory of value and the labour theory of value.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化的源泉是劳动，中国式现代化是技术价值论与劳动价值论的结合

glossary.explanation: The Party's term for China's own path to modernization, led by the Communist Party. The 20th Party Congress report (2022) listed its essential requirements.
An official policy goal that shifts emphasis from speed of growth to quality, efficiency and balance.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's formula for China's vision of international relations, stressing shared development and cooperation.

t: Grasping the dialectical thinking in the strategic thought of self-reform
zh: 科学把握自我革命战略思想中的辩证思维
paras: Wu Fulai takes up the strategic thought on the Party's self-reform that took shape after the 18th Party Congress (2012) and that the 20th Party Congress (2022) presented as the Party's "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and fall. Wu notes that scholarship has concentrated on theoretical sources, history, discourse and experience, while the dialectical thinking behind self-reform has been little studied. The author argues that this gap feeds a mistaken view that the Party has changed from a "revolutionary party" into a "governing party". The article's thesis is that self-reform follows the dialectical negation of the negation, and that this logic explains its meaning, its practice and its future course.

The article has three main parts plus a short conclusion. The first traces the changing meaning of "revolution" in Chinese and Western contexts and reads self-reform through five lenses: the subject–object relation, historical experience, contradiction, the Party's character, and escape from the historical cycle. The second identifies four pairs of dialectical unity in practice. The third sets out routes for opening a "new realm" of self-reform in the new journey.

In Wu's account, self-reform is the Party taking itself as the object of revolution. This is possible, the author says, because the Party has no special interests apart from those of the country, the nation and the people. Western parties, by contrast, are described as defending particular class interests and therefore incapable of such self-reform. In practice, Wu finds dialectical unity between self-discipline and discipline imposed from outside (including popular supervision), between consolidating foundations and innovating, between overall momentum and key priorities (with anti-corruption as the "most thorough" self-reform), and between turning the blade inward (self-reform) and outward (social revolution). Wu presents "people's supervision" and self-reform as the two complementary answers to the historical cycle, and rejects multi-party rotation and separation of powers as arguments against self-reform.

For the new journey, Wu calls for four things: combining Party leadership with full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, including the Two Establishes; regulating the use of power and improving the system of Party regulations; continuing the Party's spiritual lineage and ideals-and-convictions education; and standing with the people while innovating supervision. The conclusion holds that dialectical thinking is key to understanding the Party as a mission-driven party, and that it must keep its revolutionary character and long-term vigilance. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Party theorists ground the doctrine of self-reform in Marxist dialectics and in the Party's own historical narrative.
quoteEn: Self-reform is the key by which the Communist Party of China escapes the historical cycle and seizes the historical initiative.
quoteZh: 自我革命是中国共产党跳出历史周期率赢得历史主动的关键所在。

glossary.explanation: The Party's capacity to examine, correct and renew itself, which Xi Jinping has described since the 18th Party Congress as its most distinctive quality. The official English rendering is 'self-reform'.

The pattern of dynastic rise and collapse raised in the 1945 Yan'an conversation between Mao Zedong and Huang Yanpei. The Party names popular supervision as the first answer to it and self-reform as the second.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The official campaign since 2012 to tighten Party discipline, institutional rules and anti-corruption work.
A formula from the Party's 2021 historical resolution that affirms Xi Jinping's position as the core of the Central Committee and the Party as a whole, and the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought.
A description of the Communist Party of China as driven by a historical mission, in contrast with Western 'electoral parties' focused on winning votes.

t: On the original contributions of Chinese Marxist philosophy
zh: 论中国马克思主义哲学的原创性贡献
source: Journal of Peking University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2023 no. 2
paras: Does Chinese Marxist philosophy have any originality? Zhao Shifa takes up a question he says is much disputed at home and abroad. Some critics call Chinese Marxist philosophy a copy of the Soviet textbook system. Others reject the idea of adapting Marxist philosophy to the Chinese context, preferring "Marxist philosophy in China". Zhao argues that these critics work with too narrow a notion of originality. On a broader, practice-based notion, he holds, Chinese Marxist philosophy is an original theoretical creation.

The article has four parts. It first redefines originality. It then sets out the original content of Chinese Marxist philosophy across what Zhao calls three historic leaps: Mao Zedong's philosophy, the philosophy of the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics (Deng Xiaoping, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development), and the philosophical thinking of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The third part draws out three lessons. The fourth assesses the significance of this body of thought.

Zhao distinguishes a narrow sense of originality (first or earliest creation) from a broad one, which he equates with independent innovation arising from practice. In this broad sense originality means creative solutions to practical contradictions. It rests on the unity of critique and inheritance, of content and form, and of theory and practice. Because Marxist philosophy was combined with Chinese realities for the first time by Chinese intellectuals and communists, Zhao says, the result counts as original. He names three lessons: keeping practice at the centre, exercising the Chinese nation's subjectivity, and opposing dogmatism. He treats dogmatism as the chief enemy, citing the Wang Ming line, the "Two Whatevers" and neoliberalism as "foreign dogma". He also lists Xi's contributions to the theory of practice and dialectics, to historical materialism, to ideology and discourse power, and to the unity of Chinese and global perspectives.

Zhao concludes that Chinese Marxist philosophy enriches Marxist theory. He also says it guides the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics and offers what he calls Chinese wisdom for a new form of human civilization and a community with a shared future for mankind. He admits that its discipline, academic and discourse systems are still taking shape and that textbooks have not yet fully achieved a Chinese form. He describes Western modernity as facing internal contradictions and crisis. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language argument for the originality of Chinese Marxist philosophy, from Mao to Xi, and for the criteria it uses to judge originality.
quoteEn: Originality means excluding simple copying, plagiarism and rearrangement, shaking off the shackles of dogmatism and empiricism, and carrying out theoretical innovation on the basis of the subject's own practice, that is, independent innovation.
quoteZh: 原创意味着排除了简单地复制、抄袭与编排,摆脱了教条主义和经验主义的束缚,立足于主体自身的实践进行理论创新,也就是自主创新。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official name for the guiding ideology associated with Xi Jinping, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017 and 2018.
The official name for China's path, theory and system since reform and opening up, which stresses adapting socialism to national conditions.
The guiding concept associated with Hu Jintao, centred on people-oriented, comprehensive, coordinated and sustainable development.
A theory associated with Jiang Zemin. It holds that the Party represents advanced productive forces, advanced culture and the fundamental interests of the people.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and civilizational concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2012–13, calling for shared development and common values among nations.

A late-1970s formula holding that whatever policies Mao made and whatever instructions he gave must be followed. Deng Xiaoping's supporters opposed it in the debate on practice as the criterion of truth.

keywords: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context

t: Peasant cooperatives and common prosperity in rural areas: classical theory and Chinese practice
zh: 农民合作社促进乡村共同富裕的经典理论与中国实践
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theories, 2022 no. 10
paras: Han and Xu ask how peasant cooperatives relate to common prosperity in the countryside. They argue that the Marxist classics treated cooperatives as the necessary road for peasants towards common prosperity. On this view, cooperatives and common prosperity are bound in a relationship of mutual formation, and Chinese practice has put the idea to work.

The article has three parts. The first reviews theory: the utopian socialists (More, Saint-Simon, Fourier, Owen), Marx and Engels, and Lenin. The second sets out the "symbiosis" of cooperatives and common prosperity in their conditions of emergence, social functions and ideals. The third traces Chinese practice from the revolutionary period to the post-18th Party Congress (2012) era, drawing on examples such as Yan'an consumer cooperatives and the Zhejiang, Sichuan and Shandong models.

On theory, the authors read Marx and Engels as implying common prosperity without using the term. Cooperatives would abolish the town–country opposition and exploitation, and they should rest on public ownership of land, scaled-up operation, voluntary mutual benefit and gentle transformation of small peasants. Lenin is said to have turned cooperatives into a gradual, locally adapted route to socialism. For China, the authors claim cooperatives gave peasants land and means of production and brought them into socialist relations of production. They also credit the "two leaps" proposed by Deng Xiaoping with building a material base. In the primary, secondary and tertiary distributions, cooperatives are said to raise incomes, share value along the chain and embody a moral duty to help the weak.

The authors conclude that, under Chinese modernization, cooperatives, collective economic organisations and composite cooperative bodies can drive rural revitalisation and narrow the town–country gap. Three paths are named: high-quality development of cooperatives, comprehensive reform of supply and marketing cooperatives, and the cooperative transformation of collective economies. They cast these forms as a "third road" for the policy of letting some get rich first to lead the rest. They note that absolute poverty has been eliminated but no lasting mechanism against relative poverty exists yet. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account that links the Marxist cooperative tradition to current rural policy and to named local cooperative models.
quoteEn: The peasant cooperative is an important organisational form through which peasants move towards modernity, towards the future and towards common prosperity.
quoteZh: 农民合作社是农民走向现代性、走向未来、走向共同富裕的重要组织形式

glossary.explanation: A long-standing goal of Chinese socialism, stressed again by Xi Jinping from 2021. It means prosperity shared by all, not uniform or simultaneous wealth.
The official term for China's path of modernisation, prominent in Party discourse since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
A national strategy announced in 2017 to develop agriculture, villages and farmers' incomes.
A nationwide cooperative network, set up in 1949, that handles the circulation of farm goods and farm inputs and is promoted as a link between the Party and peasants.

t: Building a social governance community in rural revitalisation
zh: 乡村振兴中的社会治理共同体建设
source: Social Science Journal (Shehui kexue jikan), 2023 no. 2
paras: Zhao Xiaofeng asks how a social governance community can be built in the countryside during rural revitalisation. The concept was first put forward by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) and restated in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) as a community in which everyone has responsibility, does their duty and shares in the benefits. Zhao's thesis is that local government must convert its monopoly power over public services into service rights granted to social and market actors. This must be done while four "hidden traps" are avoided and a relationship model of joint participation, consultation, shared responsibility and shared benefit is built.

The article has four parts. It first sets out the starting point: the growth since reform and opening up of village committees, farmers' cooperatives, leading enterprises and rural social organisations. It then reviews governance theory, specifically delegation (principal–agent) theory and empowerment theory. Next it analyses the traps facing county and township governments, social organisations, enterprises and ordinary villagers. Finally it proposes four practical paths.

Zhao criticises delegation theory for treating governance as power and control and leaving out the people, and mutual-empowerment theory for assuming that cooperatives help government. Zhao proposes shifting from a perspective of power and control to one of rights and services. Local government is a "power-monopolising" participant, while social organisations and enterprises are "right-expanding" participants who must win service rights. The four traps follow from this. Government may take over everything, driven by administrative subcontracting and promotion tournaments. Social organisations may fall into contests over rights. Enterprise capital may expand without order and squeeze out small farmers and "backbone farmers". Villagers, increasingly individualised, may participate without rules, as in profit-driven petitioning.

Zhao proposes four mechanisms. The first is shared governance ideas under Party leadership, with the Party–people relationship as decisive. The second is joint construction: fostering more actors, avoiding both government-centred and society-centred models, and allocating or withdrawing service rights according to performance. The third is consultation and coordination, with local government as the likely coordinator and primary-level Party organisations stepping in when it fails. The fourth is benefit sharing, through common prosperity and coordinated primary, secondary and tertiary distribution, without coerced donations. Read the original if you want a sociological account of rural governance in China that draws on field observation and on the principal–agent and empowerment literatures.
quoteEn: The key to social governance is to establish institutional mechanisms for orderly participation by grassroots people, and the core of this is to deal effectively with the risks and challenges posed by the few who do not play by the rules.
quoteZh: 社会治理的关键即是要建立起基层民众有序参与的制度机制，而其核心则是要能有效应对少数人不按规则“出牌”所带来的风险和挑战。

glossary.explanation: A concept first introduced by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee in 2019. It describes a governance order in which the Party, government, enterprises, social organisations and citizens share responsibility and benefits.
A national strategy announced in 2017 to promote agricultural modernisation, rural industry, ecology, governance and organisation, and farmers' incomes.
A scholarly term for the way higher levels of government assign tasks and targets to lower levels, which carry them out with considerable discretion. It is used in Chinese political sociology.
A scholarly model in which local officials compete on measurable performance indicators for promotion by their superiors.
A Party goal of broadly shared wealth, stressed in official policy since 2021 and linked to coordinated distribution and to charitable giving.
Redistribution through voluntary donations and philanthropy, alongside market-based primary distribution and government-led secondary distribution.

t: The development, rich connotations and far-reaching significance of the contemporary Chinese view of human rights
zh: 当代中国人权观的发展脉络、丰富内涵及深远意义
paras: Xu Xianchun sets out to explain the "contemporary Chinese view of human rights", which the author presents as the theoretical counterpart of a "Chinese path of human rights development" formed since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Xu argues that this view is a major result of integrating the Marxist view of human rights with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. It guides officials in respecting and safeguarding rights and points the way forward for the cause in the new era.

The article has three parts. The first traces the sources and history of the view: Marx and Engels, traditional ideas of people-centredness, and the Party's explorations from the New Democratic Revolution through the Mao, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao periods. The second sets out the content of Xi Jinping's statements on human rights under the heading of the Party's leadership, the people's standpoint, subsistence and development rights, health, a systematic approach, vulnerable groups, rule of law and global governance. The third assesses the view's significance.

Xu's core claim is continuity. Marxist classics held that rights are social, class-based and historical, and that bourgeois human rights are both historically progressive and hypocritical. Each generation of Party leaders, in Xu's account, added to this: Mao tied rights to national independence and the people's mastery of the country; Deng stressed development and rejected "human rights over sovereignty"; Jiang named subsistence and development as the primary rights; Hu stressed a people-centred approach and the Scientific Outlook on Development. Xi's "six adherences" distil the Chinese path: Party leadership, the people's principal position, China's actual conditions, subsistence and development rights first, rule of law, and participation in global governance. Xu argues that no single model fits all countries, and that criticism of China by some Western states is a strategic effort at Westernization and containment.

Xu concludes that the view widens the Chinese path, lays a human rights foundation for Chinese modernization, and enriches the diversity of human rights civilization. It does so by promoting the "common values of all mankind" in place of Western "universal values" and by offering developing countries an alternative. The author calls for firmness and strategic resolve in following this path. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party theorists trace the genealogy of the Chinese human rights discourse from Marx to Xi Jinping.
quoteEn: The Chinese path of human rights development did not fall from the sky, was not copied from books, and is certainly not a replica of another country's path.
quoteZh: 中国人权发展道路不是从天上掉下来的，也不是从书本上抄来的，更不是别国人权发展道路的翻版。

glossary.explanation: The Party's official formulation of China's own path to modernization, stressed since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is characterised by a huge population, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical advancement, harmony with nature and peaceful development.
Xi Jinping's formulation of peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom as shared values. Official discourse presents it as an alternative to Western "universal values".
Hu Jintao-era guiding concept (2000s) that puts people first and calls for comprehensive, coordinated and sustainable development.

glossary.en: Chinese path of human rights development
glossary.explanation: The official phrase for China's approach to human rights, which stresses national conditions, the rights to subsistence and development, and Party leadership. It is set against what official discourse calls a single Western model.

keywords: Chinese path of human rights development

t: Mao Zedong's exploration of the path of Chinese modernization: process, main contributions and contemporary value
zh: 毛泽东对中国式现代化道路的探索历程、主要贡献及当代价值
source: Journal of Xiangtan University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2023 no. 2
paras: Taking its cue from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which presents Chinese modernization as the product of long exploration since 1949, Yang Xiaojun and Shao Yan ask what Mao Zedong contributed to that path. They argue that Mao was a pioneer of Chinese modernization, and that his explorations, including his errors, prepared its opening and development. They hold that studying them has theoretical and practical value for pursuing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization.

The article has three parts. The first traces Mao's exploration in three phases: the revolutionary period, when he sought national independence and industrialization; the early People's Republic, when he imitated the Soviet heavy-industry model; and the period after 1956, when he sought a path suited to China's conditions. The second lists his contributions in theory, institutions, strategy and development model. The third draws a line from Mao to Xi Jinping on theory, Party leadership and methodology.

On the authors' account, Mao's New Democracy theory supplied the first theoretical outline of modernization. The socialist transformation then built the basic economic and political institutions: public ownership, the people's congress system, multi-party cooperation and regional ethnic autonomy. Mao's strategy moved from industrialization to the "four modernizations", and from a catch-up campaign against Britain and the United States to a "two-step" plan. His model moved from "learning from the Soviet Union across the board" to independent exploration, marked by On the Ten Major Relationships and the "second integration" of Marxism with Chinese realities. The authors concede that the Great Leap Forward was a failure but say Mao reflected on it and corrected course.

For the present, the authors argue that Xi Jinping inherited and developed Mao's legacy in three ways. He built the theoretical framework of Chinese modernization, he placed the Party's overall leadership first, and he extended Mao's seeking truth from facts through investigation, problem orientation and practical action. They present the Party's self-reform as the second answer to the historical cycle of rise and fall, following Mao's "supervision by the people". They conclude that Mao's exploration is the historical and logical starting point of Chinese modernization, and that it broke the claim that capitalist modernization is the only model. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese academics now link Mao-era modernization thinking to Xi Jinping's Chinese modernization narrative.
quoteEn: Mao Zedong's in-depth exploration of and thinking on the path of Chinese modernization was without doubt the historical and logical starting point both for opening up the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics after reform and opening up, and for the advance and extension of Chinese modernization since the 18th Party Congress.
quoteZh: 毛泽东对中国式现代化道路的深入探索和思考，无疑是改革开放后中国特色社会主义道路的开辟，以及党的十八大以来中国式现代化得以推进和拓展的历史起点和逻辑起点。

glossary.explanation: The official Party concept of China's own path to modernization, set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western modernization.
Mao Zedong's theory of a transitional stage between the semi-colonial, semi-feudal old China and socialism. It is led by the Communist Party and joins several revolutionary classes.
The goal of modernizing agriculture, industry, national defence and science and technology. Zhou Enlai and Mao Zedong formulated it in the 1960s, and it was later central to reform-era policy.

Mao's call in the mid-1950s to combine Marxism-Leninism with China's concrete conditions in socialist construction, after the first combination in the revolution. It marked a move away from copying the Soviet model.
A Party principle of basing policy on actual conditions. It is associated with Mao's Yan'an-era writings and presented in Party theory as the core of Marxist method.
Xi Jinping-era term for the Party's continuing internal discipline and anti-corruption work. Official discourse presents it as the answer to the historical cycle of rise and fall.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central official goal of restoring China to national strength and international standing, usually tied to the centenary targets of 2049.

t: The theory of Chinese modernization as a major innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
zh: 中国式现代化理论是马克思主义中国化时代化的重大创新
paras: Writing in 2023, soon after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Yan Xiaofeng takes up a question of Party theory: how the theory of Chinese modernization relates to the long project of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Following Xi Jinping's remarks at a study seminar on the Congress, Yan argues that the theory is a major theoretical innovation and a major achievement in advancing that project. In this account it is also an important component of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.

The article, a commentary in a Party theoretical journal, has three parts. The first argues that opening up a new horizon for the adaptation of Marxism requires developing the theory, and traces how the Party formed it through the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second sets out the theory's contributions. The third considers its role as guidance for the new journey of building a modern socialist country in all respects.

Yan's central claim is that the Party advances the adaptation of Marxism by answering major questions of each era, and that Chinese modernization is such a question. Since the Opium War, the author holds, the Western capitalist road to modernization has proved unworkable in China. The contributions Yan lists include the claim that modernization is not Westernization and that countries may choose their own paths. Others are that Party leadership is the most essential feature, and that the Chinese features are a huge population, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical advancement, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. Yan also credits the theory with defining the essential requirements, a new form of human civilization, and a strategic layout. The article presents the Two Integrations as the fundamental route, and as the source of the theory.

Yan concludes that the new journey brings fresh strategic conditions and risks, including external challenges, deep-seated domestic contradictions and problems within the Party. These call for further theoretical answers, including to the \"questions of modernization\" Xi raised at the dialogue with world political parties. Yan calls for adherence to Xi Jinping Thought, study of the 20th Congress, and enrichment of the theory on the basis of practice. Read the original if you want to see how a Party theorist frames Chinese modernization within the official narrative of the adaptation of Marxism in the Chinese context.
quoteEn: Chinese modernization has broken the myth that "modernization equals Westernization", widened the routes by which developing countries can modernize, offered humanity a new choice for achieving modernization, and carries world significance.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化打破了“现代化=西方化”的迷思，拓展了发展中国家走向现代化的途径，为人类实现现代化提供了新的选择，具有世界意义。

glossary.explanation: The official term for China's path to modernization under Communist Party leadership, elaborated at the 20th Party Congress in 2022. It is presented as socialist and distinct from Western models.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.literal: the Sinicization and contemporization of Marxism
glossary.explanation: The official formula for the Party's effort to apply Marxism to China's conditions and to current times. 'Times' (时代化) was added to the older 'Sinicization' formula in recent years.
Formula for combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture. It is presented as the fundamental route of adapting Marxism.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's guiding ideology associated with Xi Jinping, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.
An official goal of shared wealth for all the people, described as an essential requirement of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

keywords: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context

t: Understanding the theory of Chinese modernization through historical materialism
zh: 以唯物史观理解中国式现代化理论
paras: Writing in 2023, soon after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Liu Tongfang asks how the theory of Chinese modernization should be understood from the standpoint of historical materialism. Liu argues that the theory grasps the combined situation of "changes in the world, changes of the times and changes in history", anticipates the basic direction of modernization, and links China's development to the common development of the world. In this reading it is both a major theoretical innovation and the latest major achievement of scientific socialism.

The article has four sections.
