The second examines the world-historical factors behind the revolutionary path: the rural-encirclement strategy, the interaction of world and Chinese history in shaping modern China, and the international united front. The third treats China's place in the world revolution and the global significance of the War of Resistance against Japan. Mao's texts, such as On New Democracy (1940), are read against Marx, Engels and Lenin.

The authors contend that Mao read the age as one of revolution and war, in which imperialism's contradictions were sharpening and capitalism was declining. On this basis, the revolution after the October Revolution and the May Fourth Movement was 'new democratic' and part of the proletarian socialist world revolution, so a bourgeois republic was no longer a viable prospect. They argue that 'encircling the cities from the countryside' and armed seizure of power was the Chinese form of the world revolution's general experience. In this reading, it followed from China's semi-colonial, semi-feudal conditions, and the 'Left' dogmatists erred by copying the Russian model mechanically. Mao's united-front principles combined broad alliance with differentiation, and self-reliance with foreign aid.

The authors conclude that the victory of the New Democratic Revolution was among the most significant political events of the twentieth century, alongside the October Revolution and the Second World War. In their view, it altered the global political balance and offered other colonised nations a path and experience. They propose that revisiting Mao's strategic thinking can help coordinate the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation with the world's 'great changes unseen in a century', and guide China's dealings with the outside world. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-history account of how Mao's wartime texts connected Chinese revolutionary strategy to Marxist-Leninist theories of world history and imperialism.
quoteEn: The victory of the Chinese revolution cannot be separated from Mao Zedong's strategic thinking, from a global perspective, on a series of major questions of the Chinese revolution.
quoteZh: 中国革命的胜利，离不开毛泽东以世界眼光对中国革命一系列重大问题的战略思考。

glossary.explanation: Mao Zedong's term for the stage of the Chinese revolution from about 1919 to 1949, led by the proletariat and aimed at ending imperialist and feudal domination. It was seen as a transition towards socialism.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central slogan of Party discourse, especially since 2012, for restoring China's strength and international standing.
Mao's concept of building broad alliances abroad, in particular an anti-fascist coalition during the Second World War, to support China's struggle.

glossary.en: encircling the cities from the countryside
glossary.explanation: The Chinese Communist Party's revolutionary strategy of building rural base areas and using armed struggle to eventually take the cities.

t: The historical starting point, main connotations and mission of the Chinese path to modernization
zh: 中国式现代化道路的历史起点、主要内涵与使命追求
source: Journal of Southwest University (Social Sciences Edition), 2023 no. 2
paras: Scholars disagree about when the Chinese path to modernization began, and Jiang and Wang argue that the answer shapes how its meaning and mission are understood. Taking China as a late-developing country whose modernization passed through several shifts in development model, the article contends that the founding of the People's Republic in 1949 is the historical starting point. Reform and opening up, in this reading, was a qualitative leap within a continuous process rather than a restart.

The article first reviews five candidate starting points in the literature: the Self-Strengthening Movement, the 1911 Revolution, the founding of the Communist Party, the founding of the PRC, and reform and opening up. It then surveys how scholars define the path's connotations, in formulas such as the "six unities" or "four unities", and its mission. The authors then set out five features of the path and five missions, and close with a conclusion.

The authors build the case on the nature, leadership, goals and continuity of modernization. They cite Deng Xiaoping's statements that the Four Modernizations were set under Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai and were socialist in character. The five features are: universality combined with particularity; a path forged under pressure from both Western capitalist and Soviet-style models; a socialist character; leadership by the Communist Party; and common prosperity. On this account the path is not an extension of the capitalist modernization begun in 1911, though it must still answer questions raised by the Self-Strengthening Movement and the 1911 Revolution.

The five missions the authors name are advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, meeting the people's aspiration for a better life, writing the "big article" of socialism with Chinese characteristics, creating a new form of human civilization, and making new and greater contributions to humanity. The authors present the path as transcending capitalist and traditional Soviet models and as a Chinese approach for developing countries. They add that its success demonstrates the truth of Marxism adapted to China. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language account of the debate over the starting point of Chinese modernization and the official framing of its features and missions.
quoteEn: The historical starting point of the Chinese path to modernization endows it with a specific meaning and mission; that meaning is continually enriched as the path develops, and the enriched meaning in turn shows that its pursuit of its mission is continually expanding.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化道路的历史起点赋予了它特定的内涵与使命，其内涵又在道路发展过程中不断得以丰富，而不断丰富的内涵又表明其使命追求在不断拓展。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's path of modernization under Communist Party leadership, set out in Party documents especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022). Deng Xiaoping used the phrase "Chinese-style modernization" in 1979.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing after what Party discourse calls the 'century of humiliation' that began with the Opium War.
A goal of shared affluence for all the people, treated in Party discourse as an essential requirement of socialism. Both material and cultural-spiritual wealth are included.
The goal of modernizing agriculture, industry, national defence, and science and technology. It was first proposed in the 1950s–60s and became central to Deng Xiaoping's reform programme.

glossary.en: a new form of human civilization
glossary.explanation: A phrase in Party discourse describing the civilizational outcome of Chinese modernization, set against Western capital-centred modernization. It became prominent after 2021.

t: Vigorously promoting revolutionary culture in the historical process of advancing Chinese modernization
zh: 在推进中国式现代化历史进程中大力弘扬革命文化
paras: Writing shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Fan Xichun argues that revolutionary culture is an important component of socialist culture with Chinese characteristics and a powerful source of momentum for Chinese modernization. Fan contends that building a modern socialist country and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation depend on its ideological guidance, value orientation, spiritual nourishment and cultural support. The article therefore calls for promoting revolutionary culture vigorously and for continually enriching it in practice.

The article opens by defining revolutionary culture as an advanced culture formed under Communist Party leadership across the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. It then sets out the present context: the 20th Party Congress goals of basic modernization by 2035 and a modern socialist country by mid-century, pursued amid what Fan calls profound global change, deep-seated domestic contradictions and external pressure. The main body applies a three-layer model of culture (ideas, material products, institutions and customs) and ends with a short section on adapting revolutionary culture to the times.

Fan's central move is to assign revolutionary culture a role at each of the three layers. At the level of ideas, Marxism and its Chinese theoretical achievements, communist ideals, a people-centred standpoint and core socialist values secure the nature and direction of modernization. At the level of material products, revolutionary literature, art and relics, which the article says include over 36,000 immovable sites, inspire the public. At the level of institutions, Fan points to Party leadership, whole-process people's democracy and a long lineage of revolutionary spirits, from the Jinggangshan spirit to the spirit of poverty alleviation, as the political guarantee and driving force.

Fan concludes that revolutionary culture stays vital only when it fits the demands of practice and of the age, and invokes Xi Jinping's call for creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture. The author calls for enriching its contemporary content and forms so that it becomes a mark of the new era. Fan presents this as an inherent requirement of Chinese modernization and a historical responsibility of Communists. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how Party-affiliated writers frame revolutionary culture's role in Chinese modernization, including its full catalogue of named revolutionary spirits.
quoteEn: Revolutionary culture has vitality fundamentally because it fits the demands of the social practice of its time and accords with the spiritual aspirations and values of the age.
quoteZh: 革命文化之所以具有生命力，根本在于与所处的社会实践要求相适应，与时代的精神追求和价值观念相契合。

glossary.explanation: The Party's official formulation of China's own path to modernization, elaborated at the 20th Party Congress (2022) as a path distinct from Western models.

In official discourse, the advanced culture formed under Communist Party leadership during revolution, construction and reform. It is treated as one of three components of socialist culture alongside traditional Chinese culture and advanced socialist culture.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's central national goal, associated with the Chinese Dream, of restoring China's strength and standing by mid-century.
Official term, promoted by Xi Jinping since 2019, for China's democratic model, which it describes as covering every stage of political and policy processes.
A set of twelve official values, including prosperity, democracy, patriotism and integrity, promoted since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

t: A preliminary analysis of historical trends of thought
zh: 历史思潮初析
source: Studies in Theory of History (Shixue lilun yanjiu), 2023 no. 2
paras: Yu Pei takes up a concept that, he notes, has no entry in major encyclopaedias and no agreed definition: the "historical trend of thought" (lishi sichao). He argues that such trends are a specific form of social consciousness, rooted in a society's economy, politics, culture and mass psychology, and that studying them gives theoretical and practical value for forecasting and strategic judgement in a period of world upheaval.

The article has three parts. The first defines historical trends of thought, distinguishes them from social and academic trends, and traces their evolution in the West, in modern China and in Meiji Japan. The second examines their changing "themes of the era", moving from Marx's theory of world history to the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. The third takes the postwar "global history" movement as a case of a historiographical trend, discussing Geoffrey Barraclough and L. S. Stavrianos.

Yu's central move is to apply historical materialism. Historical trends of thought are said to reflect the historical current (lishi chaoliu), which is primary and material, while the trend of thought is secondary and ideational. Yu rejects the claim that academic trends can be kept "pure" of politics, arguing that they are never outside ideology and that scholarly and social trends belong together. He also contends that no historical trend can be judged by a single standard, since it depends on one's worldview, and he cites Western claims that modernization and globalization mean Westernization. Global history is presented as a product of anti-colonial movements and the rise of developing countries after 1945, with Barraclough's rejection of Eurocentrism and Stavrianos's A Global History (later editions stressing new technology) as examples of a new era requiring new historiography.

Yu concludes that the current theme has shifted from "world history" to a community with a shared future for mankind, which he describes as enriching Marx's world-history thought. He holds that the world will remain one of "one globe, two systems" for a long time. He urges researchers to study theory, history and present conditions rigorously, so as to grasp the laws of historical development, strengthen historical confidence and contribute to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of how "trends of thought" relate to ideology, historiography and world-historical change, with global history as a worked example.
quoteEn: Academic trends of thought have never been abstract cultural concepts; they are, first of all, ideological concepts.
quoteZh: 学术思潮从来不是抽象的文化概念，而首先是一个意识形态概念。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and theoretical concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2013. It calls for countries to cooperate on shared security, prosperity and global governance.
The official term, prominent since the 20th Party Congress (2022), for China's own path of modernization as distinct from Western models.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal associated with the Chinese Dream, referring to restoring China's national strength and international standing by the mid-twenty-first century.
Yu's term for a widely influential current of ideas, often with a world-historical theme, that reflects social conditions and serves as a form of social consciousness.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: How can artificial intelligence be made to do good? Reflections on technological threats and state responsibility
zh: 人工智能如何向善：基于技术威胁与国家责任的思考
paras: Mei Lirun asks how artificial intelligence can be steered towards good when public attitudes have moved from enthusiasm, after AlphaGo's victory, to widespread anxiety about an AI threat. The article argues that, for a state whose core mission is to promote the well-being of its people, calming this anxiety is a new and unavoidable responsibility. Mei holds that the state should answer each main type of AI threat with a matching pair of measures.

The article first traces the rise of the AI threat discourse, citing warnings from Elon Musk and Stephen Hawking, a 2015 Oxford risk assessment and the spread of media alarm. It then examines three threats that Mei says attract most concern: unemployment, privacy and loss of meaning. The final section, the longest, sets out state responsibilities for each, drawing on examples from China, the United States and the European Union.

On unemployment, Mei accepts that earlier industrial revolutions created more jobs than they destroyed. Mei argues, however, that this precedent may fail now, because AI replaces white-collar as well as blue-collar work and demands higher skills. On privacy, Mei describes companies "hunting" data, which makes anonymisation weak and leaks irreversible. On meaning, Mei argues that algorithmic "information cocoons", AI's superiority in fields humans take pride in, and the handing over of decisions to algorithms narrow the space in which people find meaning through growth and autonomy.

Mei proposes that the state conduct a survey of automation ("mapping") and provide a safety net of subsidies, retraining and job information for the unemployed. For privacy, Mei calls for legislation, including AI-specific laws, and periodic special campaigns of inspection and punishment. For meaning, Mei urges the state to encourage "reverse recommendation" in algorithms and to publish "technology forecasts" of what AI can and cannot do. Mei also asks the state to promote a notion of human–machine symbiosis. Read the original if you want a Chinese political-science account of AI governance that ties public anxiety to state responsibility and cites Chinese regulatory campaigns from 2017 to 2019.
quoteEn: For a state whose core mission is to promote the well-being of its people, finding solutions that dispel the AI threat and soothe public anxiety has become a new responsibility it cannot evade.
quoteZh: 对于以增进民众福祉为核心使命的国家来说，寻找消解人工智能威胁的方案以安抚民众的忧虑便成为不可推卸的新兴责任。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese policy and media phrase for replacing workers with automated equipment. Several provinces and cities issued dedicated implementation plans for it. (In the summary, the related state survey step is called "mapping".)
A term for the closed, homogeneous information environment created when algorithms feed users only content matching their existing preferences.
Mei's proposal that recommendation algorithms also show users content outside or opposed to their preferences, to widen the range of information they receive.
Mei's proposal that the state publish regularly updated assessments of what current AI can and cannot do, and of how it is likely to develop.

t: A deeper understanding of why Marxism adapted to China and our times "works"
zh: 深刻理解中国化时代化的马克思主义行
source: Chinese Party and Government Cadres Forum (中国党政干部论坛), 2023 no. 3
paras: Taking up the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which states that the Communist Party's success and the merits of socialism with Chinese characteristics ultimately rest on Marxism "working", and specifically on Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, this theoretical commentary asks how the two claims relate. Zhang argues that this "works" can be understood from three angles: method of thought, mechanism of formation and practical results. The thesis is that adapted Marxism is a theoretical product of upholding fundamental principles while innovating, a fruit of the Two Integrations, and the key to China's "two miracles".

The article has three sections, one for each angle. It first traces the spread of Marxism-Leninism in China after the October Revolution and the founding of the Party. It then covers the move from a single "integration" to the Two Integrations. Finally it surveys the Party's record from Mao Zedong to the new era, citing Engels, Mao and the philosopher Ai Siqi along the way.

Zhang's first move treats Marxism as a method rather than a dogma. Because it offered no ready answers for a semi-colonial, semi-feudal China, the Party had to avoid mechanical application and foreign models and instead fit the theory to national conditions. Zhang calls this "upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground", the internal logic by which adapted Marxism arises. Second, Zhang argues that the combination of Marxism with Chinese reality was long studied mainly in terms of theory and mission, while cultural affinity was neglected. Drawing on Ai Siqi, Zhang says traditional Chinese culture has a deep compatibility with Marxism, which provided a cultural-psychological basis for its acceptance and fostered the creative transformation of that culture. Third, the author names adapted Marxism as the "secret code" of rapid economic growth and long-term social stability. Zhang says it guided the new-democratic revolution, the socialist market economy, the theoretical system, the institutions and the culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

Zhang concludes that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era marks a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. It is presented as the guide for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The author urges Party members to hold firm to Marxist belief and study the latest achievements of this adaptation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school-style scholarship explains the 20th Congress formula that Marxism "works" through method, the Two Integrations and developmental results.
quoteEn: Upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground embodies the unity of Marxist materialism and dialectics. It is an inevitable requirement of upholding and developing Marxism, and the internal mechanism and logic by which Marxism adapted to China and our times emerges and develops.
quoteZh: 守正创新，体现了马克思主义唯物论与辩证法的统一，是坚持和发展马克思主义的必然要求，是中国化时代化马克思主义生成和发展的内在机制和逻辑理路。

glossary.explanation: The principle of combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The second element was stressed in Xi Jinping's 2021–2023 statements.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for the Party's project of fitting Marxist theory to Chinese conditions and to the demands of each era. The 20th Party Congress added "of our times" to the older "adapting Marxism to China".

glossary.en: upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground
glossary.explanation: A formula in Party discourse for staying true to core principles, here Marxist ones, while innovating in theory and practice.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's current official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution in 2017.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A national goal in official discourse that is associated with the Chinese Dream and with achieving a modern, strong China.

glossary.zh: 社会主义市场经济体制
glossary.explanation: The economic system adopted in the 1990s that combines public ownership with market mechanisms. Official accounts credit Deng Xiaoping's reforms with establishing it.

t: Persist in using Marxism to observe, grasp and lead the times
zh: 坚持用马克思主义观察时代把握时代引领时代
source: China Party and Government Cadres Forum (中国党政干部论坛), 2023 no. 3
paras: Dong Zhenhua takes up the formula repeated in Xi Jinping's speech at the Party's centenary (2021) and in the Resolution on the Party's century of struggle: use Marxism to "observe the times, grasp the times and lead the times". Writing in 2023, soon after the 20th Party Congress, Dong argues that only by doing so can the Party keep answering the questions of China, the world, the people and the times, and produce theory that keeps pace with the age and guides practice.

The article is a short theoretical commentary in three parts. The first concerns holding to Marxism's worldview, methodology and basic standpoint. The second concerns problem awareness and a problem-oriented approach. The third concerns upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, which the author links to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Dong draws on Xi Jinping, the 20th Party Congress report, Marx and Lenin, and on episodes from Party history.

In the first part, Dong argues that the Party has kept its initiative because it applies Marxist method to analyse situations. Examples are Mao Zedong's "a single spark can start a prairie fire" after the failed uprisings, and the 1978 debate on practice as the sole criterion of truth, which Dong says opened reform and opening up. In the second part, citing Marx on problems as "the voice of the epoch", Dong holds that Marxism offers principles and methods rather than ready-made answers. Dong says the present era far exceeds what the classic authors foresaw, and that China's socialism is still in its early decades in the primary stage of socialism. In the third part, Dong treats "upholding fundamental principles" and "innovation" as two sides of one question: innovation means "continuing the discourse" in Marxism's authentic spirit, neither merely repeating texts nor starting afresh elsewhere.

Dong concludes that upholding fundamental principles means three unwaverings: Marxist basic tenets, the Party's overall leadership, and socialism with Chinese characteristics. This must go together with "saying new things" that the founders did not say. Dong calls it a solemn duty of today's Communists to keep writing new chapters of Marxism adapted to China and the times, starting from the worldview and methods of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Central Party School scholars present the logic linking Party history, problem orientation and theoretical innovation in 2023.
quoteEn: \"Innovation\" is not the bookish \"speaking in line with the texts\", still less \"speaking differently\" by setting up a separate stove apart from Marxist truth, but \"continuing the discourse\" in Marxism's authentic spirit, which is itself \"upholding fundamental principles\".
quoteZh: “创新”不是本本主义的“照着讲”，更不是离开马克思主义的真理另起炉灶“另外讲”，而是按照马克思主义的本真精神“接着讲”，这本身就是“守正”。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: Official formula for the Party's project of applying Marxist theory to Chinese conditions and developing it with contemporary practice. The phrase was given prominence in the 2021 Party resolution and the 20th Party Congress.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.

glossary.en: upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground
glossary.explanation: Official slogan for keeping to core principles, in the Party's view Marxism and Party leadership, while innovating in theory and practice.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world begun in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping.
Official thesis that China is at an early, long-lasting stage of socialist development, with underdeveloped productive forces.

t: Wang Zhen's early encounters with Chairman Mao
zh: 王震早年与毛主席的交往
paras: Written to mark the 130th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth and the 115th of Wang Zhen's, this is a historical memoir-style account rather than a research article. Li Shenming, who worked at Wang Zhen's side for over a decade, reconstructs Wang's early dealings with Mao from Wang's own oral recollections and from interviews with his old comrades and subordinates. Li presents Wang as a true Communist and Mao as a leader of exceptional breadth, openness and strategic clarity.

The article is organised chronologically in three sections. The first covers Wang's youth as a railway worker, his 1925 escort of Mao by rail handcar, and their 1930 meeting near Changsha, where Mao advised on forming the Xiangdong Independent Division. The second covers Wang's talks with Mao at the First National Soviet Congress in Ruijin (1931–32). The third covers their meeting during the Second Congress in January 1934, and the later Xiang-Gan battle at Shashi.

Li's central thread is Mao's guidance on guerrilla and mobile warfare against the 'left' line of Wang Ming and the advisers Bo Gu and Otto Braun (Li De). Mao urged Wang to use the 'sixteen-character' formula, avoid costly attritional fighting, and reject 'fortress against fortress' tactics. He also told Wang to correct the over-extension of purges, to treat captured troops generously, to study revolutionary theory, and to follow the path of encircling cities from the countryside. Li notes that Mao said all this while himself sidelined from leadership, yet voiced no complaint. Li then reports that Wang carried this guidance back to the Xiang-Gan base, and cites a veteran's testimony that it explained the victory at Shashi in April 1934.

Li concludes that the Shashi victory, achieved by Ren Bishi, Wang Zhen and Xiao Ke by applying Mao's instructions, eased pressure on the Central Soviet Area. The account also stresses Mao's personal warmth and his criticism of localism. It is offered as a tribute to both men. Read the original if you want a participant-sourced, commemorative narrative of Mao's military and political advice in the early 1930s, or want to see how Party-affiliated writers present Mao's role in the inner-Party struggle with the Wang Ming line.
quoteEn: Mao Zedong stood up and paced around the table: "Wang Zhen! There is another very important problem, which is to pay close attention to correcting the oversimplification and over-extension of the 'elimination of counter-revolutionaries'."
quoteZh: 毛泽东站了起来，在桌子边踱来踱去：“王震呢!还有个问题十分重要，这就是要十分注意纠正‘肃反’的简单化、扩大化。

t: The strategic blueprint of Chinese modernization and the elevation of its theoretical system
zh: 中国式现代化的战略擘画和理论体系升华
source: Studies on the Marxist Theory Discipline (马克思主义理论学科研究), 2023 no. 3
paras: On 7 February 2023, at a study session on the spirit of the 20th Party Congress (2022), Xi Jinping stated that a theoretical system of Chinese modernization had been "preliminarily constructed". Gu Hailiang's article is an interpretive exposition of that judgement. It argues that the formulation sums up the practical and historical logic of Chinese modernization, answers the three major questions of the era posed by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and rests on a distinctive Marxist worldview and methodology.

The article has four sections. The first traces the historical initiative behind the exploration of modernization, from the new-democratic revolution through the Mao era to reform and opening up. The second sets out the components of the theoretical system as Xi presented them, from the five features of 2020 to the 20th Party Congress report. The third links the system to the three major questions of the era, and the fourth examines the six "views" (worldview, values, view of history, view of civilization, democracy and ecology) and the relationships within the "systematic process" of modernization.

Gu's central move is to read the theory as the product of accumulated historical conditions: the revolution's "fundamental social conditions", the political premises of the socialist period, and the institutional and material base of reform and opening up. Gu cites debates of the 1920s–30s and the Four Modernizations, with Deng Xiaoping's 1979 "Chinese-style" modernization as the origin of the term. The article then lists six innovations in the Congress report: the central task, the five features, the essential requirements, the 2035 goals, the major principles and cultural roots. It argues that the Party's leadership determines the fundamental nature of Chinese modernization, and that the six "views" apply the dialectical and historical materialist worldview. They are tied to the "six musts" of Xi's thought and to six relationships, such as top-level design and practical exploration, and efficiency and fairness.

Gu concludes that the theory is a major theoretical innovation of the 20th Party Congress and a new stage in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. In this account it presents a new form of human civilization that breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Party theorists systematise the official account of Chinese modernization and trace its historical lineage.
quoteEn: Chinese modernization took shape as a \"theoretical system\" in the course of exploring the major question of the era of what kind of modern socialist great country to build and how to build it.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化是在对建设什么样的社会主义现代化强国、怎样建设社会主义现代化强国这一重大时代课题探索中成型为“理论体系”的

glossary.explanation: The official Party concept of China's own path to modernization, elaborated at the 20th Party Congress (2022). Deng Xiaoping used the related phrase "Chinese-style Four Modernizations" in 1979.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for the Party's claim to apply Marxism to China's conditions and keep renewing it. The "times" element was added in the 2021 history resolution and 2022 Congress report.

glossary.en: three major questions of the era
glossary.explanation: In the Party's formulation, the three questions Xi Jinping Thought sets out to answer: what socialism with Chinese characteristics to uphold and how, what modern socialist country to build and how, and what long-governing Marxist party to build and how.

t: The first step in the origins of Chinese civilisation, eight thousand years ago
zh: 八千年前中华文明起源迈开第一步
source: History Review (Lishi pinglun), 2022 no. 4; excerpted from Study Times, 11 July 2022
paras: Han Jianye asks when the origins of Chinese civilisation began, distinguishing them from its formation, which the author dates to the first early states on Chinese soil. The short piece argues that the first step in the origins process was already taken around 8,000 years ago. It is an excerpt from a longer article on the origin, formation and longevity of Chinese civilisation, first published in Study Times in 2022.

The article draws on archaeological finds from the Yellow River basin, the Yangtze region and the West Liao River basin. It moves from agriculture, to calendrical knowledge and belief, to social order, and then summarises what these show.

Han begins with the rough formation, by about 8,000 years ago, of two farming systems: rice in the south and millet in the north. In Han's account, China's large farmland area and this dual system secured a stable food supply. Han then cites the Jiahu site in Henan, where bone instruments may have been used for "observing celestial phenomena to determine the seasons", along with divination symbols on tortoise shells and dragon images in distant regions, which the author reads as signs of early worship of heaven and a unified cosmology. Clan cemeteries and orderly ring-ditch villages point, in Han's reading, to ancestor veneration and a settled social order.

Han concludes that by 8,000 years ago most of China had an ordered society, some social differentiation and a developed system of ideas and knowledge, including cosmology, ethics, historical consciousness, astronomy, mathematics, symbols and music. In Han's view this system forms the core of Chinese civilisation, and a cultural sphere of an "early China" was emerging. Read the original if you want a brief statement of one archaeologist's case for dating the beginnings of Chinese civilisation to the Neolithic.
quoteEn: Therefore, the first step in the origins of Chinese civilisation had already been taken 8,000 years ago.
quoteZh: 因此，8000年前已经迈开了中华文明起源的第一步。

t: Mao Zedong's successful way of turning crisis into opportunity
zh: 毛泽东化危为机的成功之道
source: Journal of Xiangtan University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2023, vol. 47 no. 2
paras: Chen and Zhang ask how Mao Zedong repeatedly turned crises facing the Chinese Communist Party into opportunities, and what this offers the Party today. They argue that his method rested on three linked capacities: advance planning, calm strategic resolve under threat, and seizing the strategic initiative. The article opens with Xi Jinping's call to "turn danger into opportunity" and presents Mao as the model for it, against a background of what it calls changes unseen in a century and rising anti-globalization.

The article is built in four sections. The first three each take one element of Mao's approach and illustrate it with episodes from the revolution and the early People's Republic: the anti-"encirclement" campaigns, the Seventh Party Congress, Third Front construction, the Khrushchev demands of 1958, Fu Zuoyi's threatened raid on Xibaipo, the response to the US blockade, the Korean War, and the campaign against schistosomiasis. The fourth section draws lessons for the present from Xi Jinping's speeches and the 20th Party Congress report (2022).

On advance preparation, the authors stress Mao's "bottom-line thinking", citing his refusal of Soviet naval proposals and the "one principle, four points" formula on Taiwan, and his claim that thorough preparation can deter an enemy. On strategic resolve, they cite his decision to delay recovering Hong Kong to keep a trade window open, the "rubber for rice" deal with Ceylon, and his insistence on despising the enemy strategically while respecting it tactically. On initiative, they say Mao held that people, not weapons, decide outcomes, and that subjective initiative must still respect objective laws. They note that the "Left" errors and the Great Leap-era setbacks came from ignoring those laws.

Chen and Zhang conclude that danger and opportunity are a unity of opposites, and that strategic initiative is the condition for turning one into the other. They call on the Party to prepare for major risks, hold firm strategic resolve and seize the initiative, citing Xi's "black swan" and "grey rhino" warnings. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars use Mao's wartime and early-PRC decisions as a template for crisis management under Xi Jinping.
quoteEn: Mao Zedong's successful way of turning crisis into opportunity profoundly reveals the basic law that the development of things is a dialectical unity of progress and twists and turns.
quoteZh: 毛泽东化危为机的成功之道深刻揭示了事物发展前进性与曲折性辩证统一的基本规律。

glossary.explanation: A phrase used in Party discourse for converting risks and setbacks into chances for advance. Xi Jinping has repeatedly urged officials to master this skill.
A way of planning that fixes the worst acceptable outcome and prepares for it, while working for the best result. It is prominent in Xi Jinping-era discourse on risk.
Holding the lead in shaping events rather than reacting to them. The authors derive it from Mao's military writings and extend it to political and economic work.
A programme from the mid-1960s that moved industry and defence facilities to China's interior to prepare for possible foreign invasion.

A summary by Zhou Enlai of Mao's instructions on Taiwan: Taiwan must be unified with China, with specified autonomy arrangements afterwards. The article treats it as a forerunner of "one country, two systems".

t: The world-historical significance of Chinese modernization
zh: 中国式现代化的世界历史意义
source: Research on Ideological Education (Sixiang jiaoyu yanjiu), 2023 no. 3
paras: Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhu Andong asks what significance Chinese modernization holds beyond the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article argues that it has major world-historical significance: it gives scientific socialism new vitality in twenty-first-century China, offers humanity a new option for achieving modernization, and offers Third World countries a theoretical and practical alternative to the Western path.

The article has three parts. It first sets out Marx's theory of world history and its two stages. It then reviews Western modernization theory and the criticisms made of it. Finally it turns to Chinese modernization, defined as socialist modernization led by the Communist Party of China. Zhu draws on Xi Jinping's remarks on the 20th Party Congress report and on Rostow's stages-of-growth model, dependency theory and world-systems theory.

Zhu reads Marx as dividing world history into a stage opened by capitalism and a transition towards a "communist" world-historical stage. Capitalism, in this account, developed the productive forces and prepared its own gravediggers. Zhu holds that no social formation exits history on its own, so the bourgeoisie presents capitalism as natural and permanent. After the Second World War the United States and other Western countries, according to Zhu, built modernization theory to keep Third World states from turning to socialism. Zhu argues that the theory erased colonial plunder and presented Western capitalism as the only route, and that neoliberal modernization later served Western, especially financial, hegemony. Zhu says dependency theory and Western left scholars such as Stiglitz and Ha-Joon Chang criticised this but did not dislodge its mainstream standing.

Zhu concludes that China's achievements and the systemic crisis of contemporary capitalism show there is no single modernization model and no universal standard. Zhu sets the five Chinese features named in the 20th Party Congress report against what the article calls Western modernization, marked by polarisation, violence and plunder. The article says China's record of rapid growth and long-term stability attracts other countries and has loosened US-led hegemonic control, making non-capitalist paths more feasible for them. Zhu holds that this moves humanity further through Marx's second stage of world history, creates a new form of human civilization and contributes to eventual communism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese Marxist scholar links Marx's world-history theory to a critique of Western modernization theory.
quoteEn: The theory of Chinese modernization not only breaks the myth that modernization equals Westernization, but also offers a more persuasive set of ideas.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化理论，不仅打破了现代化等于西方化的迷思，而且提供了一套更具有说服力的思想。

glossary.explanation: The official term for China's path of modernization under Communist Party leadership, which the 20th Party Congress (2022) summarised as having five features, including a huge population, common prosperity and peaceful development.
The term for the socialism developed by Marx and Engels, set against utopian socialism. Chinese official discourse presents Chinese modernization as its latest development.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China to national strength and prosperity, closely tied to the Chinese Dream and the 'two centenary goals'.

glossary.en: a new form of human civilization
glossary.explanation: A phrase in official discourse for the civilizational form that Chinese modernization is said to create, distinct from Western modernization.

t: Marxism and Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
zh: 马克思主义和中国化时代化的马克思主义
source: Journal of Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育导刊), 2023 no. 3
paras: Hou Huiqin takes up a question the author treats as the first-order issue for the Communist Party of China: how to understand the relationship between Marxism and Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Hou notes that doubts persist about whether Marxism is outdated, and that some tendencies pull the two apart. The article's thesis is that they form an organic unity of "one body, two sides", and that the Party must keep to two unwaverings: Marxism as guide and continued adaptation of it.

The article has three parts. The first defines the relationship through the unity of the scientific system and of the Party's guiding thought. It then sets out how the two sides interact and how their routes to knowing historical laws differ. The second part considers whether Marxism is a "foreign" culture and revisits the old debate over "substance and function" (ti–yong). The third takes up the Two Integrations, concentrating on integration with fine traditional Chinese culture.

Hou argues that Marxism supplies the general, shared theory, while its Chinese form supplies the particular, so the two cannot be separated. The founders moved from general laws to specific ones. Chinese Marxism starts from the most pressing concrete problems and moves upward to general laws. On the foreign-origin question, Hou holds that culture has a dual character, class and human, in which class character is decisive. Marxism, as the class consciousness of the working class, is a "world-historical" presence and not a foreign import. It is foreign only in two limited senses: it must be brought to a spontaneous working class from outside, and its European idiom needs localising. Hou therefore distinguishes Marxism as guiding ideology from Marxism as a cultural element. Integration with tradition must operate first at the ideological level, because tradition does not clarify or renew itself without Marxist guidance.

Hou concludes that continuing to adapt Marxism is itself the process of unifying it, and that the Two Integrations, especially with traditional culture, strengthen confidence in Chinese modernization. Hou warns against cultural revivalism, historical nihilism and any pluralism in guiding thought. The article closes by stressing that abandoning Marxism would cost the Party its soul. Read the original if you want a detailed statement of how a leading Party ideologist reads the Two Integrations and defends the unity of guiding ideology.
quoteEn: Upholding fundamental principles while innovating is the best gloss on the unity of Marxism adapted to China and our times with Marxism itself.
quoteZh: 守正创新是对中国化时代化马克思主义与马克思主义一体性的最好注解

glossary.explanation: The formula of combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The second integration was added in official discourse in recent years.
The official name for China's own path to modernization, set out by the Party at its 20th Congress (2022) as distinct from Western models.
The article's phrase for steadfastly upholding Marxism as guide while steadfastly advancing its adaptation to China and the times.

keywords: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context

t: Chinese modernization: common features and Chinese characteristics
zh: 中国式现代化：共同特征与中国特色
paras: Luo Yuting takes up a question raised by the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): how Chinese modernization can hold both the features shared by all modernizations and its own Chinese characteristics. The article argues that the two form an organic unity. A modernization with only common features, or with only Chinese characteristics, would in Luo's view not be Chinese modernization.

The article has three parts. The first defines modernization and sets out its common features. The second describes six Chinese characteristics, which Luo labels institutional, national-conditions, value, development, ecological and peace characteristics. The third discusses what the author calls China's choice, meaning how to combine the two sides in practice.

In the first part Luo defines modernization as the shift from an underdeveloped to a developed state, driven by science and technology and by socialized production. Drawing on Marx and Engels, Luo identifies four core indicators: modernized science and technology, modernized productive forces, modernized ways of life, and modernized social institutions. Chinese modernization shares these, Luo says, as the process by which China's productive forces and living standards catch up with and surpass advanced world levels. Its Chinese characteristics, following the 20th Party Congress report, are a huge population, common prosperity for all, coordinated material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. Luo adds the leadership of the Communist Party and the socialist system as institutional features. Luo treats the common features as the universal and the Chinese characteristics as the particular, and likens their combination to the dialectical link between universality and particularity in contradiction.

Luo draws three requirements from this. Production development must go together with institutional innovation, so that the socialist basic economic system is improved and polarisation under capitalist modernization is avoided. Science and technology leadership must go together with independent innovation, which Luo presents as necessary given what the article calls trade wars, tech wars and decoupling by hegemonic powers. The exploration of a path must go together with confidence in that path, and Luo contrasts it with the Western capitalist model, which the author describes as built on war, colonialism and plunder. Read the original if you want a systematic account, from a Marxist-theory scholar writing in an official-theory journal, of how Chinese modernization is placed within a general theory of modernization.
quoteEn: A modernization with only the common features of modernization and no Chinese characteristics, or with only Chinese characteristics and none of the common features of modernization, is not Chinese modernization.
quoteZh: 只有现代化的共同特征而没有中国特色，或者只有中国特色而没有现代化的共同特征，都不是中国式现代化。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's modernization path under Communist Party leadership. The 20th Party Congress report (2022) described it with five features and presented it as an alternative to Western modernization.
An official goal of prosperity shared by all people, presented as an essential requirement of socialism. It is set against polarisation between rich and poor.

t: The value and significance of Mao Zedong's speech at the opening ceremony of Yan'an University
st: With a discussion of the Chinese logic of running higher education institutions in the Yan'an period
zh: 毛泽东《在延安大学开学典礼上的讲话》的价值与意义
zhSub: 兼论延安时期高等院校办学的中国逻辑探索
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theory, 2022 no. 9
paras: Prompted by Xi Jinping's April 2022 remarks at Renmin University of China that Chinese universities should take root in Chinese soil rather than copy foreign models, Zeng Luping returns to Mao Zedong's speech at the opening of the reorganised Yan'an University in May 1944. The author argues that the speech sets out a Chinese 'logic' of running universities: institutions must first serve the Party's central tasks, national strategy and economic and social needs. In wartime conditions, this meant serving the anti-Japanese base areas.

The article has four parts. It first reviews the history of Yan'an University, from its founding in 1941 through the mergers of 1943 and 1944, and places it within the Yan'an Rectification Movement. It then analyses the speech's content, traces its roots in Mao's educational thought, and finally examines the university's practice and legacy under seven headings: educational policy, disciplines, management, curriculum, links with practical work units, research, and productive labour.

Zeng contrasts two logics. Western-influenced universities, including most pre-1949 Chinese ones, followed a 'disciplinary logic' in which scholarly output is the measure of success. The Rectification Movement, in the author's account, criticised this and established a 'social-demand logic', with 'new-type regularisation' acceptable only if consistent with adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. Zeng reads Mao's speech, with its concrete targets for self-sufficiency, literacy and public health, as a rejection of dogmatism that applies the principle of seeking truth from facts. The author stresses that this does not abolish disciplines or scholarship, but subordinates them to the Party's central tasks.

Zeng concludes that Yan'an University embodied the 'Yan'an model' of higher education and that, after 1949, its principles shaped the new China's system: Marxist guidance, education serving proletarian politics and combined with productive labour, Party committee leadership with presidential responsibility, and priority for engineering. The author holds that the 1952 reorganisation of departments fully applied the social-demand logic. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese account of Yan'an-era university history and of how Party scholarship links it to current calls for a distinctively Chinese higher education.
quoteEn: Under the special social conditions of modern Chinese history, the social-demand logic of running Chinese higher education institutions must take precedence over the disciplinary logic.
quoteZh: 在中国近现代历史的特殊社会现实条件下，中国高等院校办学的社会需求逻辑必须高于学科逻辑。

glossary.literal: Yan'an campaign to rectify work styles
glossary.explanation: A Party-wide ideological campaign launched in 1942 under Mao Zedong's leadership, directed against subjectivism, dogmatism and sectarianism and aimed at unifying the Party around Mao's line.
A principle that Mao made central to Mao Zedong Thought and that later Party leaders reaffirmed, meaning that policy should proceed from actual conditions rather than from doctrine.
The author's term for the principle that universities should first serve national strategy and economic and social needs, contrasted with a 'disciplinary logic' centred on scholarly output.
A Yan'an-era formulation for regular, systematic education that remains tied to Chinese revolutionary conditions, as opposed to copying existing university models.

The approach to higher education developed in the Communist-led base areas in the 1940s, stressing service to practical work, unity of theory and practice, and combining education with productive labour.

t: The historical contribution of the "Two Integrations" and its practical requirements
zh: “两个结合”的历史贡献及实践要求
paras: Xu Fengzhen asks what the formula of integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture, the Two Integrations, contributes to the theory of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article treats it as an original theoretical creation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Xu argues that it unites content and method, and epistemology and practice, and that it opens a new stage in the adaptation of Marxism.

The article is organised around five angles: concept, theory, history, cognition and practice. It first traces the discourse on adapting Marxism from Li Dazhao, Chen Weishi, Zhang Wentian and Ai Siqi to Mao Zedong and the post-1949 formulations. It then examines how Marxism came to be chosen in China, the stages of integration from the New Democratic Revolution to the new era, and two mistaken ways of thinking. It ends with methodological requirements.

Xu's core claims are that the Two Integrations reorganises earlier wording into a unified framework. "Marxism" replaces "Marxism-Leninism", "China's specific realities" absorbs earlier stage-specific formulas, and fine traditional culture is placed alongside those realities. Xu describes the structure as "one body, three wings" (theory, practice, culture) and "one root, two foundations". Xu explains the affinity between Marxism and the Communist Party through five points: people-centred stance, human emancipation, revolutionary character, the highest programme of communism, and practicality. Xu also points to correspondences between Marxism and Chinese traditional thought. Xi's rejection of the "template" and "master copy" views serves as the corrective to dogmatism and cultural nihilism. Xu contrasts the periods before and after the Zunyi Conference as positive and negative lessons.

In practice, Xu calls for close study of Marx's original texts, for strengthening both the Marxist "root" and the two Chinese "foundations", and for pursuing creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture. Xu proposes extending adaptation to parts of Marxism beyond philosophy, such as Marx's thinking on modernization, party building and the united front. The author also proposes moving from one-to-one mutual adaptation to a one-to-two form, with the three elements reinforcing one another. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese academic account of how the Two Integrations is theoretically framed and what research agenda it sets for studies of the adaptation of Marxism.
quoteEn: The process of the "Two Integrations" is the process by which the "original version" of Marxism is creatively transformed into a localised "Chinese version".
quoteZh: “两个结合” 的过程，就是马克思主义的 “原生版” 被创造性地转化为本土化的 “中国版” 的过程。

glossary.explanation: The formula of integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The second integration, with traditional culture, was added to Party doctrine under Xi Jinping.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official description of the Party's ongoing project of fitting Marxism to Chinese conditions and to the present era.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into its constitution in 2017 and the state constitution in 2018.
The official term for the parts of China's cultural heritage regarded as worth inheriting, as distinct from elements judged outdated.

glossary.zh: 创造性转化、创新性发展
glossary.explanation: A formula associated with Xi Jinping for treating traditional culture: adapting it to contemporary needs and developing it in new directions.

t: Marx's view of the modern and the theoretical foundations of the new path of Chinese modernization
zh: 马克思的现代观与中国式现代化新道路的学理基础
paras: Marx never defined "the modern" in one place, and the authors argue that existing scholarship has treated only fragments of his scattered remarks. Zhuang and Gu set out to reconstruct Marx's view of the modern as a systematic whole. They contend that this view supplies the fundamental theoretical basis for the new path of Chinese modernization.

The article has four parts. It first sets out Marx's methodological principles, then the main dimensions through which he presents the content of the modern. It next examines his understanding of the modern as a historical process, and finally draws out implications for Chinese modernization. Marx's own texts, including the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, the Manifesto and Capital, are the main evidence.

In the authors' reading, Marx understands the modern first as a transformation in how people exist, from dependence on persons to independence resting on dependence on things. He compares classical and modern society along four dimensions: handwork giving way to machine production, widening exchange that makes history world history, natural economy giving way to commodity economy (with labour-power sold as a commodity), and the reversal of town–country relations. The authors then argue that Marx treats the arrival of modernity as lawlike and unavoidable, as both progressive and historically narrow, and as uneven across countries. Late-developing countries may enjoy advantages, and Marx's remark that a society can shorten and lessen the birth-pangs implies several possible routes into modernity.

From this the authors conclude that modernization is essentially a transformation of human existence, with one goal but many possible paths. Because historical conditions have changed, they argue, China cannot repeat the Western European route, which relied on internal dispossession and external plunder. They hold that the uneven course of modernity makes a new path both possible and necessary. They describe Chinese modernization as socialist modernization, which must complete tasks that capitalism completed in the West while serving the people as a whole. In their account it is the direct theoretical result of socialism with Chinese characteristics and points towards a new form of civilization. Read the original if you want a close, text-based account of how Chinese Marxist scholars derive a theory of modernization from Marx's writings.
quoteEn: The goal of modernization is singular in nature, namely a fundamental transformation of the human condition, while the specific paths and means of achieving it are plural.
quoteZh: 现代化发展的目标指向，在性质上是单一的，即实现人的生存状态的根本变革，而实现这种变革的具体路径和方式是多元的。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's account of China's own path to modernity, set out in Party documents especially since 2021–22. It is presented as distinct from Western models.

The official designation for China's system and theory since the reform era. The article reads it both as socialism with national features and as a socialism marked by a particular stage of development.

t: Theoretical features and historical evolution of the contemporary adaptation of Marxism to the needs of our times
st: On Marxism's "timeliness" (shidaihua) from scientific socialism to Xi Jinping Thought
zh: 马克思主义时代化的理论特征和历史演进
paras: He Haigen and Sun Daiyao examine what it means to "adapt Marxism to the needs of our times" (Marxism's shidaihua) and trace how this has unfolded historically. Taking up the 20th Party Congress (2022) call to keep writing new chapters of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, they argue that shidaihua is an internal requirement of Marxist development. In their account it means combining Marxism with the features of an era so that it answers the questions that era poses.

The article first sets out a conceptual framework. It distinguishes the "big era", defined by a social formation such as capitalism and lasting centuries, from "small eras" defined by shifting themes, principal contradictions and technological change. It then divides the history of Marxism into three stages tied to the three scientific and technological revolutions: the birth of scientific socialism, the "Russian stage" of Leninism, and the "Chinese stage". It closes with four features of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.

The authors argue that shidaihua requires a real need and objective conditions, and that it must not depart from the direction of the big era, the transition from capitalism to socialism, or it would degenerate. In their reading, the first technological revolution gave socialism a material basis, moving it from utopia to science. The second, with the shift to monopoly capitalism, produced Lenin's analysis of imperialism and Russia as a weak link; the authors cite figures on foreign capital in Russia. The third, they say, changed the class structure in the West and exhausted the Soviet model, which they illustrate with East–West German comparisons. They contend that Deng Xiaoping's reassessment of the era as one of "peace and development" opened the Chinese stage.

For the present, the authors identify four features of Xi Jinping Thought. It grasps what has changed and what has not in the era: peace and development remain the theme, while the world faces changes unseen in a century and a new technological revolution. It treats nationalisation and timeliness as an inseparable "two-in-one". It keeps answering the basic questions of socialism within the big era. It responds to the "question of the world" through a community with a shared future for mankind and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-school account of how Chinese theorists periodise Marxism's development and link it to technological revolutions.
quoteEn: The nationalisation and the timeliness of Marxism are an inseparable "two-in-one", and timeliness is the precondition for nationalisation.
quoteZh: 马克思主义的民族化和时代化是不可分割的“二元一体”，时代化是民族化的前提条件
keywords: adaptation of Marxism to the times

t: Upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
zh: 守正创新推进马克思主义中国化时代化
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2023, Deng Chundong takes up one of the "six musts" set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): the requirement to uphold fundamental principles and break new ground. Deng argues that this pairing is the key to enriching Marxism and to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The two sides are held to be dialectically united and inseparable.

The article has three parts. The first draws on the history of world socialism and of the Communist Party of China to show why the pairing matters. The second sets out what upholding fundamental principles requires, namely the \"three unwaverings\". The third explains how innovation should proceed, in four directions: following objective laws, starting from China's realities, answering the questions of the era, and guiding new practice with the Party's innovative theory.

Deng contends that abandoning fundamental principles betrays Marxism and leads socialism to setbacks, while dogmatism leaves socialism stagnant. The three unwaverings are: the basic tenets of Marxism, the Party's overall leadership, and socialism with Chinese characteristics. Deng insists that rigid adherence to old formulas or past mistakes is not real upholding of principles. Equally, policies that depart from the Marxist standpoint or from the basic socialist system, or that copy the governance models of Western capitalist countries, are not real innovation. Innovation, in this reading, means respecting objective laws, combining Marxism with China's circumstances and with fine traditional Chinese culture, studying contemporary capitalism and Marxism outside China selectively, and developing the theory of Chinese modernization.

Deng concludes that the strength of the Party and of socialism with Chinese characteristics ultimately rests on Marxism, in its Chinese and contemporary form. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented as the Marxism of contemporary China and of the twenty-first century. Deng calls for arming the whole Party with it and for opening new horizons through the Two Integrations. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party theorists in 2023 explained the relationship between orthodoxy and innovation in the Party's theoretical work.
quoteEn: In essence, both upholding fundamental principles and innovation are a steadfast adherence to Marxism, which reveals objective laws, and through innovation new laws are continually revealed.
quoteZh: 守正与创新，本质上都是对揭示客观规律的马克思主义的坚守，并通过创新不断揭示新的规律。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: Official formula for the Party's project of applying Marxism to Chinese conditions and updating it for the present era. The "times" element was added to the older "Sinification of Marxism" in recent Party documents.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's current official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.
The formula of combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture.
The Party's official concept of a distinctive path to modernization, set out prominently in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022).
The official name for China's socialist path and system since the reform era, associated with Deng Xiaoping.

keywords: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context
upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground

t: Opening up a new realm of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
zh: 开辟马克思主义中国化时代化新境界
paras: He Xinyuan asks how Marxism can keep guiding practice in individual countries, and answers that it must be localised and adapted to its era. The article argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era achieved a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. In He's account, it thereby opened up a new realm of that process.

The article has three parts. The first presents localisation and timeliness as a general law of the world socialist movement, citing Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and Kim Il Sung–Kim Jong Il-ism and Ho Chi Minh Thought in Korea and Vietnam. The second examines the Two Integrations. The third sets out the basic guidelines for continuing the work on the new journey, drawing on the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022).

He contends that the Two Integrations are a law-like understanding of the process. These are combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The first, in He's reading, is the Party's most valuable experience, and dogmatism and bookishness caused earlier setbacks. The second is described as a distinctive feature, resting on a claimed high degree of fit between scientific socialism's values and traditional Chinese culture. He holds that the Two Integrations are specific to China yet also universal, offering a basic guide for working-class parties elsewhere. For the new journey, He lists six principles: putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, staying true to fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, systems thinking, and a global vision. These rest on dialectical and historical materialism.

He concludes that theoretical innovation has no end and that the Party must keep adapting Marxism through the Two Integrations and these principles. He claims that the Two Integrations will also open broad prospects for Marxism's localisation in other countries. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars present the Two Integrations and the guidelines for adapting Marxism after the 20th Party Congress.
quoteEn: The Two Integrations also reflect universality, and can provide a basic guide for the working-class parties of other countries in upholding and applying Marxism.
quoteZh: “两个结合”也体现出普遍性，能为其他国家的工人阶级政党坚持和运用马克思主义提供基本遵循。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for the Party's ongoing effort to fit Marxism to Chinese conditions and to each era. It is presented as the source of the Party's successive theoretical systems.

Xi Jinping's formula, first stated in 2021, for combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. It was written into the Party's 2021 historical resolution.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology since 2017, written into the Party and state constitutions. It is presented as the latest stage of the adaptation of Marxism in China.
Hu Jintao-era guiding concept that stresses people-centred, comprehensive and sustainable development. It is part of the theoretical lineage the article lists.
Jiang Zemin-era theory holding that the Party represents advanced productive forces, advanced culture and the fundamental interests of the people.

t: Three "coats" of historical nihilism
zh: 历史虚无主义的三件“外套”
paras: Zhao Guanghui, in a short commentary, asks how historical nihilism has changed form now that it is under pressure. The author argues that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), its spread has been checked, so it has become more concealed and has put on new "coats". These are "secret history", "art" and "scholarship". Each coat makes its claims more persuasive.

The piece takes the three coats in turn. It opens with Xi Jinping's call, at the Party history study and education mobilisation meeting, to oppose historical nihilism openly and to clarify vague understandings of major issues in Party history. It then gives a short section to each coat and closes with a general assessment of the shift in method.

Zhao argues that "secret history" exploits the public appetite for hidden political and personal details. In the author's account, it turns policy disputes among Party leaders into power struggles and invites readers to take fiction as reliable history. Under the "art" coat, the author says, artistic form is used to carry ideological content, through "playful retellings", the mocking of the sublime and a calligraphy example that builds a "upright" image of Chiang Kai-shek. The "scholarship" coat, Zhao claims, uses academic reflection and selective sources to dismantle historical materialism, the theory of five social formations and class analysis, and to undermine the historical basis of Party leadership.

Zhao concludes that historical nihilism has moved from crude defamation of heroes to forging history by treating a detail as the whole, detached from its context. The author calls on readers to use their judgement so as to see the mainstream, the essence and the general trend. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese official scholarship classifies and rebuts the forms of historical nihilism.
quoteEn: Treating "historical details" apart from their historical context, or magnifying them into the "historical whole", in fact reconstructs or even forges history.
quoteZh: 但将“历史细节”脱离历史语境对待，或将之放大为“历史整体”，其实是重构甚至伪造了历史。

glossary.explanation: In official Chinese usage, a label for views seen as denying or belittling the Party's history, revolutionary figures and the socialist path. Party leaders have called for opposing it, especially since the 2010s.
A nationwide campaign launched in 2021, around the Party's centenary, to study the history of the Communist Party of China.
The Marxist theory that material production and social relations drive historical development.
The schema of primitive, slave, feudal, capitalist and socialist or communist society, a standard framework in Chinese Marxist historiography.

t: On the methodological innovation of the Two Integrations in advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
zh: 论“两个结合”对推动马克思主义中国化时代化的方法论创新
paras: Li Hongwei takes up the Two Integrations, first announced by Xi Jinping at the Party's centenary in 2021 and set out systematically in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). The article argues that existing scholarship has mostly traced their history, content, results and experience, and that their epistemological and methodological contribution has been little examined. Li's thesis is that the Two Integrations are both a worldview and a methodology, and that they carry out methodological innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times.

The article is organised around four classic disputes that the Two Integrations are said to resolve: space and time (differences between cultures), substance and function (ti and yong), knowing and doing, and things and people. Each section pairs a conceptual problem with a method. Li draws on Chinese philosophical categories, Mao Zedong's, Deng Xiaoping's and Xi Jinping's statements, and passages from Marx, and traces the move from the earlier single "integration" with Chinese reality to the present two-part formula.

First, Li holds that integration works by seeking common ground while preserving differences. Marxism and fine traditional Chinese culture, though of different origin, are said to share features such as an orientation to practice, an ideal of great harmony, and a belief that the people make history. Integration is described as a chemical-like reaction, not simple addition, and as guarded against both dogmatism and cultural nihilism. Second, on substance and function, Li reads the Two Integrations as giving Marxism's basic principles the leading role, with Chinese reality as the site of theoretical and practical innovation and fine traditional culture as a source of spirit and wisdom. This is presented as an answer to the late-Qing formula "Chinese learning for substance, Western learning for application" and as an expression of cultural confidence. Third, Li argues that integration must be carried out in practice. Theorists and Party cadres are named as its key agents, and formalism and detached theorising are criticised.

Li adds that the Two Integrations must serve the people. In content they should be close to the people, and in form they should be welcome to them, meaning plain language and a Chinese style. Li links this to Chinese modernization, to a community with a shared future for mankind, and to a "new form of human civilization". The article concludes that the Two Integrations have underpinned the Party's achievements over a century and remain necessary for high-quality development, common prosperity and building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how Chinese theorists frame the Two Integrations as a methodology, with its sources in Chinese philosophy and Party texts.
quoteEn: The Two Integrations are both a worldview and a methodology.
quoteZh: “两个结合”既是世界观，又是方法论。

glossary.explanation: The formula of combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Xi Jinping first stated it in this form in 2021 and elaborated it at the 20th Party Congress in 2022.

A pair of categories from Chinese philosophy, used since the late Qing in debates on Chinese versus Western learning. The formula "Chinese learning for substance, Western learning for application" made Confucian values the core and Western technology the tool.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official name for the project of fitting Marxism to China's conditions and to the present era. It is the stated aim of the Party's theoretical work.
The Party's official term for China's own path to modernity, set out at the 20th Party Congress in 2022.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and theoretical concept promoted by Xi Jinping since the early 2010s. It calls for shared global governance and cooperation among states.
An official economic goal stressing quality, innovation and efficiency over growth rates alone.
An official goal of broadly shared prosperity, emphasised in Party policy under Xi Jinping.

t: Innovations in major-country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics in the new era, seen from a historical perspective
zh: 从历史发展的视角看新时代中国特色大国外交的创新
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (Dangdai shijie yu shehui zhuyi), 2023 no. 1
